EXPOSÉ XVIII
THE GLOBAL DUALITY FORMULAby P. Deligne
0. Introduction

0.1. The present exposé is devoted to Poincaré duality. This duality is built on the model of VERDIER [1], who treats the case of locally compact separated topological spaces. We show a priori that the functor \(Rf_!\) of Exposé XVII admits a right adjoint \(Rf^!\), and we establish a good number of its properties before computing it more explicitly in the case of smooth morphisms.
The possibility of such a construction seems to rest on the following properties of the functor \(Rf_!\)
a) For the existence of an adjoint \(Rf^!\) and its formal properties:

1. (I) the functor \(Rf_!\) commutes with base change;
  2. (II) the functors \(R^i f_!\) commute with filtered inductive limits; they are zero for \(i\) large enough;
  3. (III) the functor \(Rf_!\) can be computed "at the level of complexes", i.e. from a functor between categories of complexes.
b) For the computation of this adjoint in the case where \(f\) is smooth:
1. (IV) the computation of \(Rf_!((\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})_U)\) for \(U\) "small".

0.2. In § 3, n° 1, which is independent of §§ 1, 2, we construct the functor \(Rf^!\); here we use constructions special to the situation, and not only (I), (II) and (III). This makes this n° rather unpleasant; the author confesses that he did not always fully understand what was going on.
§ 2 is devoted to point (IV); it is purely formal starting from § 1, where the cohomology of curves is studied.

In § 1, we establish considerably more than is necessary for § 2, by also studying the case of continuous coefficients. This section was deeply influenced by SERRE [1]. The points useful for the sequel are:
a) n° 1.1, devoted to the trace morphism in the case of curves, and generalized in 2.9;

b) the effacement theorem 1.6.9. The reader willing to accept a transcendental argument may read n° 1.6, from 1.6.6 (2nd proof) onward, independently of n°s 1.2 to 1.5. The essential ingredient of 1.6.9 is one or another form of Poincaré duality for smooth curves over an algebraically closed field, together with the acyclicity lemma XV 2.6 (preliminary to the smooth base change theorem XVI 1.1). Its conclusion is generalized in 2.17.
n° 3.2 gathers the fruits of § 2.

0.3. Verdier's method in Poincaré duality allows one to define the functor \(Rf^!\) for \(f\) compactifiable. The counterpart of this generality is that the compatibilities to be checked are unfamiliar, and sometimes, even for the most trivial ones such as 3.2.3, have outlandish proofs. The author admits not having proved as many of them as he should have.

The interested reader will be able, without difficulty, starting from the appendix to Exposé XVII, to extend the definition of \(Rf^!\) to the case of separated morphisms of finite type with target a coherent scheme (i.e. quasi-compact quasi-separated).

0.4. The main result 3.2.5 is stated in concrete terms which would allow one to return formally to the point of view that was that of the oral seminar, where the functor \(Rf^!\) was defined only for morphisms admitting a factorization through a smooth morphism and an immersion. A sketch of the proof from the oral seminar will be found in VERDIER [2].
1. Cohomology of curves.
1.1. The trace morphism.

1.1.1. Let \(n\) be an integer \(\geqslant 1\) and \(X\) a scheme on which \(n\) is invertible. The sheaf \(\mu_n\) (IX 3.1) on \(X\) is then a locally free sheaf of modules of rank 1 over the constant sheaf of rings \(\mathbb{Z}/n\). For \(i \in \mathbb{Z}\), we denote by the notation \(\mathbb{Z}/n\,(i)\) its \(i\)th tensor power.
\[(1.1.1.1)\qquad \mathbb{Z}/n\,(i) = \underline{\operatorname{Hom}}(\mathbb{Z}/n, \mathbb{G}_m)^{\otimes i} \;.\]
If \(n = dn'\), the exponentiation map by \(d\) establishes an isomorphism
\[\mu_n \otimes_{\mathbb{Z}/n} \mathbb{Z}/n' \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \mu_{n'} \;,\]
whence isomorphisms, called canonical:
\[(1.1.1.2)\qquad \mathbb{Z}/n\,(i) \otimes_{\mathbb{Z}/n} \mathbb{Z}/n' \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \mathbb{Z}/n'\,(i) \;.\]
If \(F\) is an abelian sheaf such that \(nF = 0\), we set
\[(1.1.1.3)\qquad F(i) = F \otimes_{\mathbb{Z}/n} \mathbb{Z}/n\,(i) \;.\]

If already \(n'F = 0\), the isomorphism (1.1.1.2) allows one to identify \(F \otimes_{\mathbb{Z}/n} \mathbb{Z}/n\,(i)\) and \(F \otimes_{\mathbb{Z}/n'} \mathbb{Z}/n'\,(i)\), so that \(F(i)\) depends only on \(F\) and not on the choice of \(n\). More generally, if \(F\) is a torsion sheaf prime to the residue characteristics of \(X\) (XVII 0.13), and if \({}_m F\) is the kernel of multiplication by \(m\) in \(F\), we define \(F(i)\) as the inductive limit, for \(m\) invertible on \(X\) tending multiplicatively to infinity
\[(1.1.1.4)\qquad F(i) = \varinjlim_m {}_m F(i) \;.\]

The functor \(F \mapsto F(i)\) is exact. If \(f : Y \to X\) is a morphism of schemes (resp. a quasi-compact quasi-separated morphism of schemes), and if \(F\) is a torsion sheaf on \(X\) (resp. on \(Y\)), prime to the residue characteristics of \(X\), then \(f^*(F(i)) \simeq (f^*F)(i)\) (resp. \((f_*F)(i) \simeq f_*(F(i))\)). If \(\mathcal{A}\) is a sheaf of rings on \(X\), annihilated by \(n\) invertible on \(X\), it extends to an exact functor \(K \mapsto K(i)\) from \(D(X,\mathcal{A})\) to \(D(X,\mathcal{A})\). This functor commutes with the inverse image functors and the direct image functors.
The functors \(F \mapsto F(i)\) are sometimes called the functors of "Tate twist".

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 1.1.2

A flat curve over a scheme \(S\) is a morphism \(f : X \to S\) that is flat, of finite presentation, and separated, with fibres purely of dimension one.
The expression "purely of dimension one" does not exclude the empty scheme. Contrary to EGA II 7.4.2, we allow here a curve over a field to be empty, but we require it to be separated.
When \(S\) is the spectrum of a field, we shall speak simply of a curve over \(S\); a curve over a field is quasi-projective.

1.1.3. Let \(X\) be a curve over an algebraically closed field \(k\) of characteristic exponent \(p\) prime to an integer \(n \geqslant 1\). Suppose first that \(X\) is reduced, and let \(\overline{X}\) be a complete curve over \(k\) of which \(X\) is a dense open. The complement \(Y = \overline{X} - X\) is of dimension 0. The exact cohomology sequence (XVII 5.1.16.3) therefore induces an isomorphism
\[(1.1.3.1)\qquad H^2_c(X, \mathbb{Z}/n(1)) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } H^2_c(\overline{X}, \mathbb{Z}/n(1)) \;.\]
We have moreover an isomorphism IX 4.7 (given by Kummer theory)
\[(1.1.3.2)\qquad H^2_c(\overline{X}, \mathbb{Z}/n(1)) \simeq \operatorname{Pic}(\overline{X})/n \simeq (\mathbb{Z}/n)^c\]
where \(c\) denotes the set of irreducible components of \(X\), or of \(\overline{X}\), which amounts to the same thing.

If \(X\) is no longer necessarily reduced, and if \(c\) is the set of its irreducible components, we denote, for \(i \in c\), by \(n_i\) the multiplicity of \(X\) at the generic point \(\eta_i\) of the \(i\)th irreducible component of \(X\):
\[n_i = \operatorname{lg}(\mathcal{O}_{X,\eta_i}) \;.\]

It is known that the restriction map from \(H^2_c(X, \mathbb{Z}/n(1))\) to \(H^2_c(X_{\mathrm{red}}, \mathbb{Z}/n(1))\) is an isomorphism, whence, via (1.1.3.1) and (1.1.3.2) applied to \(X_{\mathrm{red}}\), a canonical isomorphism between \(H^2_c(X, \mathbb{Z}/n(1))\) and \((\mathbb{Z}/n)^c\). We denote by \(\mathrm{Tr}_X\) or simply \(\mathrm{Tr}\) the composite arrow
\[(1.1.3.3)\qquad \mathrm{Tr} : H^2_c(X, \mathbb{Z}/n(1)) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } (\mathbb{Z}/n)^c \xrightarrow{\ t\ } \mathbb{Z}/n \;,\]
where
If \(F\) is an abelian group annihilated by \(n\), we have an isomorphism
\[H^2_c(X, F(1)) \xleftarrow{\ \sim\ } F \otimes H^2_c(X, \mathbb{Z}/n(1))\]
and hence, via (1.1.3.3), a trace morphism
If \(n = n'd\), the diagram

\[(1.1.3.5)\qquad \xymatrix{ 0 \ar[r] & \mu_n \ar[r] \ar[d]^{x^d} & \mathbb{G}_m \ar[r]^{x^n} \ar[d]^{x^d} & \mathbb{G}_m \ar[r] \ar@{=}[d] & 0 \\ 0 \ar[r] & \mu_{n'} \ar[r] & \mathbb{G}_m \ar[r]_{x^{n'}} & \mathbb{G}_m \ar[r] & 0 }\]
is commutative, and therefore so is the diagram
\[(1.1.3.6)\qquad \xymatrix{ H^2_c(X, \mathbb{Z}/n(1)) \ar[r]^-{\sim} \ar[d] & (\mathbb{Z}/n)^c \ar[d] \\ H^2_c(X, \mathbb{Z}/n'(1)) \ar[r]_-{\sim} & (\mathbb{Z}/n')^c }\]
by the definition IX 4.7 of the isomorphism (1.1.3.2).

The arrow (1.1.3.4) thus depends only on \(F\), and not on the choice of the integer \(n\) prime to \(p\) such that \(nF = 0\). By passage to the limit, we define it for every torsion abelian group \(F\) prime to \(p\).
The following lemma follows immediately from the definitions.

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 1.1.4

Under the preceding hypotheses, if, for \(i \in c\), \(U_i\) is a non-empty open of \(X\) contained in the \(i\)th irreducible component, the diagram

\[\xymatrix@R=2.2em@C=0.6em{ \bigoplus_{i \in c} H^2_c(U_i, F(1)) \ar[rr]^-{\sim} \ar[dr]_{\bigoplus \mathrm{Tr}_{U_i}} & & H^2_c(X, F(1)) \ar[dl]^{\mathrm{Tr}_X} \\ & F & }\]

is commutative.

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 1.1.5

Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be two curves over an algebraically closed field \(k\), \(u : X \to Y\) a quasi-finite and flat morphism, and \(n\) an integer prime to the characteristic exponent \(p\) of \(k\). The following diagram, in which \(\mathrm{Tr}_u\) is the arrow (XVII 6.2.3), is then commutative

\[\xymatrix@R=2.2em@C=0.6em{ H^2_c(X, \mathbb{Z}/n(1)) \ar[rr]^-{\mathrm{Tr}_u} \ar[dr]_{\mathrm{Tr}_X} & & H^2_c(Y, \mathbb{Z}/n(1)) \ar[dl]^{\mathrm{Tr}_Y} \\ & \mathbb{Z}/n & }\]

Lemma 1.1.4 allows one to reduce to the case where \(X\) and \(Y\) are irreducible, with \(X_{\mathrm{red}}\) and \(Y_{\mathrm{red}}\) moreover smooth. If \(e\) (resp. \(f\)) is the multiplicity of \(X\) (resp. \(Y\)) at the generic point, and if \(e = df\), the triangles marked \(+\) in the following diagram are commutative:

\[\xymatrix@R=2.2em@C=0.5em{ H^2_c(X, \mathbb{Z}/n(1)) \ar[rr]^-{\sim} \ar[dd]_{\mathrm{Tr}_u} \ar[dr]^-{\mathrm{Tr}_X} & & H^2_c(X_{\mathrm{red}}, \mathbb{Z}/n(1)) \ar[dd]^{d.\mathrm{Tr}_{u_{\mathrm{red}}}} \ar[dl]_-{e.\mathrm{Tr}_{X_{\mathrm{red}}}} \\ & \mathbb{Z}/n & \\ H^2_c(Y, \mathbb{Z}/n(1)) \ar[rr]_-{\sim} \ar[ur]_-{\mathrm{Tr}_Y} & & H^2_c(Y_{\mathrm{red}}, \mathbb{Z}/n(1)) \ar[ul]^-{f.\mathrm{Tr}_{Y_{\mathrm{red}}}} }\]
Its outline is commutative, as is deduced from the commutativity of the diagram

\[\xymatrix{ u_! \mathbb{Z}/n_X(1) \ar[r]^-{\sim} \ar[d]_{\mathrm{Tr}_u} & u_{\mathrm{red}!}\, \mathbb{Z}/n_{X_{\mathrm{red}}}(1) \ar[d]^{d.\mathrm{Tr}_{u_{\mathrm{red}}}} \\ \mathbb{Z}/n_Y(1) \ar[r]_-{\sim} & \mathbb{Z}/n_{Y_{\mathrm{red}}}(1) }\]
It suffices to check this last compatibility at the generic point of \(Y\), which is trivial.

Let \(\overline{X}\) and \(\overline{Y}\) be the complete non-singular curves containing \(X_{\mathrm{red}}\) and \(Y_{\mathrm{red}}\) as dense opens (EGA II 7.4.11). The morphism \(u_{\mathrm{red}}\) extends to a flat morphism \(\overline{u} : \overline{X} \to \overline{Y}\) (EGA II 7.4.9) and, by 1.1.4, it suffices to check 1.1.5 for \(\overline{u}\).
By (XVII 6.3.18.2), the diagram of sheaves on \(Y\), in which \(N\) denotes the norm,

\[\xymatrix{ 0 \ar[r] & \overline{u}_*\mu_n \ar[r] \ar[d]_{\mathrm{Tr}_u} & \overline{u}_*\mathbb{G}_m \ar[r]^{x^n} \ar[d]^N & \overline{u}_*\mathbb{G}_m \ar[r] \ar[d]^N & 0 \\ 0 \ar[r] & \mu_n \ar[r] & \mathbb{G}_m \ar[r]_{x^n} & \mathbb{G}_m \ar[r] & 0 }\]
is commutative, and therefore so is the diagram
\[\xymatrix{ \operatorname{Pic}(X)/n \ar[r]^-{\sim} \ar[d]_N & H^2_c(X, \mathbb{Z}/n(1)) \ar[d]^{\mathrm{Tr}_u} \\ \operatorname{Pic}(Y)/n \ar[r]_-{\sim} & H^2_c(Y, \mathbb{Z}/n(1)) }\]

and it remains to note that if \(\mathcal{L}\) is an invertible sheaf of degree 1 on \(X\), its norm is again of degree 1 (this fact resulting from the compatibility EGA IV 21.10.7, taking into account the definition EGA IV 21.5.5 of the norm of a divisor).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 1.1.6

It is possible in one and only one way to define, for every compactifiable flat curve \(f : X \to S\) and every torsion sheaf \(F\) on \(S\), prime to the residue characteristics of \(S\), a trace morphism

\[\mathrm{Tr}_f : R^2 f_!(f^*F(1)) \to F \;,\]

functorial in \(F\), of formation compatible with every base change (cf. XVII 6.2.3, (VAR 2)) and which, for \(S\) the spectrum of an algebraically closed field, coincides with the trace morphism (1.1.3.4).
The trace morphism \(\mathrm{Tr}_f\) is given to us fibre by fibre; its uniqueness is therefore clear.

Let \(p : \mathbb{P}^1_S \to S\) be the projective line over \(S\) and \(n\) an integer invertible on \(S\). We have \(\operatorname{Pic}_S(\mathbb{P}^1_S) = \mathbb{Z}_S\), whence by Kummer theory (IX 3.2) a morphism \(\mathbb{Z}/n \to R^2 p_* \mathbb{Z}/n(1)\), which one checks fibre by fibre (XII 5.2) to be an isomorphism. Its inverse \(\mathrm{Tr}_p\) induces fibre by fibre the trace morphism (1.1.3.4).

Let \(f : X \to S\) be a flat curve over \(S\) such that there exists a quasi-finite and flat \(S\)-morphism \(u\) from \(X\) to \(\mathbb{P}^1_S\). By virtue of 1.1.5, the composite morphism \(\mathrm{Tr}_p \circ \mathrm{Tr}_u\) (XVII 6.2.3) has as its fibre at any geometric point of \(S\) the trace morphism (1.1.3.4). In particular, it does not depend on the choice of \(u\).

Suppose that \(X\) is a union of open subschemes \(U_i\) such that there exists a quasi-finite and flat morphism from \(U_i\) to \(\mathbb{P}^1_S\). If \(\alpha_i\) (resp. \(\alpha_{ij}\)) is the inclusion of \(U_i\) (resp. \(U_{ij} = U_i \cap U_j\)) into \(X\), the sequence
\[\sum R^2(f\alpha_{ij})_! \, \mathbb{Z}/n(1) \rightrightarrows \sum R^2(f\alpha_i)_! \, \mathbb{Z}/n(1) \to R^2 f_! \, \mathbb{Z}/n(1) \to 0 \;.\]

is exact, by (XVII 6.2.8) and the right exactness of \(R^2 f_!\) (since \(R^3 f_! = 0\)). One checks fibre by fibre, by 1.1.5, that the sum of the trace morphisms \(\sum_i R^2(f\alpha_i)_! \, \mathbb{Z}/n(1) \to \mathbb{Z}/n\) factors through a trace morphism \(\mathrm{Tr}_f\) from \(R^2 f_! \, \mathbb{Z}/n(1)\) to \(\mathbb{Z}/n\) which, fibre by fibre, induces (1.1.3.4).

For a general \(X\), let \(j : X' \to X\) be the largest open of \(X\) such that \(f|X'\) is a Cohen-Macaulay morphism (cf. EGA IV 12.1.1 (vi)). Every point \(x\) of \(X'\) has a neighbourhood \(U_x\) in \(X'\) such that there exists a quasi-finite \(S\)-morphism \(u_x\) from \(U_x\) to \(\mathbb{P}^1_S\). This morphism is automatically flat (EGA IV 11.3.10 and 15.4.2) and \(X'\) therefore satisfies the preceding hypotheses. Moreover, \(X'\) is dense fibre by fibre in \(X\); the morphism from \(R^2(fj)_! \, \mathbb{Z}/n(1)\) to \(R^2 f_! \, \mathbb{Z}/n(1)\) is therefore an isomorphism, as one sees fibre by fibre, and the composite arrow
\[\mathrm{Tr}_f : R^2 f_! \, \mathbb{Z}/n(1) \xleftarrow{\ \sim\ } R^2(fj)_! \, \mathbb{Z}/n(1) \xrightarrow{\ \mathrm{Tr}_{fj}\ } \mathbb{Z}/n\]
induces fibre by fibre (1.1.3.4).
If \(F\) satisfies \(nF = 0\), we have (XVII 5.2.6)
\[(1.1.6.1)\qquad R^2 f_! \, \mathbb{Z}/n(1) \otimes F \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } R^2 f_!(f^*F(1))\]
and we define \(\mathrm{Tr}_f\) as the composite arrow
\[\mathrm{Tr}_f : R^2 f_!(f^*F(1)) \xleftarrow{\ \sim\ } R^2 f_! \, \mathbb{Z}/n(1) \otimes F \to F \;.\]

In the general case, we define \(\mathrm{Tr}_f\) as the inductive limit of the trace morphisms relative to the sheaves \(F_n\) for \(n\) invertible on \(S\). These arrows induce fibre by fibre (1.1.3.4) and therefore commute with every base change, q.e.d.
One checks fibre by fibre, with the help of 1.1.4, 1.1.5 and (1.1.6.1), the following results:

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 1.1.7

Let \(f : Y \to S\) be a compactifiable flat curve over \(S\), \(u : X \to Y\) a quasi-finite flat morphism of finite presentation, and \(F\) a torsion sheaf on \(S\), with torsion prime to the residue characteristics of \(S\). The following diagram is commutative:

\[\xymatrix@C=3em{ R^2(fu)_!(fu)^*F(1) = R^2 f_!(u_! u^*)f^*F(1) \ar[r]^-{\mathrm{Tr}_u} \ar[d]_{\mathrm{Tr}_{fu}} & R^2 f_! f^* F(1) \ar[d]^{\mathrm{Tr}_f} \\ F \ar@{=}[r] & F }\]

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 1.1.8

Let \(u : Y \to S\) be a quasi-finite flat morphism of finite presentation, \(f : X \to Y\) an \(S\)-compactifiable flat curve (XVII 3.2.1), and \(F\) as in 1.1.7. The following diagram is commutative:

\[\xymatrix@C=3em{ R^2(uf)_!(uf)^*F(1) = u_! R^2 f_! f^* u^* F(1) \ar[r]^-{\mathrm{Tr}_f} \ar[d]_{\mathrm{Tr}_{uf}} & u_! u^* F \ar[d]^{\mathrm{Tr}_u} \\ F \ar@{=}[r] & F }\]
One checks similarly, starting from (1.1.3.2):

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 1.1.9

If \(f : X \to S\) is a compactifiable smooth curve, and if the geometric fibres of \(f\) are irreducible, then the trace morphism (1.1.6) is an isomorphism.
1.2. \(1\)-acyclicity of projective space.
In this n°, we always use in principle the fppf topology (XVII 0.10).

1.2.1. Let \(\varepsilon\) be a locally free Module on a scheme \(S\), assumed everywhere of rank \(\geqslant 2\), \(p : \mathbb{P}(\varepsilon) \to S\) the corresponding projective bundle, and \(G\) an abelian sheaf on the big fppf site of \(S\) (XVII 0.10). Each pair \((K_0, \varphi)\) formed of a torsor \(K_0\) under \(G\) and a homomorphism \(\varphi : \mathbb{G}_{m,S} \to G\) defines a \(p^*G\)-torsor \(K(K_0, \varphi)\) on \(\mathbb{P}(\varepsilon)\), the sum of \(K_0\) and the image under \(\varphi\) of the \(\mathbb{G}_m\)-torsor \(\Theta(1)\).
\[(1.2.1.1)\qquad K(K_0, \varphi) = K_0 + \varphi\Theta(1) \;.\]
We make the pairs \((K_0, \varphi)\) into a category by setting

\[\operatorname{Hom}((K_0, \varphi), (K_0', \varphi')) = \begin{cases} \varnothing & \text{if } \varphi \neq \varphi' \\ \operatorname{Hom}(K_0, K_0') & \text{if } \varphi = \varphi' \;. \end{cases}\]

The torsor \(K(K_0, \varphi)\) then depends functorially on \((K_0, \varphi)\). It is compatible with localization, and therefore defines a functor from the stack over \(S\) of pairs \((K_0, \varphi)\) to the stack over \(S\) of \(p^*G\)-torsors on \(\mathbb{P}(\varepsilon)\) (\(=\) the stack whose sections over \(U/S\) are the \(p^*G\)-torsors on \(U \times_S \mathbb{P}(\varepsilon)\)). These stacks are stacks in groupoids (\(=\) every morphism over a \(U/S\) is an isomorphism).

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 1.2.2

Under the hypotheses 1.2.1, if \(G\) is a flat commutative group scheme of finite presentation over \(S\), then the functor \(K\) of 1.2.1 is an equivalence.
1.2.2.1 This statement is equivalent to the conjunction of
\[G \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } p_*p^*G \quad\text{and}\quad \operatorname{Hom}(\mathbb{G}_m, G) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } R^1 p_* p^*G \;.\]

Indeed, a morphism of stacks in groupoids is an equivalence if and only if it induces an isomorphism on the sheaf generated by the presheaf of isomorphism classes of objects (2nd formula) and an isomorphism on the sheaf of automorphisms of an arbitrary local object (1st formula).
We shall give two proofs (1.2.4 and 1.2.5) of full faithfulness.

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 1.2.3

Let \(f : X \to S\) be a proper and flat morphism. Assume that \(f_*\mathcal{O}_X = \mathcal{O}_S\) universally and \(R^1 f_*\mathcal{O}_X = 0\) universally. Then every \(S\)-morphism from \(X\) to an \(S\)-group scheme of finite type \(G\) factors through \(f\) and a section of \(G\); more precisely, \(G \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } f_*f^*G\).
It suffices to prove the 1st assertion.

By the rigidity lemma (Mumford [1, 6.1 pg 115]; note that Mumford does not use the noetherian hypothesis made on \(S\)), it suffices to treat the case where \(S\) is the spectrum of an algebraically closed field. Suppose first that \(G\) is an abelian scheme, and let \(G^\vee\) be the dual abelian scheme. Since \(G = G^{\vee\vee}\), giving \(\varphi : X \to G\) is equivalent to giving an invertible sheaf \(\mathcal{L}\) on \(X \times G^\vee\), trivialized along \(X \times \{e\}\) and algebraically equivalent to zero on the fibres of the projection \(\operatorname{pr}_1\) of \(X \times G^\vee\) onto \(X\). If \(x : S \to X\) is a rational point of \(X\), we have \(\mathcal{L} \sim \operatorname{pr}_2^*(x \times G^\vee)^*\mathcal{L} \otimes \mathcal{M}\), with \(\mathcal{M}\) trivialized along \(x \times G^\vee\) and \(X \times \{e\}\). Giving \(\mathcal{M}\) is equivalent to giving a morphism of schemes from \(G^\vee\) to \(\operatorname{Pic}_{X/S}\), sending \(e\) to \(e\). Since \(H^1(X, \mathcal{O}_X) = 0\), we have \(\operatorname{Pic}^0_{X/S} = 0\), \(\mathcal{M} \sim 0\) and \(\mathcal{L} \sim \operatorname{pr}_2^*\mathcal{L}'\) with \(\mathcal{L}'\) equivalent to zero on \(G^\vee\), hence defining \(g \in G(S)\) such that \(\varphi = g \circ f\).
In the general case, \(G\) is an extension of an abelian scheme \(A\) by an affine group \(G_0\). The preceding result reduces us to the case where \(A = 0\), and we then have
\[\operatorname{Hom}_S(\operatorname{Spec}(H^0(X, \mathcal{O}_X)), G) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \operatorname{Hom}_S(X, G) \;.\]

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 1.2.4

Under the hypotheses 1.2.1, if \(G\) is a group scheme of finite presentation over \(S\) or is defined by a quasi-coherent sheaf on \(S\), then the functor (1.2.1.1) is fully faithful.

A. Let us prove that if \(K(K_0, \varphi)\) is isomorphic to \(K(K_0', \varphi')\), then \(\varphi = \varphi'\). For \(G\) quasi-coherent, we have \(\varphi = \varphi' = 0\), and the assertion is vacuous. For \(G\) of finite presentation, by (SGA 3 IX 5.1), it suffices to prove the assertion for \(S\) the spectrum of an algebraically closed field \(k\). Let then \(T\) be the largest subtorus of \(G\), and \(H = G/T\). The exact cohomology sequence yields

\[0 \to H^0(\mathbb{P}(\varepsilon), T) \to H^0(\mathbb{P}(\varepsilon), G) \xrightarrow{\ \alpha\ } H^0(\mathbb{P}(\varepsilon), H) \xrightarrow{\ \delta\ } H^1(\mathbb{P}(\varepsilon), T) \xrightarrow{\ \beta\ } H^1(\mathbb{P}(\varepsilon), G) \;.\]

By 1.2.3, \(H^0(\mathbb{P}(\varepsilon), G) \sim G(k)\) and \(H^0(\mathbb{P}(\varepsilon), H) \sim H(k)\), so that \(\alpha\) is surjective and \(\delta\) zero. If \(Y(T) = \operatorname{Hom}(\mathbb{G}_m, T)\), we have \(T \sim \mathbb{G}_m \otimes Y(T)\) and \(H^1(\mathbb{P}(\varepsilon), T) \sim Y(T)\). The injectivity of \(\beta\) therefore expresses the injectivity of the canonical arrow, defined by \(\Theta(1)\), \(\operatorname{Hom}(\mathbb{G}_m, G) \simeq \operatorname{Hom}(\mathbb{G}_m, T) \to H^1(\mathbb{P}(\varepsilon), G)\), and this proves the assertion.

B. To prove that the functor 1.2.1.1 is fully faithful is a local question on \(S\). We therefore reduce to assuming that \(\mathbb{P}(\varepsilon)/S\) admits a section \(s\). If \(K(K_0, \varphi)\) is isomorphic to \(K(K_0', \varphi')\), we have \(\varphi = \varphi'\) by A and \(K_0 \sim s^*K(K_0, \varphi) \sim s^*K(K_0', \varphi') \sim K_0'\). Thanks to the formula
\[(1.2.4.1)\qquad \operatorname{Hom}(K(K_0, \varphi), K(K_0', \varphi')) \sim \operatorname{Hom}(K(K_0 - K_0', \varphi - \varphi'), G_{\mathbb{P}(\varepsilon)}) \;,\]
it only remains for us to show that
\[\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathrm{tors}}(G, G) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathrm{tors}}(p^*G, p^*G) \;.\]
This follows from 1.2.3.
1.2.5. Here is another, more kunnutesque, proof of full faithfulness. The question is local on \(S\); by (1.2.4.1), it therefore suffices to check that
\[\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb{P}(\varepsilon)}(G, K(G, \varphi)) \begin{cases} = \varnothing & \text{if } \varphi \neq 0 \\ \xleftarrow{\ \sim\ } G & \text{if } \varphi = 0 \;. \end{cases}\]
This is exactly what the following lemma expresses:

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 1.2.6

Let \(\varepsilon\) be a locally free module everywhere of rank \(\geqslant 2\) on \(S\), \(G\) a group scheme of finite presentation over \(S\), \(\varphi : \mathbb{G}_m \to G\) a homomorphism of groups, \(V(\varepsilon)\) the vector bundle defined by \(\varepsilon\), \(V(\varepsilon)^\times\) the corresponding punctured vector bundle, and \(\Psi : V(\varepsilon)^\times \to G\) an \(S\)-morphism satisfying the following identity between \(S\)-morphisms from \(\mathbb{G}_m \times V(\varepsilon)^\times\) to \(G\):

\[\Psi(\lambda v) = \varphi(\lambda)\Psi(v) \;.\]

Then \(\varphi = e\), and \(\Psi\) factors through the projection \(p\) of \(\mathbb{P}(\varepsilon)\) onto \(S\).

It suffices to prove the second assertion. One reduces immediately to the case \(S\) noetherian, then, by (SGA 3 IX 5.1) and the rigidity lemma (Mumford [1, 6.1 pg 115]) applied to \(\mathbb{P}(\varepsilon)\), to the case where \(S\) is the spectrum of a field. Let \(n\) be an integer, \(W_n\) and \(G_n\) the infinitesimal neighbourhoods of the \(n\)th order of the zero section in \(V(\varepsilon)\) and \(G\), \(\mathfrak{g}_n\) the affine algebra of \(G_n\), and \(P_n(\Psi) : V(\varepsilon)^\times \to \operatorname{Hom}_S(W_n, G)\) the principal part of the \(n\)th order of \(\Psi\). Every section of \(\operatorname{Hom}_S(W_n, G)\) defines, by right translation by the inverse of the image of the zero section, a homomorphism from \(W_n\) to \(G_n\) sending \(o\) to \(e\); this defines
\[\Psi_1 = P_n(\Psi).\Psi^{-1} : V(\varepsilon)^\times \to \operatorname{Hom}_S(W_n, G_n) \;.\]

The hypothesis implies that \(\Psi_1\) commutes with the homotheties, which we let act on the second member by transport of structure from their action on \(W_n \subset V(\varepsilon)\). The affine algebra of \(W_n\) is \(\sum_{i=0}^n \operatorname{Sym}^i(\varepsilon)\). In view of its homogeneity, \(\Psi_1\) is therefore defined by a section, on \(\mathbb{P}(\varepsilon)\), of the \(\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}(\varepsilon)}\)-module
\[\sum_{i=0}^n p^*\operatorname{Hom}(\mathfrak{g}_n, \operatorname{Sym}^i(\varepsilon))(-i) \;.\]
The components of index \(i > 0\) of this module have no section other than the zero section, and we conclude that
This, being valid for every \(n\), implies that \(\Psi\) factors through a section of \(G\).
This second proof extends to prove the following analytic variant of 1.2.4. When \(G\) is affine, the proof of 1.2.2 can be carried out independently of this variant.

1.2.7. Let \(L\) be the field of fractions of a complete discrete valuation ring \(\mathcal{O}\), \(U_m\) the rigid analytic group "generic fibre" of the formal completion of \(\mathbb{G}_m\), and \(\widehat{\Theta(1)}\) the \(U_m\)-torsor on \(\mathbb{P}^r_L\), the formal completion of \(\Theta(1)\). If \(G\) is a rigid analytic group over \(L\), the functor \((K_0, \varphi) \mapsto p^*K_0 + \varphi\widehat{\Theta(1)}\) (cf. 1.2.1) is a fully faithful functor from the category of pairs \((K_0, \varphi)\) formed of a \(G\)-torsor on \(\operatorname{Spec}(L)\) and \(\varphi \in \operatorname{Hom}(U_m, G)\), to the category of \(p^*G\)-torsors on \(\mathbb{P}^r_L\).

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 1.2.8

Let \(k\) be a field of characteristic exponent \(p\) and \(f : X \to \operatorname{Spec}(k)\) a proper scheme over \(k\) satisfying \(H^0(X, \mathcal{O}_X) = k\) and \(\operatorname{Pic}^\tau_X = 0\). For every affine commutative group scheme of finite type \(G\) over \(k\), containing no tori, we have \(R^1 f_*(f^*G) = 0\).

It suffices to show that after every base change \(c : S \to \operatorname{Spec}(k)\), the functor \(f^*\) from the category of \(G\)-torsors on \(S\) to that of \(G\)-torsors on \(X_S\) is an equivalence. This problem is local on \(\operatorname{Spec}(k)\), so that to solve it we may reduce to the case where \(X\) has a rational point, where \(G\) is a successive extension of groups \(\mathbb{G}_a\), \(\alpha_p\), \(\mu_p\), \(\mathbb{Z}/p\) and \(\mathbb{Z}/\ell_i\) for \(\ell_i\) prime to \(p\), and where \(\mathbb{Z}/\ell_i \sim \mu_{\ell_i}\).

It is known that \(\operatorname{Lie}(\operatorname{Pic}_X) = H^1(X, \mathcal{O}_X) = 0\). By 1.2.3 and the existence of a section, the functors \(f^*\) under consideration are fully faithful; it therefore suffices to prove that \(R^1 f_*(f^*G) = 0\), or, by dévissage, that
\[R^1 f_*\mathbb{G}_a = R^1 f_*\alpha_p = R^1 f_*\mu_p = R^1 f_*\mathbb{Z}/p = R^1 f_*\mathbb{Z}/\ell_i = 0 \;.\]

For \(\mathbb{G}_a\), this follows from the fact that \(H^1(X, \mathcal{O}_X) = 0\). The case of \(\alpha_p\) (resp. \(\mathbb{Z}/p\)) is deduced from it via 1.2.3, by the long exact cohomology sequence defined by the exact sequence
\[0 \to \alpha_p \to \mathbb{G}_a \xrightarrow{\ x^p\ } \mathbb{G}_a \to 0 \qquad (\text{resp. } 0 \to \mathbb{Z}/p \to \mathbb{G}_a \xrightarrow{\ x - x^p\ } \mathbb{G}_a \to 0 \ (p \neq 1)) \;.\]

The case of \(\mathbb{Z}/\ell_i\) (resp. of \(\mu_p\)) is deduced from the isomorphism \(\mathbb{Z}/\ell_i \sim \mu_{\ell_i}\), from 1.2.3, and from the long exact sequence deduced from the Kummer exact sequence
\[0 \to \mu_n \to \mathbb{G}_m \to \mathbb{G}_m \to 0 \;.\]

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 1.2.9

Let \(S\) be a local artinian scheme, \(\bar{s}\) a geometric point of \(S\), \(f : X \to S\) a proper and flat morphism, and \(G\) a flat commutative group scheme of finite type over \(S\). Assume \(f\) smooth or \(G\) affine. If \(H^0(X_{\bar{s}}, \mathcal{O}) = k(\bar{s})\), if \(\operatorname{Pic}^\tau_{X_{\bar{s}}} = 0\) and \(G_{\bar{s}}\) contains no subgroup \(\mathbb{G}_m\), then the functor \(f^*\) from the category of \(G\)-torsors on \(S\) to that of \(f^*G\)-torsors on \(X\) is an equivalence.

a. The problem posed is local on \(S\) when one takes as localization morphisms the finite and flat morphisms \(u : S' \to S\). This allows one to assume that \(f\) admits a section \(x\). The functor \(f^*\) is then fully faithful, by 1.2.3 and the existence of \(x\), and it remains to show that every torsor, trivialized along \(x\), is trivial.

b. Suppose that \(S\) is the spectrum of a field. If \(G\) is affine, the assertion follows from 1.2.8. If \(X\) is smooth, and if \(G\) is an extension of an abelian variety \(A\) by an affine group \(G_0\), we denote by \(G^n\) the inverse image of \({}_n A\) in \(G\). The group \(H^1(X, A)\) is torsion (Raynaud [1, XIII 2.6]), hence the union of the images of the \(H^1(X, {}_n A)\). The group \(H^1(X, G)\) is thus the union of the images of the \(H^1(X, G^n)\). Since the groups \(G^n\) are affine, we again conclude by 1.2.8.

c. Let us prove the general case (assuming the existence of a section \(x\)) by induction on the length of \(S\). Let \(i : S_0 \hookrightarrow S\) be a subscheme defined by an ideal \(I\) of square zero and of length 1.

The \(G\)-torsors \(P\) on \(X\) such that \(x^*P\) is trivial are, by the induction hypothesis, deformations of the trivial \(G\)-torsor \(P_0\) on \(X \times S_0\). If \(G\) is smooth, and if \(L\) is the Lie algebra of \(G_{\bar{s}}\), these deformations are classified by
which proves 1.2.9 in this case.

For \(G\) flat over \(S\), this argument generalizes in terms of the Lie complex \(L\) of \(G_{\bar{s}}\). If \(\mathrm{L}\Lambda(G_s/k(s))\) is the relative cotangent complex of \(G_s\), this complex \(L \in D^b(k(s))\) is the dual of \(\mathrm{L}e^*(\mathrm{L}\Lambda(G_s/k(s)))\). We have \(H^i(L) = 0\) for \(i \neq 0, 1\).

The deformations over \(S\) (resp. over \(X\)) of the trivial \(G\)-torsor over \(S_0\) (resp. over \(X_0\)) are classified by \(H^1(L \otimes I)\) (resp. by \(H^1(X_s, f^*(L \otimes I))\)) (Illusie [1]). By hypothesis, we have \(H^1(X_s, H^0(f^*(L \otimes I))) = 0\) (since \(H^1(X_s, \mathcal{O}) = 0\)) and \(H^1(L \otimes I) \sim H^0(X_s, \underline{H}^1(f^*(L \otimes I)))\). We conclude that
\[H^1(L \otimes I) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } H^1(X_s, f^*(L \otimes I)) \;,\]

which means that every deformation over \(X\) of the trivial \(G\)-torsor over \(X_0\) is the inverse image of one and only one deformation to \(S\) of the trivial \(G\)-torsor over \(S_0\). If this deformation is trivial along a section, it is therefore trivial, which proves 1.2.9.

1.2.10. Let us prove 1.2.2 when \(S\) is artinian. Let \(T\) be the largest subtorus of \(G\); since we already have full faithfulness (1.2.4), the problem is local on \(S\) for the étale topology: we may assume \(T\) diagonalizable: \(T \sim \mathbb{G}_m^n\). By 1.2.3 and 1.2.9, the exact cohomology sequence yields
\[R^1 p_* T \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } R^1 p_* G \;,\]
and the assertion follows, since it is trivial for \(G = T\) and \(\operatorname{Hom}(\mathbb{G}_m, T) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \operatorname{Hom}(\mathbb{G}_m, G)\) (cf. 1.2.2.1).
1.2.11. Let us prove 1.2.2 when \(S\) is noetherian local complete. Let \(s\) be a section of \(p\).

If \(K\) is a \(G\)-torsor on \(\mathbb{P}(\varepsilon)\), there exists by 1.2.10 a unique pair \((\widehat{\varphi}, \widehat{\psi})\) formed of a formal homomorphism \(\widehat{\varphi} : \mathbb{G}_m \to G\) and a formal isomorphism \(\widehat{\psi} : p^*s^*K + \widehat{\varphi}\Theta(1) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \widehat{K}\). If \(G\) is affine, then \(\widehat{\psi}\) is algebraizable (SGA 3 IX 7.1). Let us provisionally admit that, as will be proved in (1.2.2.13), \(\widehat{\varphi}\) is always algebraizable to \(\varphi : \mathbb{G}_m \to G\).

If \(K_0 = s^*K\), and if \(K_1 = p^*K_0 + \varphi\Theta(1)\), we have a formal isomorphism \(\widehat{\psi} : \widehat{K_1} = \widehat{K(K_0, \varphi)} \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \widehat{K}\), i.e. a formal trivialization of \(K - K_1\). By virtue of formal GAGA, this section is algebraic, which proves 1.2.11. More precisely, if \(G\) is quasi-affine, then \(K - K_1\) is representable and one uses EGA III 5.1.4. In the general case, one proceeds similarly with the algebraic space \(K - K_1\).
1.2.2.12. Algebraicity of \(\widehat{\varphi}\): preliminary verification for a base trait.
Suppose that \(S\) is a complete trait, \(S = \operatorname{Spec}(V)\), and let \(L\) be the field of fractions of \(V\).
a) Over \(L\), there exists a unique triple \((K_{0L}, \varphi_L, \psi_L)\):
\[\psi_L : K(K_{0L}, \varphi_L) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } K|\operatorname{Spec}(L) \;.\]

b) By (1.2.10) (1.2.2.11), and with the notation of 1.2.7, we have a rigid analytic map \(\widehat{\varphi_L} : U_m \to \widehat{G}\), a \(\widehat{G}\)-torsor \(\widehat{K_0}\), and a rigid analytic isomorphism
\[\widehat{\psi} : p^*\widehat{K_0} + \widehat{\varphi_L}\,\widehat{\Theta(1)} \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \widehat{K} \;.\]

By the uniqueness assertion 1.2.7, \(\widehat{\varphi_L}\) is identified with the map deduced from \(\varphi_L\). The formal morphism \(\widehat{\varphi}\) of 1.2.11 therefore induces on \(\mu_n\) a map which coincides with the map deduced from the algebraic map \(\varphi_L : \mathbb{G}_m \to G\).
1.2.2.13. Algebraicity of \(\widehat{\varphi}\).
The formal map \(\widehat{\varphi} : \mathbb{G}_m \to G\) of 1.2.11 induces, for \(\ell\) invertible on \(S\), maps
\[\varphi_\ell : T_\ell(\widehat{\mathbb{G}_m}) = T_\ell(\mathbb{G}_m) \to T_\ell(G) \;.\]

By (1.2.2.12) and (EGA II 7.1.9), for every point \(t\) of \(S\), there exists an algebraic morphism \(\varphi_t : \mathbb{G}_{m_t} \to G_t\) such that \(T_\ell(\varphi_t) = T_\ell(\varphi)_t\). By (SGA 3 XV 4.1 bis), \(\widehat{\varphi}\) is therefore algebraizable.

1.2.14. Let us prove 1.2.2. By passage to the limit, we reduce to the case \(S\) noetherian, then \(S\) noetherian local with affine algebra \(A\). Let \(s\) be a section of \(p\). Let \(K\) be a \(G\)-torsor on \(\mathbb{P}(\varepsilon)\). Over \(S' = \operatorname{Spec}(\widehat{A})\), there exists one and only one homomorphism \(\varphi' : \mathbb{G}_{m,S} \to G_S\) such that the inverse image \(K'\) of \(K\) on \(\mathbb{P}(\varepsilon) \times_S S'\) is of the form \(K(K_0', \varphi')\). This homomorphism \(\varphi'\) descends to \(\varphi : \mathbb{G}_m \to G\). To prove the essential surjectivity of the functor 1.2.1, we are free to replace \(K\) by \(K - \varphi\Theta(1)\), i.e. to assume that \(\varphi = 0\). Over \(S'\), there then exists one and only one isomorphism \(\psi : p'^*s^*K' \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } K'\), inducing the identity on the section \(s\). This morphism descends to \(S\) (fpqc descent of morphisms of fppf torsors), and this proves 1.2.2.

blocks.title: Variants
blocks.html:
Variants 1.2.15

The conclusion of 1.2.2 is still valid in the following cases.

(i) \(G\) is defined by a quasi-coherent Module on \(S\).

(ii) \(G\) is the inverse image of a torsion sheaf on the small étale site of \(S\).
In case (i), the arrows (1.2.2.1) are isomorphisms by the base change theorem for a proper morphism and the simple connectedness of \(\mathbb{P}^r_k\) for \(k\) algebraically closed.
In case (ii), the fact that the arrows (1.2.2.1) are isomorphisms is standard, taking into account that the fppf cohomology of \(G\) coincides with its cohomology for the étale topology.
1.3. Integration of torsors.
1.3.1 Let \(S\) be a scheme and \(G\) an abelian sheaf on the big fppf site of \(S\), satisfying the following 3 conditions.
\((1.3.1.1)\) (i) For every projective space \(p : \mathbb{P}_S \to S\), with \(r \geqslant 1\), we have, in the big fppf site of \(S\) (XVII 0.10)
\[G \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } p_*p^*G \quad\text{and}\quad \operatorname{Hom}(\mathbb{G}_m, G) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } R^1 p_*p^*G \;.\]

(ii) For every \(n\) and every smooth affine \(S\)-morphism \(f : X \to T\), if \(K_1\) and \(K_2\) are two \(G\)-torsors on \(\operatorname{Sym}^n_T(X)\), the set \(\operatorname{Hom}(K_1, K_2)\) is identified with the set of symmetric morphisms from the inverse image of \(K_1\) on \((X/T)^n\) to the inverse image of \(K_2\) on \((X/T)^n\).
This condition is equivalent to the conjunction of:
(ii') \(\operatorname{Hom}_S(\operatorname{Sym}^n_T(X), G) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \operatorname{Hom}_S((X/T)^n, G)^{\mathfrak{S}_n}\), and
(ii") If the inverse image on \((X/T)^n\) of a torsor \(K\) on \(\operatorname{Sym}^n_T(X)\) admits a symmetric section, then \(K\) is trivial.
(iii) \(G\) satisfies either condition (XVII 6.3.21.1), or conditions (XVII 6.3.24.1) and (XVII 6.3.24.2).
The conclusion of 1.2.2 is therefore valid (cf. 1.2.2.1), as is the formulary XVII 6.3.26.

Condition (i) is discussed in 1.2.2 and 1.2.15. Condition (ii) is satisfied as soon as \(G\) is representable of finite presentation, or the inverse image of a sheaf on the small étale site of \(S\), or flat quasi-coherent. Condition 1.3.1.1 is therefore satisfied in each of the following cases.
\((1.3.1.2)\) (a) \(G\) is smooth of finite presentation (1.2.2 and XVII 6.3.21.1).
(b) \(G\) is the inverse image of a torsion sheaf on the small étale site of \(S\) (1.2.15 (ii) and XVII 6.3.21.1).
(c) \(G\) is affine, and the kernel of an epimorphism of smooth groups (1.2.2 and XVII 6.3.3.1).
(d) \(G\) is defined by a flat quasi-coherent sheaf on \(S\) (1.2.15 (i) and XVII 6.3.21.1).

1.3.2. Let \(f : X \to S\) be a projective and smooth curve over a scheme \(S\), with non-empty connected geometric fibres. Let \(\mathcal{L}\) be an invertible sheaf on \(X\) "sufficiently" relatively ample in the following sense.
\((1.3.2.1)\) For every geometric point \(s\) of \(S\), if \(X_s\) is of genus \(g\), then
\[\deg_{X_s}(\mathcal{L}) > 2g - 2 \;,\]
\[\deg_{X_s}(\mathcal{L}) \geqslant 1 \text{ if } g = 0, \text{ and } \deg_{X_s}(\mathcal{L}) \geqslant 2 \text{ if } g = 1 \;.\]

We then have \(R^1 f_*\mathcal{L} = 0\), and \(f_*\mathcal{L}\) is locally free, of formation compatible with every base change, and everywhere of rank \(\geqslant 2\). If a section \(s\) of \(f_*\mathcal{L}\) vanishes at no point, the scheme \(D_s\) of zeros of \(s\), regarded as a section of \(\mathcal{L}\) on \(X\), is a relative divisor (EGA IV 21.15.2), finite locally free over \(S\) since \(X/S\) is of relative dimension 1. We have canonically
\[s : \mathcal{O}(D_s) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \mathcal{L} \;.\]

The divisor \(D_s\) depends on \(s\) only up to multiplication by a section of \(\mathcal{O}_S^\times\). The preceding construction therefore provides us with a relative divisor \(Z_\mathcal{L}\) on the scheme deduced from \(X\) by the base change
\[p : \mathbb{P}(f_*(\mathcal{L})^\vee) \to S \;.\]

Let \(K\) be a torsor under \(G_X\), and let \(K|Z_\mathcal{L}\) be its inverse image on \(Z_\mathcal{L}\). The trace of this torsor (XVII 6.3.26), from \(Z_\mathcal{L}\) to \(\mathbb{P}(f_*(\mathcal{L})^\vee)\), is a torsor \(K_\mathcal{L}\) on \(\mathbb{P}(f_*(\mathcal{L})^\vee)\):
\[K_\mathcal{L} = \operatorname{Tr}_{Z_\mathcal{L}/\mathbb{P}}(K|Z_\mathcal{L}) \;.\]

By virtue of 1.2.2, there exists a triple, unique up to unique isomorphism, formed of a \(G\)-torsor \(\langle\mathcal{L}, K]\) on \(S\), a morphism \(\varphi_{\mathcal{L}, K} : \mathbb{G}_m \to G\), and an isomorphism
\[K_\mathcal{L} \simeq p^*\langle\mathcal{L}, K] + \varphi_{\mathcal{L}, K}\Theta(1) \;.\]
1.3.3. If we denote the composition of torsors additively, we have canonically
\[(1.3.3.1)\qquad \langle\mathcal{L}, K_1 + K_2] = \langle\mathcal{L}, K_1] + \langle\mathcal{L}, K_2]\]
\[(1.3.3.2)\qquad \varphi_{\mathcal{L}, K_1 + K_2} = \varphi_{\mathcal{L}, K_1} + \varphi_{\mathcal{L}, K_2} \;.\]

Let \(\mathcal{L}_1\) and \(\mathcal{L}_2\) be two invertible sheaves on \(X\) satisfying (1.3.2.1), and \(\mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}_1 \otimes \mathcal{L}_2\). The tensor product of sections defines a morphism

\[\xymatrix@C=1em@R=2.4em{ & \mathbb{P}(f_*(\mathcal{L}_1)^\vee) \times_S \mathbb{P}(f_*(\mathcal{L}_2)^\vee) \ar[rr]^-{\pi} \ar[dl]_{\operatorname{pr}_1} \ar[d]|{\operatorname{pr}_2} \ar@/^3pc/[dd]|(0.65){p_{12}} & & \mathbb{P}(f_*(\mathcal{L})^\vee) \ar[dd]^{p} \\ \mathbb{P}(f_*(\mathcal{L}_1)^\vee) \ar[dr]_{p_1} & \mathbb{P}(f_*(\mathcal{L}_2)^\vee) \ar[d]|{p_2} & & \\ & S \ar@{=}[rr] & & S }\]
We have \(\pi^*Z \simeq Z_{\mathcal{L}_1} + Z_{\mathcal{L}_2}\), whence an isomorphism (XVII 6.3.27.1)
\[(1.3.3.3)\qquad \pi^*K_\mathcal{L} \simeq \operatorname{pr}_1^*K_{\mathcal{L}_1} + \operatorname{pr}_2^*K_{\mathcal{L}_2} \;.\]
We have a canonical isomorphism
\[\pi^*\Theta(1) \simeq \operatorname{pr}_1^*\Theta(1) \otimes \operatorname{pr}_2^*\Theta(1) \;,\]
so that (1.3.3.3) is rewritten as

\[\begin{aligned} \pi^*(p^*\langle\mathcal{L}, K] + \varphi_{\mathcal{L}, K}\Theta(1)) &\simeq p_{12}^*\langle\mathcal{L}, K] + \operatorname{pr}_1^*\varphi_{\mathcal{L}, K}\Theta(1) + \operatorname{pr}_2^*\varphi_{\mathcal{L}, K}\Theta(1) \\ &\simeq p_{12}^*\langle\mathcal{L}_1, K] + p_{12}^*\langle\mathcal{L}_2, K] + \operatorname{pr}_1^*\varphi_{\mathcal{L}_1, K}\Theta(1) + \operatorname{pr}_2^*\varphi_{\mathcal{L}_2, K}\Theta(1) \;. \end{aligned}\]
We deduce from this, by a double application of 1.2.2, a canonical isomorphism
\[(1.3.3.4)\qquad \langle\mathcal{L}_1 \otimes \mathcal{L}_2, K] \simeq \langle\mathcal{L}_1, K] + \langle\mathcal{L}_2, K]\]
and an identity
\[\varphi_{\mathcal{L}_1 \otimes \mathcal{L}_2, K} = \varphi_{\mathcal{L}_1, K} = \varphi_{\mathcal{L}_2, K} \;.\]
We thus see that \(\varphi_{\mathcal{L}, K}\) depends only on \(K\), and we set
\[(1.3.3.5)\qquad \deg(K) = \varphi_{\mathcal{L}, K} \;.\]
We therefore have
\[(1.3.3.6)\qquad K_\mathcal{L} \simeq p^*\langle\mathcal{L}, K] + \deg(K)\Theta(1) \;.\]

Let \(\mathcal{U}\) be an invertible sheaf, locally a direct summand of \(f_*\mathcal{L}\), defining a section \(u\) of \(\mathbb{P}((f_*\mathcal{L})^\vee)\). Let \(D_u\) be the relative divisor defined by the invertible local sections of \(\mathcal{U}\).
\[u_S^*\Theta(1) \simeq \mathcal{U}_S^\vee\]
and we therefore deduce from 1.3.3.6 that
\[(1.3.3.8)\qquad u^*K_\mathcal{L} = \operatorname{Tr}_{D/S}(K) \simeq \langle\mathcal{L}, K] - \deg(K)\mathcal{U} \;.\]
We leave to the reader the task of verifying the compatibility:

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 1.3.4

The following diagram of isomorphisms 1.3.3.1 and 1.3.3.4 is commutative

\[\xymatrix@C=1em@R=2.6em{ \langle\mathcal{L}_1 \otimes \mathcal{L}_2, K_1 + K_2] \ar[r]^-{\sim} \ar@{=}[d] & \langle\mathcal{L}_1 \otimes \mathcal{L}_2, K_1] + \langle\mathcal{L}_1 \otimes \mathcal{L}_2, K_2] \ar[d]^{\wr} \\ \langle\mathcal{L}_1, K_1 + K_2] + \langle\mathcal{L}_2, K_1 + K_2] \ar[r]_-{\sim} & \langle\mathcal{L}_1, K_1] + \langle\mathcal{L}_2, K_1] + \langle\mathcal{L}_1, K_2] + \langle\mathcal{L}_2, K_2] }\]

The isomorphisms (1.3.3.1) and (1.3.3.4) are moreover compatible with the associativity and commutativity isomorphisms, in a sense which we leave to the reader to make explicit. The formula (1.3.3.4) then allows one to extend by "linearity" the definition of \(\langle\mathcal{L}, K]\) when \(\mathcal{L}\) no longer necessarily satisfies condition (1.3.2.1).
1.3.5. For every relative divisor \(D\) on \(X\), we set
\[(1.3.5.0)\qquad \operatorname{Tr}_{D/S}(K) = \operatorname{Tr}_{D/S}(K|D) \;.\]

If \(\mathcal{O}(D)\) satisfies (1.3.2.1), the section 1 of \(\mathcal{O}(D)\) is a section of \(f_*\mathcal{O}(D)\), and as such generates an invertible sheaf, locally a direct summand of \(f_*\mathcal{O}(D)\), of which it defines a trivialization. The isomorphism 1.3.3.8 therefore provides us with an isomorphism
\[(1.3.5.1)\qquad \langle\mathcal{O}(D), K] \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \operatorname{Tr}_{D/S}(K) \;.\]
One checks immediately that the diagrams

\[(1.3.5.2)\qquad \xymatrix@C=2em{ \langle\mathcal{O}(D), K_1 + K_2] \ar[r]^-{\sim} \ar[d]^{\wr} & \operatorname{Tr}_{D/S}(K_1 + K_2) \ar[d]^{\wr} \\ \langle\mathcal{O}(D), K_1] + \langle\mathcal{O}(D), K_2] \ar[r]^-{\sim} & \operatorname{Tr}_{D/S}(K_1) + \operatorname{Tr}_{D/S}(K_2) }\]
and

\[(1.3.5.3)\qquad \xymatrix@C=2em{ \langle\mathcal{O}(D_1 + D_2), K] \ar[r]^-{\sim} \ar[d]^{\wr} & \operatorname{Tr}_{D_1 + D_2/S}(K) \ar[d]^{\wr} \\ \langle\mathcal{O}(D_1), K] + \langle\mathcal{O}(D_2), K] \ar[r]^-{\sim} & \operatorname{Tr}_{D_1/S}(K) + \operatorname{Tr}_{D_2/S}(K) }\]
(XVII 6.3.27.1) are commutative. This allows one, by linearity, to define the isomorphism (1.3.5.1) for every relative divisor.
1.3.6. Let \(D\) and \(E\) be two effective relative Cartier divisors, and let \(f\) be a rational function such that
\[\operatorname{div}(f) = D - E \;,\]
i.e. an isomorphism between \(\mathcal{O}(D)\) and \(\mathcal{O}(E)\). The isomorphism \(f\) between \(\mathcal{O}(D)\) and \(\mathcal{O}(E)\) defines, by (1.3.5.1), an isomorphism
\[(1.3.6.1)\qquad \langle f, K] : \operatorname{Tr}_{D/S}(K) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \operatorname{Tr}_{E/S}(K) \;.\]
We have, by 1.3.5.2 for the second formula:
\[\langle fg, K] = \langle f, K].\langle g, K]\]
\[\langle f, K_1 + K_2] = \langle f, K_1] + \langle f, K_2] \;.\]

If \(\lambda\) is a section of \(\mathcal{O}_S^\times\), then, for every invertible sheaf \(\mathcal{L}\) on \(X\), multiplication by \(\lambda\) is an automorphism of \(\mathcal{L}\). By transport of structure, this automorphism induces on the two members of 1.3.3.8 automorphisms which are deduced from one another via the isomorphism 1.3.3.8. We deduce from this that
\[\langle\lambda, K] = \deg(K)(\lambda) \;,\]
if \(\deg(K) \neq 0\), the isomorphism \(\langle f, K]\) between \(\operatorname{Tr}_{D/S}(K)\) and \(\operatorname{Tr}_{E/S}(K)\) therefore depends on the choice of \(f\).

Let \(\lambda \in \Gamma(S, \mathcal{O}_S^\times)\), \(g \in \Gamma(S, G)\), \(\mathcal{L}\) an invertible sheaf on \(X\), and \(K\) a \(G\)-torsor on \(X\). If \(\langle\lambda, g]\) is the automorphism of \(\langle\mathcal{L}, K]\) deduced by transport of structure from the automorphisms \(\lambda\) of \(\mathcal{L}\) and \(g\) of \(K\), then \(\langle\lambda, g]\), identified with a section of \(G\), is given by \(\langle\lambda, g] = \langle\lambda, K] + \langle\mathcal{L}, g]\); since \(\langle\mathcal{O}(D), g] = \operatorname{Tr}_{D/S}(g)\), we draw from the preceding formula that
\[(1.3.6.2)\qquad \langle\lambda, g] = \deg(K)(\lambda) + \deg(\mathcal{L}).g \;.\]

1.3.7. Let \(f : X \to S\) be a projective and smooth curve over \(S\) and \(G\) a group over \(S\) satisfying 1.3.1.1. If \(X \xrightarrow{f_0} T \xrightarrow{\pi} S\) is the Stein factorization of \(f\), then \(\pi\) is an étale covering of \(S\) and the sheaf \(f_*\mathbb{G}_m\) is the torus \(\prod_{T/S}\mathbb{G}_m\). Locally on \(S\) (for the étale topology), \(X\) is a sum of a family of curves \((X_i)_{i \in I}\) over \(S\) with non-empty connected geometric fibres. If \(K\) is a torsor under \(G\) and \(\mathcal{L}\) an invertible sheaf on \(X\), we then set
\[\langle\mathcal{L}, K] = \sum_i \langle\mathcal{L}|X_i, K|X_i]\]

and we define the degree of \(K : f_*\mathbb{G}_m = \mathbb{G}_m^I \to G\) as having the coordinates \(\deg(K|X_i) : \mathbb{G}_m \to G\). The local constructions globalize and provide functors and morphisms
\[(1.3.7.1)\qquad \langle\mathcal{L}, K]_{X/S} = \operatorname{Tr}_{T/S}(\langle\mathcal{L}, K]_{X/T})\]
\[(1.3.7.2)\qquad \deg(K) : f_*\mathbb{G}_m = \prod_{T/S}\mathbb{G}_m \to G : \deg_{X/S}(K) = \prod_{T/S} \deg_{X/T}(K) \;.\]
For \(\lambda\) an automorphism of \(\mathcal{L}\), defined by an element \(\lambda_0\) of \(\Gamma(T, \mathcal{O}_T^\times)\), we have
\[(1.3.7.3)\qquad \langle\lambda, K] = \deg(K)(\lambda) \;.\]
We define the total degree of \(K\) as the composite
\[\operatorname{deg\,tot}(K) : \mathbb{G}_m \to f_*\mathbb{G}_m \xrightarrow{\ \deg(K)\ } G \;.\]
The preceding results yield:

Summary 1.3.8. : For every smooth projective curve \(f : X \to S\), we have a functor \(\langle\ ,\ ]\), whose formation is compatible with all base change, which to an invertible sheaf \(\mathcal{L}\) on \(X\) and a torsor \(K\) under \(f^*G\) associates a torsor \(\langle\mathcal{L}, K]\) under \(G\) on \(S\). This functor is equipped with the following additional structures and satisfies the following conditions:

(1.3.8.1) \(\langle\mathcal{L}, K]\) is biadditive in \(\mathcal{L}\) and \(K\); the biadditivity isomorphisms are compatible with the associativity and commutativity isomorphisms, with base change, satisfy the compatibility (1.3.4), and are compatible with the isomorphisms (1.3.8.2) below (via XVII 6.3.25.3 and XVII 6.3.27.1).
(1.3.8.2) For every effective relative divisor \(E\) on \(X/S\), we have a canonical isomorphism
\[\langle\mathcal{O}(E), K] \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \operatorname{Tr}_{E/S}(K|E) \;.\]
(1.3.8.3) The degree 1.3.7.2 satisfies, for \(\lambda \in f_*\mathbb{G}_m\) an automorphism of \(\mathcal{L}\),
\[\langle\lambda, K] = \deg(K)(\lambda) \;.\]
For \(\lambda \in \mathbb{G}_m(S)\), the total degree satisfies
\[\langle\lambda, K] = \operatorname{deg\,tot}(K)(\lambda) \;.\]
Likewise, for \(g \in G(S)\) we have \(\langle\mathcal{L}, g] = \deg(\mathcal{L}).g\) .
We deduce a canonical isomorphism:
\[(1.3.8.4)\qquad \langle f^*\mathcal{L}, K] \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \operatorname{deg\,tot}(K)(\mathcal{L}) \;.\]
It follows immediately from the definitions that for every homomorphism \(\Psi : G \to G'\), we have a canonical isomorphism, compatible with the preceding data:
\[(1.3.8.5)\qquad \langle\mathcal{L}, \Psi(K)] \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \Psi(\langle\mathcal{L}, K]) \;.\]
(1.3.8.6) Let \(u : X \to Y\) be a flat morphism between smooth projective curves over \(S\). We then have isomorphisms compatible with biadditivity and with base change:
— For \(\mathcal{L}\) an invertible sheaf on \(X\) and \(K\) a \(G_Y\)-torsor on \(Y\), we have
\[\langle\mathcal{L}, u^*K] \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \langle N_{X/Y}(\mathcal{L}), K] \;.\]
— For \(\mathcal{L}\) an invertible sheaf on \(Y\) and \(K\) a \(G_X\)-torsor on \(X\), we have
\[\langle u^*\mathcal{L}, K] \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \langle\mathcal{L}, \operatorname{Tr}_{X/Y}K] \;.\]

Moreover, these isomorphisms satisfy an obvious compatibility for a composite \(uv\) of morphisms of curves; for \(\mathcal{L} = \mathcal{O}(E)\), they are identified with the isomorphisms (XVII 6.3.27.2)
\[\operatorname{Tr}_{E/S}(u^*K) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \operatorname{Tr}_{u_*E/S}(K)\]
\[\operatorname{Tr}_{u^*E/S}(K) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \operatorname{Tr}_{E/S} \operatorname{Tr}_{X/Y}K \;.\]

It remains to prove 1.3.8.6. We reduce to the case where \(X\) and \(Y\) have nonempty connected geometric fibres, and we note that the explicit formulas above yield, for each section \(s\) of \(\mathcal{L}\) which does not vanish as a section of the direct image of \(\mathcal{L}\), an isomorphism \(\Psi_s\) of the desired type, homogeneous in \(s\), and therefore independent of \(s\) for \(\mathcal{L}\) satisfying (1.3.2.1). The general case follows.

1.3.9. Under the hypotheses 1.3.7, we have seen (1.3.8) that every \(G\)-torsor \(K\) on \(X\) defines a functor \(\langle\times, K]\), denoted below by \(F(\times)\), equipped with the following additional data and satisfying the following conditions:
(i) \(F\) is a morphism of fppf stacks over \(S\) (XVII 0.10 and Giraud [1])
— with source the stack whose \(T\)-objects, for \(T\) an \(S\)-scheme, are the invertible sheaves on \(X_T\)
— with target the stack of \(G\)-torsors.

(ii) The functor \(F\) is equipped with additivity isomorphisms \(F(\mathcal{L}_1 \otimes \mathcal{L}_2) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } F(\mathcal{L}_1) + F(\mathcal{L}_2)\), functorial, compatible with the associativity and commutativity isomorphisms, and compatible with base change.

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 1.3.10

Under the hypotheses of 1.3.7, the functor

\[\Phi : K \mapsto \langle\times, K]\]

is an equivalence between the category of \(G\)-torsors on \(X\) and the category of morphisms of stacks considered in (1.3.9).
We easily reduce to the case where \(X\) has nonempty connected fibres.

Let \(F\) satisfy 1.3.9 (i) and (ii). For every \(S\)-scheme \(T\) and every section \(t\) of \(X_T/T\), we again denote by \(t\) the relative divisor \(t(S)\). Then \(F(\mathcal{O}(t))\) is a \(G_T\)-torsor on \(T\). We denote by \(\Psi(F)\) the torsor thus obtained on \(X\), for \(t\) the "universal point" of \(X\), with values in \(X\), defined by the identity map of \(X\) into \(X\). For every section \(t\) as above, we have
\[(1.3.10.1)\qquad F(\mathcal{O}(t)) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } t^*\Psi(F) \;.\]

The isomorphism 1.3.8.2 provides an isomorphism of functors \(\Psi \circ \Phi \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \operatorname{Id}\). Let us construct an isomorphism \(\Phi \circ \Psi \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \operatorname{Id}\).
For each section \(t\) of \(X_T\) over \(T\), the isomorphism (1.3.10.1) is an isomorphism
\[F(\mathcal{O}(t)) \xrightarrow{\ \alpha\ } \langle\mathcal{O}(t), \Psi(F)] \;.\]
By addition, each family \(t_1 \ldots t_n\) of sections of \(X_T\) over \(T\) defines an isomorphism
\[F(\mathcal{O}(\textstyle\sum t_i)) \xrightarrow{\ \alpha\ } \langle\mathcal{O}(\textstyle\sum t_i), \Psi(F)] \;,\]
and by 1.3.9 (ii), this isomorphism does not depend on the order of the \(t_i\) .

Take \(T = (X/S)^n\) and for \(t_1 \ldots t_n\) the universal \(n\)-tuple of sections. If \(T' = \operatorname{Sym}^n_S(X)\), we then have on \(X_T\) a divisor \(\sum t_i\), which is the inverse image of the divisor \(\sum t_i\) on \(X_{T'}\). Over \(T\), \(\alpha\) is a symmetric isomorphism
\[\alpha : F(\mathcal{O}(\textstyle\sum t_i)) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \langle\mathcal{O}(\textstyle\sum t_i), \Psi(F)]\]
between torsors that are inverse images of torsors on \(T'\). By hypothesis (1.3.1.1)(ii), this isomorphism comes from one and only one isomorphism on \(T'\)
\[\alpha : F(\mathcal{O}(\textstyle\sum t_i)) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \langle\mathcal{O}(\textstyle\sum t_i), \Psi(F)] \qquad (\text{on } T') \;.\]
By XVII 6.3., we thus have, for every relative divisor \(D\) on \(X\), an isomorphism
\[(1.3.10.2)\qquad \alpha_D : F(\mathcal{O}(D)) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \langle\mathcal{O}(D), \Psi(F)] \;,\]
additive in \(D\), and whose formation is compatible with all base change.

Let \(\mathcal{L}\) be a sufficiently ample invertible sheaf on \(X\) in the sense of 1.3.2.1. Each everywhere-nonzero section \(s\) of \(f_*\mathcal{L}\) defines, with the notation of 1.3.2, an isomorphism
\[s : \mathcal{O}(D_s) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \mathcal{L} \;,\]
whence, by (1.3.10.2), an isomorphism
\[(1.3.10.3)\qquad \alpha_s : F(\mathcal{L}) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \langle\mathcal{L}, \Psi(F)] \;.\]
Let us prove that this isomorphism does not depend on \(s\). Indeed:
(i) The formation of \(\alpha_s\) is compatible with all base change
(ii) There exists a homomorphism \(\varphi : \mathbb{G}_m \to G\) such that
\[\alpha_{\lambda s} = \varphi(\lambda).\alpha_s\]
(by the functoriality of the two sides of (1.3.10.3)).

We necessarily have \(\varphi = 0\), for otherwise the torsor on \(\mathbb{P}((f_*\mathcal{L})^\vee)\) that is the inverse image of \(F(\mathcal{L}) - \langle\mathcal{L}, \Psi(F)]\) would be of degree \(\neq 0\). The \(\alpha_s\) therefore define a morphism from \(\mathbb{P}((f_*\mathcal{L})^\vee)\) to \(G\), and the latter is constant by hypothesis ((1.3.1.1)(i)). We may thus set \(\alpha_\mathcal{L} = \alpha_s\) .

The isomorphisms \(\alpha_\mathcal{L}\) thus form an isomorphism of functors between the restrictions of the functors \(F\) and \(\langle\times, \Psi(F)]\) to the sufficiently ample sheaves. This isomorphism is compatible with the additivity isomorphisms, which allows us to extend it by linearity to all invertible sheaves and completes the construction of
\[\alpha : \Phi \circ \Psi \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \operatorname{Id} \;.\]

blocks.title: Example
blocks.html:
Example 1.3.11

: \(G = \mathbb{G}_m\). Under the hypotheses 1.3.7, and in the special case where \(G = \mathbb{G}_m\), we write \(\langle\ ,\ \rangle\) rather than \(\langle\ ,\ ]\); if \(\mathcal{L}\) and \(\mathcal{U}\) are two invertible sheaves on \(X\), then \(\langle\mathcal{L}, \mathcal{U}\rangle\) is an invertible sheaf on \(S\). Moreover, we have isomorphisms (1.3.8.2)

\[\langle\mathcal{O}(D), \mathcal{U}\rangle \simeq N_{D/S}(\mathcal{U}) \;.\]
If \(D\) and \(E\) are disjoint effective relative divisors, then \(\mathcal{O}(E)|D\) is canonically isomorphic to \(\mathcal{O}\), whence an isomorphism
\[(1.3.11.1)\qquad \sigma_{D,E} : \langle\mathcal{O}(D), \mathcal{O}(E)\rangle \simeq N_{D/S}(\mathcal{O}(E)|D) \simeq N_{D/S}(\mathcal{O}) \simeq \mathcal{O} \;.\]

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 1.3.12

Let \((D_i)_{i=1,2}\) and \(E\) be effective relative divisors, with \(D_i\) disjoint from \(E\) (\(i = 1, 2\)). Let \(f\) be a rational function satisfying \(\operatorname{div}(f) = D_1 - D_2\), i.e. an isomorphism \(f : \mathcal{O}(D_1) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \mathcal{O}(D_2)\). The following diagrams of isomorphisms are commutative

\[(1.3.12.1)\qquad \xymatrix@C=3em{ \langle\mathcal{O}(D_1), \mathcal{O}(E)\rangle \ar[r]^-{\sigma_{D_1, E}} \ar[d]_{\langle f, \mathcal{O}(E)\rangle} & \mathcal{O} \ar[d]^{N_{E/S}(f)} \\ \langle\mathcal{O}(D_2), \mathcal{O}(E)\rangle \ar[r]_-{\sigma_{D_2, E}} & \mathcal{O} }\]

\[(1.3.12.2)\qquad \xymatrix@C=3em{ \langle\mathcal{O}(E), \mathcal{O}(D_1)\rangle \ar[r]^-{\sigma_{E, D_1}} \ar[d]_{\langle\mathcal{O}(E), f\rangle} & \mathcal{O} \ar[d]^{N_{E/S}(f)} \\ \langle\mathcal{O}(E), \mathcal{O}(D_2)\rangle \ar[r]_-{\sigma_{E, D_2}} & \mathcal{O} }\]
Formula (1.3.12.2) simply expresses the commutativity of the diagram
\[\xymatrix@C=3em{ N_{E/S}(\mathcal{O}(D_1)) \ar[r]^-{\sim} \ar[d]_{N_{E/S}(f)} & \mathcal{O} \ar[d]^{N_{E/S}(f)} \\ N_{E/S}(\mathcal{O}(D_2)) \ar[r]_-{\sim} & \mathcal{O} }\]

For every \(S\)-scheme \(T\) and every invertible sheaf \(\mathcal{L}\) on \(X_T\), set \(F(\mathcal{L}) = N_{E_T/T}(\mathcal{L})\). The hypotheses of 1.3.10 are satisfied by this functor, so that there exists a unique invertible sheaf \(\mathcal{M}\) equipped with an isomorphism of functors compatible with biadditivity:
\[N_{E_T/T}(\mathcal{L}) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \langle\mathcal{L}, \mathcal{M}\rangle \;.\]
Moreover, if \(d : T \to X_T\) is a section of \(X\) over \(T\), we have canonically
\[d^*\mathcal{M} \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } N_{E_T/T}(\mathcal{O}(d)) \;.\]
Taking for \(d\) the universal section of \(X\), \(\Delta : X \to X_X\), we find
\[\mathcal{M} \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } N_{E_X/X}(\mathcal{O}(\Delta)) \;.\]
Locally on \(S\), \(E\) is a sum of sections \(E = \sum t_i\) (XVII 6.3); for such an \(E\), we have
\[N_{E_X/X}(\mathcal{O}(\Delta)) = \bigotimes t_i^*\mathcal{O}(\Delta) = \sum \mathcal{O}(t_i) = \mathcal{O}(E) \;,\]
and this isomorphism, being independent of the order of the \(t_i\), defines a canonical isomorphism
\[(1.3.12.3)\qquad N_{E_X/X}(\mathcal{O}(\Delta)) \sim \mathcal{O}(E) \;,\]
so that
\[(1.3.12.4)\qquad N_{E_T/T}(\mathcal{L}) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \langle\mathcal{L}, \mathcal{O}(E)\rangle \;.\]
The isomorphism (1.3.12.3) is compatible with biadditivity, with base change, and is characterized by the fact that, moreover, for every section \(d\) of \(X_T\) over \(T\), the isomorphism
\[N_{E/T}(\mathcal{O}(d)) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \langle\mathcal{O}(d), \mathcal{O}(E)\rangle \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } d^*\mathcal{O}(E)\]
is the inverse image of the universal isomorphism (1.3.12.3). In particular, for \(d\) disjoint from \(E\), the diagram

\[\xymatrix{ N_{E/T}(\mathcal{O}(d)) \ar[r]^-{\sim} \ar@{=}[d] & \langle\mathcal{O}(d), \mathcal{O}(E)\rangle \ar[r]^-{\sim} & d^*\mathcal{O}(E) \ar@{=}[d] \\ N_{E/T}(\mathcal{O}(d)) \ar@{=}[rr] & & d^*\mathcal{O}(E) }\]
is commutative. By addition, we deduce that for \(D\) disjoint from \(E\), the diagram

\[(1.3.12.5)\qquad \xymatrix{ N_{E/T}(\mathcal{O}(D)) \ar[r]^-{\sim} \ar@{=}[d] & \langle\mathcal{O}(D), \mathcal{O}(E)\rangle \ar[r]^-{\sim} & N_{D/T}(\mathcal{O}(E)) \ar@{=}[d] \\ \mathcal{O} \ar@{=}[rr] & & \mathcal{O} }\]
is commutative. The arrow \(\sigma_{E, D_1}\) is therefore the composite of the inverse of 1.3.12.4 and an obvious arrow
\[\langle\mathcal{O}(D), \mathcal{O}(E)\rangle \xleftarrow{\ \sim\ } N_{E/S}(\mathcal{O}(D)) \to \mathcal{O}\]
and 1.3.12.2 follows immediately, since 1.3.12.4 is functorial.
From 1.3.12 we deduce (cf. SERRE [1] Ch III prop 7 pg 46)

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 1.3.13

Let \((D_i)_{i=1,2}\) and \((E_i)_{i=1,2}\) be effective relative divisors, with \(D_i\) disjoint from \(E_j\), \(f\) a rational function satisfying \(\operatorname{div}(f) = D_1 - D_2\) and \(g\) a rational function satisfying \(\operatorname{div}(g) = E_1 - E_2\). We then have

\[N_{E_1/S}(f).N_{E_2/S}(f)^{-1} = N_{D_1/S}(g).N_{D_2/S}(g)^{-1}\]

or briefly

\[(1.3.13.1)\qquad f(\operatorname{div}(g)) = g(\operatorname{div}(f)) \;.\]
This formula, in the form
expresses, via (1.3.12.1) and (1.3.12.2), the commutativity of the diagram

\[\xymatrix@C=3em{ \langle\mathcal{O}(D_1), \mathcal{O}(E_1)\rangle \ar[r]^-{\langle\mathcal{O}(D_1), g\rangle} \ar[d]_{\langle f, \mathcal{O}(E_1)\rangle} & \langle\mathcal{O}(D_1), \mathcal{O}(E_2)\rangle \ar[d]^{\langle f, \mathcal{O}(E_2)\rangle} \\ \langle\mathcal{O}(D_2), \mathcal{O}(E_1)\rangle \ar[r]_-{\langle\mathcal{O}(D_2), g\rangle} & \langle\mathcal{O}(D_2), \mathcal{O}(E_2)\rangle }\]

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 1.3.14

For \(G = \mathbb{G}_m\), the degree (1.3.7.2) coincides with the usual degree of invertible sheaves.
It suffices to compare formulas (1.3.7.3) and (1.3.12.1) for \(f\) the inverse image of \(f_0 \in \Gamma(S, \mathcal{O}_S^\times)\).
1.3.15. For any sufficiently ample \(\mathcal{L}\) and \(\mathcal{M}\), there exist locally on \(S\) disjoint divisors \(D\) and \(E\) and isomorphisms
\[\alpha : \mathcal{L} \to \mathcal{O}(D) \quad\text{and}\quad \beta : \mathcal{M} \to \mathcal{O}(E) \;.\]
We denote by \(\tau\) the isomorphism that makes the following diagram commute

\[\xymatrix@C=3em{ \langle\mathcal{L}, \mathcal{M}\rangle \ar[r]^-{\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle} \ar[d]_{\wr}^{\tau} & \langle\mathcal{O}(D), \mathcal{O}(E)\rangle \ar[r]^-{\sigma_{D,E}} & \mathcal{O} \ar@{=}[d] \\ \langle\mathcal{M}, \mathcal{L}\rangle \ar[r]_-{\langle\beta,\alpha\rangle} & \langle\mathcal{O}(E), \mathcal{O}(D)\rangle \ar[r]_-{\sigma_{E,D}} & \mathcal{O} }\]
It follows from 1.3.12 that this isomorphism does not depend on the particular choice of \(D, E\), \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\); it therefore globalizes to a canonical isomorphism
\[(1.3.15.1)\qquad \tau : \langle\mathcal{L}, \mathcal{M}\rangle \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \langle\mathcal{M}, \mathcal{L}\rangle \;.\]
This isomorphism satisfies \(\tau^2 = 1\); it is compatible with biadditivity, since (1.3.11.1) is, and extends by linearity to arbitrary invertible sheaves.
It follows from (1.3.12.5) that the morphism (1.3.12.4) is identified with the composite
\[N_{E_T/T}(\mathcal{L}) \xleftarrow{\ \sim\ } \langle\mathcal{O}(E), \mathcal{L}\rangle \xrightarrow{\ \tau\ } \langle\mathcal{L}, \mathcal{O}(E)\rangle\]
(check this for \(\mathcal{L} = \mathcal{O}(D)\) with \(D\) disjoint from \(E\)).

Summary 1.3.16. For every smooth projective curve \(f : X \to S\), we have a functor \(\langle\ ,\ \rangle\), whose formation is compatible with all base change, which to two invertible sheaves \(\mathcal{L}\) and \(\mathcal{M}\) on \(X\) associates an invertible sheaf \(\langle\mathcal{L}, \mathcal{M}\rangle\) on \(S\). This functor is equipped with the following additional structures and satisfies the following conditions:
1.3.16.1. With the notation of 1.3.8, for \(G = \mathbb{G}_m\), we have
\[\langle\mathcal{L}, \mathcal{M}\rangle = \langle\mathcal{L}, \mathcal{M}] \;,\]

in particular, \(\langle\mathcal{L}, \mathcal{M}\rangle\) is biadditive in \(\mathcal{L}, \mathcal{M}\) in the sense made precise in 1.3.8.1, and this biadditivity is compatible with that of the right-hand side of a canonical isomorphism (functorial in \(\mathcal{M}\))
\[\langle\mathcal{O}(E), \mathcal{M}\rangle \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } N_{E/S}(\mathcal{M}) \;.\]
1.3.16.2. We have a symmetry isomorphism
\[\tau : \langle\mathcal{L}, \mathcal{M}\rangle \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \langle\mathcal{M}, \mathcal{L}\rangle \;,\]

functorial in \(\mathcal{L}\) and \(\mathcal{M}\), compatible with base change, with the biadditivity isomorphisms, and satisfying \(\tau^2 = 1\). It makes the following diagram commute, for \(D\) and \(E\) disjoint divisors:

\[\xymatrix@C=1.4em@R=2.4em{ N_{D/S}(\mathcal{O}(E)) \ar[d]_{\wr} & \langle\mathcal{O}(D), \mathcal{O}(E)\rangle \ar[l] \ar[rr]^-{\tau} & & \langle\mathcal{O}(E), \mathcal{O}(D)\rangle \ar[r] & N_{E/S}(\mathcal{O}(D)) \ar[d]^{\wr} \\ \mathcal{O} \ar@{=}[rrrr] & & & & \mathcal{O} }\]
These formulas imply formulas (1.3.12.1) (1.3.12.2) (1.3.13.1) and

(1.3.16.3) For \(a, b \in \Gamma(S, \mathcal{O}_S^\times)\), denoting by \(\langle a, b\rangle\) the automorphism of \(\langle\mathcal{L}, \mathcal{M}\rangle\)—identified with a section of \(\mathbb{G}_m\)—obtained by functoriality from the automorphisms \(a\) and \(b\) of \(\mathcal{L}\) and \(\mathcal{M}\), we have
\[\langle a, b\rangle = a^{\deg(\mathcal{M})}\, b^{\deg(\mathcal{L})} \;.\]
(1.3.16.4) If \(\mathcal{L}_0\) (resp. \(\mathcal{M}_0\)) is an invertible Module on \(S\), we have a canonical isomorphism
\[\langle f^*\mathcal{L}_0, \mathcal{M}\rangle \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \mathcal{L}_0^{\otimes\deg(\mathcal{M})}\]
\[(\text{resp.} \qquad \langle\mathcal{L}, f^*\mathcal{M}_0\rangle \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \mathcal{M}_0^{\otimes\deg(\mathcal{L})} \qquad) \;.\]

1.3.16.5. If \(u : X \to Y\) is a finite flat morphism of smooth projective curves over \(S\), then, for \(\mathcal{L}\) an invertible sheaf on \(X\) and \(\mathcal{M}\) an invertible sheaf on \(Y\), the isomorphisms 1.3.8.6
\[\langle\mathcal{L}, u^*\mathcal{M}\rangle \sim \langle N_{X/Y}\mathcal{L}, \mathcal{M}\rangle\]
\[\langle u^*\mathcal{M}, \mathcal{L}\rangle \sim \langle\mathcal{M}, N_{X/Y}\mathcal{L}\rangle\]
are deduced from one another by the symmetry (1.3.16.2) (check this for \(\mathcal{L} = \mathcal{O}(E)\) and \(\mathcal{M} = \mathcal{O}(F)\) with \(E\) and \(F\) disjoint).
1.3.16.6. For \(\mathcal{L}\) an invertible sheaf on \(X\), the symmetry arrow
\[\tau : \langle\mathcal{L}, \mathcal{L}\rangle \to \langle\mathcal{L}, \mathcal{L}\rangle\]
is multiplication by \((-1)^{\deg(\mathcal{L})}\).
1.3.17. It remains to prove 1.3.16.6. We give two proofs, the first making use of the theory of the determinant (SGA 6 XI ).
First proof : Let \(u : T \to S\) be a finite locally free morphism. If \(\mathcal{L}\) is an invertible sheaf on \(T\), we have an isomorphism
\[(1.3.17.1)\qquad N_{T/S}(\mathcal{L}) \simeq \det(u_*\mathcal{L})\, \det(u_*\mathcal{O}_T)^{-1}\]
uniquely determined by the following three conditions:
a) its formation is compatible with base change;
b) for \(\mathcal{L} = \mathcal{O}_T\), it is the identity morphism of \(\mathcal{O}_S\);
c) it is functorial in \(\mathcal{L}\).
Let \(D\) and \(E\) be two effective relative divisors on \(X\), \(i\) the inclusion of \(D\) into \(X\), and \(u\) the projection of \(D\) onto \(S\). The short exact sequence
\[0 \to \mathcal{O}(-E) \to \mathcal{O} \to \mathcal{O}_E \to 0\]
allows us to interpret the isomorphism
\[\langle\mathcal{O}(D), \mathcal{O}(-E)\rangle \simeq N_{D/S}(\mathcal{O}(-E)) \simeq \det(u_*i^*\mathcal{O}(-E))\, \det(u_*i^*\mathcal{O})^{-1}\]
as an isomorphism
\[\langle\mathcal{O}(D), \mathcal{O}(-E)\rangle \simeq \det Ru_*(Li^*\mathcal{O}_E)^{-1} \simeq \det Rf_*(\mathcal{O}_D \overset{L}{\otimes} \mathcal{O}_E)^{-1} \;.\]
or
\[(1.3.17.2)\qquad \langle\mathcal{O}(D), \mathcal{O}(E)\rangle \simeq \det Rf_*(\mathcal{O}_D \overset{L}{\otimes} \mathcal{O}_E) \;.\]

For \(D\) and \(E\) disjoint, we have \(\mathcal{O}_D \overset{L}{\otimes} \mathcal{O}_E = \mathcal{O}\), and the resulting isomorphism of \(\langle\mathcal{O}(D), \mathcal{O}(E)\rangle\) with \(\mathcal{O}_S\) is the one already considered. We deduce that, for \(D\) and \(E\) disjoint, the symmetry \(\tau\) and the symmetry isomorphism \(\mathcal{O}_D \overset{L}{\otimes} \mathcal{O}_E \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \mathcal{O}_E \overset{L}{\otimes} \mathcal{O}_D\) are compatible via (1.3.17.2). By specialization, this remains true for arbitrary \(D\) and \(E\).
When \(D = E\) is defined by an ideal \(I\), we have

\[\begin{aligned} \underline{H}^0(\mathcal{O}_D \overset{L}{\otimes} \mathcal{O}_D) &= \mathcal{O}_D && \text{symmetry} = +1 \\ \underline{H}^{-1}(\mathcal{O}_D \overset{L}{\otimes} \mathcal{O}_D) &= I/I^2 && \text{symmetry} = -1 \\ \underline{H}^i(\mathcal{O}_D \overset{L}{\otimes} \mathcal{O}_D) &= 0 && \text{for } i \neq 0, -1 \;. \end{aligned}\]
Consequently, the arrow
\[\tau : \langle\mathcal{O}(D), \mathcal{O}(D)\rangle \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \langle\mathcal{O}(D), \mathcal{O}(D)\rangle\]
and 1.3.16.6 follows.

Second proof : By reduction to a "universal" case, we may assume that \(S\) is reduced. This case reduces to the one where \(S\) is the spectrum of an algebraically closed field \(k\). In this case, let \(X_1\), \(X_2\), \(Y_1\) and \(Y_2\) be four divisors on \(X\), \(f\) and \(g\) two rational functions, and suppose that
\[\operatorname{div}(f) = X_2 - X_1\]
\[\operatorname{div}(g) = Y_2 - Y_1\]
\[(X_1 \cup Y_2) \cap (X_2 \cup Y_1) = \varnothing \;.\]
The maps \(f\) and \(g\) then define
\[\langle f, g\rangle : \langle\mathcal{O}(X_1), \mathcal{O}(Y_1)\rangle \to \langle\mathcal{O}(X_2), \mathcal{O}(Y_2)\rangle \;.\]
Both sides are canonically isomorphic to \(k\) (1.3.11.1), so that \(\langle f, g\rangle\) is identified with an element of \(k^\times\).

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 1.3.18

We have

\[\langle f, g\rangle = \prod_{x \in X_1 \cup Y_2} (-1)^{v_x(f) v_x(g)} \left(g^{v_x(f)}/f^{v_x(g)}\right)(x) \;.\]

Let us show that (1.3.18) implies (1.3.16.6). We may assume that \(\mathcal{L} \sim \mathcal{O}(X) \sim \mathcal{O}(Y)\) with \(X\) and \(Y\) effective, and that \(X \cap Y = \varnothing\). Let \(f\) be a function such that \(\operatorname{div}(f) = Y - X\). The commutative diagram

\[\xymatrix@C=3em{ \langle\mathcal{L}, \mathcal{L}\rangle \ar[r]^-{\tau} \ar@{=}[d] & \langle\mathcal{L}, \mathcal{L}\rangle \ar@{=}[d] \\ \langle\mathcal{O}(X), \mathcal{O}(Y)\rangle \ar[r]_-{\langle f, f^{-1}\rangle} & \langle\mathcal{O}(Y), \mathcal{O}(X)\rangle }\]
shows that
\[\tau = \langle f, f^{-1}\rangle = \prod_{x \in X} (-1)^{v_x(f)^2} = (-1)^{\deg(\mathcal{L})} \;.\]
Let us prove 1.3.18. We reduce to assuming \(X_i\) and \(Y_i\) very ample. There then exist factorizations \(f = f_1 f_2\); \(g = g_1 g_2\) with
\[\begin{aligned} \operatorname{div}(f_1) &= X' - X_1 & \operatorname{div}(g_1) &= Y' - Y_1 \\ \operatorname{div}(f_2) &= X_2 - X' & \operatorname{div}(g_2) &= Y_2 - Y' \;, \end{aligned}\]
the divisors \(X'\), \(Y'\) and \(X_1 \cup X_2\), \(Y_1 \cup Y_2\) being disjoint.
We denote by \(\langle\ ,\ \rangle^\times\) the right-hand side of (1.3.18) and prove that
\[\langle f, g\rangle^\times = \langle f_1, g_1\rangle^\times \cdot \langle f_2, g_2\rangle^\times \;.\]
By Serre [1], we have
We deduce that
\[\langle f_1, g_1\rangle^\times \cdot \langle f_2, g_2\rangle^\times = g_1(X_1)\, f_1(Y')\, g_2(X')\, f_2(Y_2) \;.\]
\[\prod_{X_1 \cup X' \cup Y' \cup Y_2} (-1)^{v_x(f_1) v_x(g_2)} \left(f_1^{v_x(g_2)} \cdot f_2^{-v_x(f_1)}\right)(x)\]
\[\prod_{X_1 \cup Y_2} (-1)^{v_x(f) v_x(g)} \left((f_1 f_2)^{v_x(g_2)} \cdot (g_1 g_2)^{-v_x(f_1)}\right)(x) = \langle f_1 f_2, g_1 g_2\rangle^\times \;.\]

By the functoriality of \(\langle\ ,\ \rangle\) we have \(\langle f, g\rangle = \langle f_1, g_1\rangle\langle f_2, g_2\rangle\), and one checks easily that \(\langle f_i, g_i\rangle = \langle f_i, g_i\rangle^\times\). The lemma follows.
1.4. Strictly commutative Picard stacks.
Some results of "general topology" will be needed in order to express the results of 1.3 by a "universal coefficient formula".
The results of this section are suggested in a letter from A. Grothendieck to J.L. Verdier (1966).
The notions of associativity and commutativity for bifunctors (see below) were introduced by MAC LANE.
1.4.1. Let \(C\) be a category, \(F : C \times C \to C\) a functor, and
\[\sigma : F(F(X,Y), Z) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } F(X, F(Y,Z))\]
an isomorphism of trifunctors. We say that the pair \((F, \sigma)\) is an associative functor, or that \(\sigma\) is an associativity datum on \(F\), if the following condition is satisfied

(Ass) For any family \((X_i)_{i \in I}\) of objects of \(C\), and denoting by \(e : I \to M(I)\) the canonical map from \(I\) into the free monoid (without unit) generated by \(I\), there exist a map \(\underline{F} : M(I) \to \operatorname{Ob}C\), isomorphisms \(a_i : \underline{F}(e_i) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } X_i\) and isomorphisms \(a_{g,h} : \underline{F}(gh) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } F(\underline{F}(g), \underline{F}(h))\) such that the diagrams

\[(1.4.1.1)\qquad \xymatrix@C=1.2em{ \underline{F}(f(gh)) \ar[r]^-{a_{f,gh}} \ar@{=}[d] & F(\underline{F}(f), \underline{F}(gh)) \ar[r]^-{a_{g,h}} & F(\underline{F}(f), F(\underline{F}(g), \underline{F}(h))) \\ \underline{F}((fg)h) \ar[r]_-{a_{fg,h}} & F(\underline{F}(fg), \underline{F}(h)) \ar[r]_-{a_{f,g}} & F(F(\underline{F}(f), \underline{F}(g)), \underline{F}(h)) \ar[u]_{\sigma} }\]
are commutative.
We will not need to use the fact that the axiom (Ass) is equivalent to "the pentagon axiom", namely that the following diagram is commutative
\[\xymatrix@R=2em@C=1em{ & F(F(X,Y), F(Z,T)) \ar[dl] \ar[dr] & \\ F(X, F(Y, F(Z,T))) & & F(F(F(X,Y),Z), T) \ar[d] \\ F(X, F(F(Y,Z), T)) \ar[u] & & F(F(X, F(Y,Z)), T) \ar[ll] }\]
Now suppose given functorial isomorphisms
\[\sigma_{X,Y,Z} : F(F(X,Y), Z) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } F(X, F(Y,Z))\]
\[\tau_{X,Y} : F(X,Y) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } F(Y,X) \;.\]
We say that \(\sigma\) and \(\tau\) make \(F\) an associative and strictly commutative functor if the following condition is satisfied.

(Ass.s.Com) For any family \((X_i)_{i \in I}\) of objects of \(C\), and denoting by \(e : I \to N(I)\) the canonical map from \(I\) into the free abelian monoid (without unit) generated by \(I\), there exist a map \(\underline{F} : N(I) \to \operatorname{Ob}C\), isomorphisms \(a_i : \underline{F}(e_i) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } X_i\) and isomorphisms \(a_{g,h} : \underline{F}(gh) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } F(\underline{F}(g), \underline{F}(h))\) such that the diagram (1.4.1.1) is commutative, as well as the diagram

\[(1.4.1.2)\qquad \xymatrix@C=2em{ \underline{F}(gh) \ar[r]^-{a_{g,h}} \ar@{=}[d] & F(\underline{F}(g), \underline{F}(h)) \ar[d]^{\tau} \\ \underline{F}(hg) \ar[r]_-{a_{h,g}} & F(\underline{F}(h), \underline{F}(g)) }\]
We will not need to use the fact that this axiom is equivalent to the conjunction of
1) the pentagon axiom
2) \(\tau_{X,X} : X + X \to X + X\) is the identity
3) \(\tau_{Y,X} \circ \tau_{X,Y} : X + Y \to Y + X \to X + Y\) is the identity
4) the hexagon axiom: the diagram

\[\xymatrix@R=1.8em@C=0.5em{ & X + (Y + Z) \ar[dr]^{\sigma} & \\ (X + Y) + Z \ar[ur]^{\sigma} \ar[d]_{\tau} & & X + (Z + Y) \ar[d]^{\sigma} \\ Z + (X + Y) \ar[dr]_{\sigma} & & (X + Z) + Y \ar[dl]^{\tau} \\ & (Z + X) + Y & }\]
is commutative.
Note that condition 2) is not very often satisfied in practice (whence the terminology strictly commutative).

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 1.4.2

A strictly commutative Picard category \(\mathscr{P}\) is a nonempty category all of whose morphisms are isomorphisms, equipped with a functor \(+ : \mathscr{P} \times \mathscr{P} \to \mathscr{P} : (X, Y) \mapsto X + Y\) and functorial isomorphisms

\[\sigma : (X + Y) + Z \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } X + (Y + Z)\]

\[\tau : X + Y \to Y + X\]

making \(+\) an associative and strictly commutative functor, and such moreover that for every \(X \in \operatorname{Ob}\mathscr{P}\), the functor \(Y \mapsto X + Y\) is an equivalence of categories.
The reader will verify that

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 1.4.3

If \((X_i)_{i \in I}\) is a family of objects of a strictly commutative Picard category \(\mathscr{P}\), there exist a map \(\Sigma : \mathbb{Z}^{(I)} \to \operatorname{Ob}\mathscr{P}\), isomorphisms \(a_i : \Sigma(e_i) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } X_i\) and \(a_{\underline{n},\underline{m}} : \Sigma(\underline{n} + \underline{m}) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \Sigma(\underline{n}) + \Sigma(\underline{m})\) such that the diagrams of type (1.4.1.1) and (1.4.1.2) are commutative. The system \((\Sigma, (a_i), (a_{\underline{n},\underline{m}}))\) is unique up to unique isomorphism, and is functorial in \((X_i)_{i \in I}\).

1.4.4 A strictly commutative Picard category admits, up to unique isomorphism, one and only one neutral object, which we may define here as a pair \((e, \varphi)\) consisting of an object \(e\) and an isomorphism \(\varphi : e + e \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } e\). If \((e, \varphi)\) is a neutral object, there exists one and only one isomorphism of functors
\[\alpha_s : e + X \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } X\]
making the diagram commute
\[\xymatrix@C=3em{ e + (e + X) \ar[d]_{e + \alpha_s} & (e + e) + X \ar[l]_-{\sigma} \ar[d]^{\varphi} \\ e + X \ar@{=}[r] & e + X }\]

One defines similarly \(\alpha_d : X + e \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } X\), and \(\varphi\) is a special case of both \(\alpha_s\) and \(\alpha_d\); \(\tau\) exchanges \(\alpha_s\) and \(\alpha_d\). The group \(\operatorname{Aut}(e)\) is abelian, and for every \(X \in \operatorname{Ob}\mathscr{P}\), the functors \(X +\) and \(+ X\) establish the same isomorphism between \(\operatorname{Aut}(e)\) and \(\operatorname{Aut}(X)\).

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 1.4.5

A strictly commutative Picard stack \(\mathscr{P}\) on a site \(\mathscr{S}\) is a stack in groupoids \(\mathscr{P}\) on \(\mathscr{S}\) (GIRAUD [1]), equipped with a functor \(+ : \mathscr{P} \times_\mathscr{S} \mathscr{P} \to \mathscr{P}\) and isomorphisms of functors

\[\tau_{x,y} : x + y \to y + x\]

\[\sigma_{x,y,z} : (x + y) + z \to x + (y + z)\]

which, for every \(U \in \operatorname{Ob}\mathscr{S}\), make \(\mathscr{P}(U)\) a strictly commutative Picard category.

In what follows, we speak simply of a Picard stack, without specifying "strictly commutative". By 1.4.4, every Picard stack \(\mathscr{P}\) admits a global "neutral object" \(e\), and \(\operatorname{Aut}(e)\) is an abelian sheaf.
