1.4.6. An additive functor \(F : \mathscr{P}_1 \to \mathscr{P}_2\) between Picard stacks on \(\mathscr{S}\) is an \(\mathscr{S}\)-functor (necessarily cartesian) equipped with an isomorphism of functors
\[F(x + y) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } F(x) + F(y)\]
making the diagrams commute
\[\xymatrix@C=3em{ F(x + y) \ar[r] \ar[d]_{F(\tau)} & F(x) + F(y) \ar[d]^{\tau} \\ F(y + x) \ar[r] & F(y) + F(x) }\]
and

\[\xymatrix@C=1.6em{ F((x + y) + z) \ar[r] \ar[d]_{F(\sigma)} & F(x + y) + F(z) \ar[r] & (F(x) + F(y)) + F(z) \ar[d]^{\sigma} \\ F(x + (y + z)) \ar[r] & F(x) + F(y + z) \ar[r] & F(x) + (F(y) + F(z)) }\]
A morphism of additive functors \(u : F \to G\) is a morphism of \(\mathscr{S}\)-functors (automatically an isomorphism) making the diagram commute
\[\xymatrix@C=3em{ F(x + y) \ar[r]^-{u_{x+y}} \ar[d] & G(x + y) \ar[d] \\ F(x) + F(y) \ar[r]_-{u_x + u_y} & G(x) + G(y) }\]
1.4.7. If \(\mathscr{P}_1\) and \(\mathscr{P}_2\) are two Picard stacks on \(\mathscr{S}\), the Picard stack \(\operatorname{HOM}(\mathscr{P}_1, \mathscr{P}_2)\) is the following Picard stack:
a) if \(U \in \operatorname{Ob}\mathscr{S}\), its objects over \(U\) are the additive functors from \(\mathscr{P}_1|U\) to \(\mathscr{P}_2|U\); the morphisms are the morphisms of additive functors;
b) we define the sum of two additive functors \(F_1\) and \(F_2\) by the formula \((F_1 + F_2)(x) = F_1(x) + F_2(x)\); the structural isomorphism is the one making the diagram commute

\[\xymatrix@C=1.5em@R=3em{ (F_1 + F_2)(x + y) \ar[rr]^-{\text{structural}} \ar@{=}[d] & & (F_1 + F_2)(x) + (F_1 + F_2)(y) \ar@{=}[d] \\ F_1(x + y) + F_2(x + y) \ar[dr] & & F_1(x) + F_2(x) + F_1(y) + F_2(y) \\ & F_1(x) + F_1(y) + F_2(x) + F_2(y) \ar[ur]_-{\tau} & }\]
c) the associativity and commutativity isomorphisms are defined via the analogous isomorphisms in \(\mathscr{P}_2\).

1.4.8. If \(\mathscr{P}_1\), \(\mathscr{P}_2\) and \(\mathscr{P}\) are three Picard stacks, a biadditive functor from \(\mathscr{P}_1 \times \mathscr{P}_2\) to \(\mathscr{P}\) is an \(\mathscr{S}\)-functor \(F\) from \(\mathscr{P}_1 \times_\mathscr{S} \mathscr{P}_2\) to \(\mathscr{P}\), equipped with isomorphisms of functors
such that
a) For \(x_1\) (resp. \(x_2\)) fixed, \(F(x_1, \times)\) (resp. \(F(\times, x_2)\)) satisfies the compatibilities of 1.4.3.
b) For \(U \in \operatorname{Ob}\mathscr{S}\), \(x_1, y_1 \in \operatorname{Ob}\mathscr{P}_1(U)\) and \(x_2, y_2 \in \operatorname{Ob}\mathscr{P}_2(U)\), the diagram
is commutative.
For example, the canonical functor
\[\operatorname{HOM}(\mathscr{P}_1, \mathscr{P}_2) \times \mathscr{P}_1 \to \mathscr{P}_2 : (F, x) \mapsto F(x)\]
is biadditive.

One shows as in 1.4.7 that the biadditive functors from \(\mathscr{P}_1 \times \mathscr{P}_2\) to \(\mathscr{P}\) form a Picard stack \(\operatorname{HOM}(\mathscr{P}_1, \mathscr{P}_2 ; \mathscr{P})\).

We will see in (1.4.20) that there exists a "2-universal" biadditive functor \(\mathscr{P}_1 \times \mathscr{P}_2 \to \mathscr{P}_1 \otimes \mathscr{P}_2\); more precisely, there exist a Picard stack \(\mathscr{P}_1 \otimes \mathscr{P}_2\) and a biadditive functor \(\otimes : \mathscr{P}_1 \times \mathscr{P}_2 \to \mathscr{P}_1 \otimes \mathscr{P}_2\) such that for every Picard stack \(\mathscr{P}\), the functor defined by \(\otimes\):
\[(1.4.8.1)\qquad \operatorname{HOM}(\mathscr{P}_1 \otimes \mathscr{P}_2, \mathscr{P}) \to \operatorname{HOM}(\mathscr{P}_1, \mathscr{P}_2 ; \mathscr{P})\]
is an equivalence. This stack is unique up to unique equivalence (up to unique isomorphism).

1.4.9. Let \(u : \mathscr{S}_1 \to \mathscr{S}_2\) be a morphism of sites. The direct image \(u_*\mathscr{P}\) of a Picard stack \(\mathscr{P}\) on \(\mathscr{S}_1\) is the Picard stack on \(\mathscr{S}_2\) defined by
\[u_*\mathscr{P}(V) = \mathscr{P}(u^*V) \;.\]

Its objects over \(V \in \operatorname{Ob}\mathscr{S}_2\) are the objects of \(\mathscr{P}\) over \(u^*V\); its morphisms, its addition law, and its compatibility isomorphisms are those of \(\mathscr{P}\). The direct image \(u_*\) is a 2-functor.

1.4.10. A Picard prestack \(\mathscr{P}\) on a site \(\mathscr{S}\) is a prestack \(\mathscr{P}\) on \(\mathscr{S}\) (Giraud [1]), equipped with a functor \(+ : \mathscr{P} \times_\mathscr{S} \mathscr{P} \to \mathscr{P}\) and associativity and commutativity isomorphisms \(\sigma\) and \(\tau\), such that for each \(U \in \operatorname{Ob}\mathscr{S}\), \(\mathscr{P}(U)\) is a (strictly commutative) Picard category. If \(\mathscr{P}_1\) and \(\mathscr{P}_2\) are two Picard prestacks, one defines in the obvious way (cf. 1.4.6, 1.4.7) the additive functors from \(\mathscr{P}_1\) to \(\mathscr{P}_2\) and the Picard prestack \(\operatorname{HOM}(\mathscr{P}_1, \mathscr{P}_2)\) that they form. If \(\mathscr{P}\) is a Picard prestack, and \(j : \mathscr{P} \to a\mathscr{P}\) the stack it generates, there exists, up to essentially unique equivalence, one and only one pair consisting of a Picard stack structure on \(a\mathscr{P}\) and an additive functor structure on \(j\); equipped with these data, the pair \((j, a\mathscr{P})\) is called the Picard stack generated by \(\mathscr{P}\). For every Picard stack \(\mathscr{P}_1\), we have an equivalence
\[(1.4.10.1)\qquad \operatorname{HOM}(a\mathscr{P}, \mathscr{P}_1) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \operatorname{HOM}(\mathscr{P}, \mathscr{P}_1) \;.\]

1.4.11. We denote by \(C^{[-1,0]}(\mathscr{S})\) the category of complexes of abelian sheaves \(K\) on \(\mathscr{S}\) such that \(K^i = 0\) for \(i \notin [-1, 0]\). To every complex \(K \in \operatorname{Ob}C^{[-1,0]}(\mathscr{S})\)
there is associated the following Picard prestack \(\operatorname{pch}(K)\):
(I) For \(U \in \operatorname{Ob}\mathscr{S}\), we have \(\operatorname{Ob}\operatorname{pch}(K)(U) = K^0(U)\).
(II) If \(x, y \in K^0(U)\), an arrow from \(x\) to \(y\) is an element \(f\) of \(K^{-1}(U)\) such that \(df = y - x\) .
(III) The composition law for arrows is the addition law in \(K^{-1}(U)\).
(IV) The functor \(+\) is given by the addition law in \(K^0(U)\) and \(K^{-1}(U)\).
(V) The associativity and commutativity isomorphisms are provided by the zero element of \(K^{-1}(U)\) .

We denote by \(\operatorname{ch}(K)\) the Picard stack generated (1.4.10) by the Picard prestack \(\operatorname{pch}(K)\). The sheaf \(\underline{H}^0(K)\) is interpreted as the following associated sheaf
\[(1.4.11.1)\qquad \underline{H}^0(K) \simeq a(U \mapsto \text{group of isomorphism classes of objects of } \operatorname{ch}(K)(U)) \;.\]
On the other hand,
\[(1.4.11.2)\qquad \underline{H}^{-1}(K) \simeq \operatorname{Aut}(e)\]
1.4.12. Every morphism of complexes \(f : K \to L\) induces an additive functor \(\operatorname{pch}(f) : \operatorname{pch}(K) \to \operatorname{pch}(L)\), whence an additive functor
\[\operatorname{ch}(f) : \operatorname{ch}(K) \to \operatorname{ch}(L)\]

It follows from (1.4.11.1) and (1.4.11.2) that \(\operatorname{ch}(f)\) is an equivalence if and only if \(f\) is a quasi-isomorphism. We deduce from 1.4.10.1 that for two morphisms \(f, g : K \to L\), we have
\[\operatorname{Hom}(\operatorname{ch}(f), \operatorname{ch}(g)) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \operatorname{Hom}(\operatorname{pch}(f), \operatorname{pch}(g)) \;.\]

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 1.4.13

(I) For every Picard stack \(\mathscr{P}\), there exists a complex \(K\) such that \(\mathscr{P} \simeq \operatorname{ch}(K)\).

(II) For every additive functor \(F : \operatorname{ch}(K) \to \operatorname{ch}(L)\), there exist a quasi-isomorphism \(k : K' \to K\) and a morphism \(\ell : K' \to L\) such that \(F \simeq \operatorname{ch}(\ell)\operatorname{ch}(k)^{-1}\).
Let us prove (I). Let \((k_i, U_i)_{i \in I}\) be a family such that
(a) \(k_i \in \operatorname{Ob}\mathscr{P}(U_i)\);
(b) every object of \(\mathscr{P}\) is locally isomorphic to an inverse image of one of the \(k_i\).

Set \(K^0 = \bigoplus_{i \in I} \mathbb{Z}_{U_i}\) . We deduce from 1.4.3 that there exists an additive functor \(F\) from \(\operatorname{ch}(0 \to K^0)\) to \(\mathscr{P}\) sending the basis \(e_i\) of \(\mathbb{Z}_{U_i}\) to \(k_i\). Lemma 1.4.16

Let \(L \in \operatorname{Ob} C^{[-1,0]}(\mathscr{S})\) be such that \(L^{-1}\) is injective.

(I) \(\operatorname{pch}(L)\) is already a stack.

(II) For \(K \in \operatorname{Ob} C^{[-1,0]}(\mathscr{S})\), every additive functor \(F : \operatorname{ch}(K) \to \operatorname{ch}(L)\) is isomorphic to a functor \(\operatorname{ch}(f)\) for \(f\) a morphism from \(K\) to \(L\).

(I) For any \(U \in \operatorname{Ob}\mathscr{S}\) and \(x \in L^0(U)\), the sheaf of pairs formed by a local section \(\ell\) of \(L^0|U\) and an isomorphism between \(x\) and \(\ell\) is a principal homogeneous space under \(L^{-1}\); it therefore admits a section, and \(j : \operatorname{pch}(L) \to \operatorname{ch}(L)\) is surjective on the isomorphism classes of objects, hence an equivalence.

(II) Let \(L'\) be a complex of injectives, equipped with a quasi-isomorphism \(\varphi : L \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } L'\), such that \(\varphi^i\) is an isomorphism for \(i \leqslant -1\). By 1.4.13, and [C.D], there exists a diagram commutative up to homotopy
\[\xymatrix@C=3em{ L \ar[r]^-{\sim}_-{\varphi} & L' \\ K' \ar[r]_-{\sim}^-{\psi} \ar[u]^{f_0} & K \ar[u]_{f_1} }\]

such that \(F \simeq \operatorname{ch}(f_0)\, \operatorname{ch}(\psi)^{-1}\). Moreover, \(K = \tau_{\leqslant 0}K\) and \(L = \tau_{\leqslant 0}L'\), so that \(f_1\) factors through \(f : K \to L\), and \(F \simeq \operatorname{ch}(f)\).

1.5. The universal coefficient formula.

1.5.1. Let \(f : X \to S\) be a projective smooth curve over \(S\). We shall denote by \(\operatorname{PIC}(X/S)\) the Picard stack on the big fppf site of \(S\) (XVII 0.10), the direct image (1.4.9) of the stack of invertible sheaves on \(X\). We have
\[(1.5.1.1)\qquad \operatorname{PIC}(X/S) = f_*\operatorname{ch}\mathbb{G}_m[1]\]
\[(1.5.1.2)\qquad \operatorname{PIC}(X/S)^\flat = \tau_{\leqslant 0}\, Rf_*(\mathbb{G}_m[1]) \;.\]

Each section \(t\) of \(X\) defines an invertible sheaf \(\mathcal{O}(t)\) on \(X\). With the notation of 1.4.24 (cf. 1.4.24. a\(\leftrightarrow\)b), this construction, being compatible with every base change, defines a morphism of Picard stacks over \(S\)
\[(1.5.1.3)\qquad \operatorname{ch} \mathbb{Z}^{(X)} \to \operatorname{PIC}(X/S) \;.\]
If \(C\) is any Picard stack over \(S\), the morphisms (1.5.1.3) and (1.4.24.1) define an additive functor
\[(1.5.1.4)\qquad \operatorname{HOM}(\operatorname{PIC}(X/S), C) \to \operatorname{HOM}(\operatorname{ch}(\mathbb{Z}^{(X)}), C) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } f_*f^*C \;.\]
By applying the construction \(\flat\), the functor 1.5.1.3 defines a morphism
\[(1.5.1.5)\qquad \mathbb{Z}^{(X)} \to \tau_{\leqslant 0}\, Rf_* \mathbb{G}_m[1] \to Rf_* \mathbb{G}_m[1] \;,\]
and the functor 1.5.1.4 has, by 1.4.24.2, as its analogue a morphism
\[(1.5.1.6)\qquad R\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}(\tau_{\leqslant 0}\, Rf_*(\mathbb{G}_m[1]), K) \to Rf_*f^*K \;.\]

If \(C\) is the stack \(\operatorname{ch}(G[1])\) of torsors under a group \(G\) satisfying (1.3.1.1), theorem 1.3.10 asserts that the functor 1.5.1.4 is an equivalence, the inverse equivalence being the one that associates to a torsor \(K\) under \(G_X\) the additive functor \(\langle\times, K]\). That (1.5.1.4) is an equivalence amounts to saying that the morphism deduced from 1.5.1.4 or 1.5.1.6
\[(1.5.1.7)\qquad \tau_{\leqslant 1}\, R\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}(\tau_{\leqslant 0}\, Rf_*(\mathbb{G}_m[1]), G) \to \tau_{\leqslant 1}\, Rf_*f^*G\]
is an isomorphism.

blocks.html:
Theorem 1.5.2

(universal coefficient formula).

Let \(f : X \to S\) be a projective smooth curve over \(S\), \(C\) a Picard stack over \(S_{\mathrm{fppf}}\) and \(K = C^\flat\) (1.4.15). Suppose that \(K\) is locally isomorphic (in \(D^+(S_{\mathrm{fppf}})\)) to complexes of the form \(G_{-1} \to G_0\), where the sheaves \(G_i\) satisfy (1.3.1.1). Then

(I) The functor 1.5.1.4

\[(1.5.2.1)\qquad \operatorname{HOM}(\operatorname{PIC}(X/S), C) \to f_*f^*C\]

is an equivalence of Picard stacks.

(II) The morphism deduced from (1.5.1.6) or (1.5.1.4)

\[(1.5.2.2)\qquad \tau_{\leqslant 0}\, R\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}(\tau_{\leqslant 0}\, Rf_*(\mathbb{G}_m[1]), K) \to \tau_{\leqslant 0}\, Rf_*f^*K\]

is an isomorphism.
This theorem makes \(\tau_{\leqslant 0}\, Rf_*(\mathbb{G}_m[1])\) play the role played by homology in the classical universal coefficient formula.

It is clear that, for each stack \(C\), we have (I)\(\leftrightarrow\)(II), and both (I) and (II) are local in nature on \(S\). If \(C\) is of the form \(\operatorname{ch}(G[1])\), then the theorem follows from 1.3.10, as noted above. It remains to show that if \(K\) is of the form
and if (1.5.2.2) is an isomorphism for \(G_{-1}[1]\) and \(G_0[1]\), then (1.5.2.2) is an isomorphism for \(K\). To verify this, it suffices to compare the long exact cohomology sequence
with the analogous long exact sequence for the left-hand side of (1.5.2.2), and to apply the five lemma.
1.5.3. Let \(u\) be a flat morphism of projective smooth curves over \(S\)

\[(1.5.3.2)\qquad \xymatrix@C=3em{ \operatorname{HOM}(\operatorname{PIC}(Y/S), C) \ar[r] \ar[d]_{\operatorname{HOM}(N_{X/Y}, C)} & f_{2*}f_2^*C \ar[d]^{u^*} \\ \operatorname{HOM}(\operatorname{PIC}(X/S), C) \ar[r] & f_{1*}f_1^*C }\]

\[(1.5.3.4)\qquad \operatorname{Tr}_u : f_{1*}f_1^* \operatorname{ch}(G[1]) \to f_{2*}f_2^* \operatorname{ch}(G[1])\]
and 1.3.8.6 provides us with an isomorphism making the following diagram essentially commutative

1.5.4. With the notation of 1.5.2, let \(G\) be an abelian sheaf on \(S\) satisfying 1.3.1.1. Locally on \(S\) for the étale topology, we have (non-canonically)

b) The second morphism 1.5.4.2 is the degree 1.3.7.2.

1.5.5. When, in 1.5.2.2, one takes \(K = \mathbb{G}_m[1]\), theorem 1.5.2 appears as a self-duality theorem for \(\tau_{\leqslant 0}(Rf_*\mathbb{G}_m[1])\). Any complex representing \(\tau_{\leqslant 0}\, Rf_*\mathbb{G}_m[1]\) admits a canonical filtration in three steps, the successive quotients being, up to unique quasi-isomorphism
\[\operatorname{Pic}_{X/S}/\operatorname{Pic}^0_{X/S} \;, \quad \operatorname{Pic}^0_{X/S} \;, \quad (f_*\mathbb{G}_m)[1] \;.\]

To the preceding self-duality there corresponds a duality (with values in \(\mathbb{G}_m\)) between \(\operatorname{Pic}_{X/S}/\operatorname{Pic}^0_{X/S}\) and \(f_*\mathbb{G}_m\), and a self-duality (with values in \(\mathbb{G}_m[1]\)) on \(\operatorname{Pic}^0_{X/S}\) (self-duality of the Jacobian).

1.5.6. The situation is distinctly less favourable for smooth curves over \(S\): \(f : X \to S\) which one does not assume proper over \(S\). It seems that the additive group behaves in an uncontrollable way. The preceding arguments nevertheless extend to the case of smooth curves obtained from a proper curve over \(S\) by removing a part finite over \(S\), for \(G\) a torsion étale sheaf, with torsion prime to the residue characteristics of \(S\). Lemma 1.5.7

Let \(p : X \to S\) be the projection of a standard affine space over \(S\), and \(G\) a torsion abelian sheaf on \(S_{\text{ét}}\), prime to the residue characteristics of \(S\). We again denote by \(G\) the inverse image of \(G\) on the site \(S_{\mathrm{fppf}}\). Then the functor \(p^*\) is an equivalence of categories between the category of torsors under \(G\) on \(S_{\text{ét}}\) (or on \(S_{\mathrm{fppf}}\), which amounts to the same (Grothendieck [1])), and the category of torsors under \(G_X\) on \(X\).

1.5.8. Let \(\bar{f} : \overline{X} \to S\) be a proper morphism of finite presentation with fibres purely of dimension one, \(Y\) a subscheme of \(\overline{X}\) finite over \(S\), defined by an ideal \(\underline{m}\), and suppose that \(X = \overline{X} - Y\) is a smooth curve over \(S\). Let, on the other hand, \(G\) be a torsion sheaf on \(S_{\text{ét}}\), prime to the residue characteristics of \(S\). We shall again denote by \(G\) the sheaf on the big fppf site of \(S\) (XVII 0.10) which is the inverse image of \(G\).

Let \(\mathbb{G}_m(\underline{m})\) be the subsheaf of \(\mathbb{G}_{mX}\) formed by the sections equal to 1 on \(Y\). A torsor under \(\mathbb{G}_m(\underline{m})\) is identified with an invertible sheaf on \(\overline{X}\), trivialized on \(Y\). Every relative divisor on \(X\), finite over \(S\), defines such an invertible sheaf. Locally on \(S\) for the étale topology, there exist such divisors giving rise to relatively ample invertible sheaves.

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 1.5.9

Under the hypotheses 1.5.8, with \(S\) affine, let \(\mathcal{O}_{\overline{X}}(1)\) be a relatively ample invertible sheaf on \(\overline{X}\), trivialized along \(Y\), and let \(\mathcal{M}\) be an invertible sheaf on \(\overline{X}\), trivialized along \(Y\). For every point \(s \in S\), there exists an integer \(n_0\) such that for every integer \(n \geqslant n_0\) and every section \(m_s\) of \(\mathcal{M}(n) \otimes k(s)\) on the fibre \(\overline{X}_s\), equal to 1 on \(Y_s\), there exists a section \(m\) of \(\mathcal{M}(n)\) equal to 1 on \(Y\), which lifts \(m_s\).

One reduces to the case \(S\) noetherian (since a family of surjective morphisms remains a family of surjective morphisms under base change). Let \(\mathcal{N}\) be the coherent sheaf of local sections of \(\mathcal{M}\) vanishing on \(\overline{X}_s\) and \(Y\). For each \(n\), the local solutions to the given problem form a principal homogeneous space under \(\mathcal{N}(n)\), so that the obstruction to lifting \(m_s\) lies in \(H^1(X, \mathcal{N}(n)) = H^0(S, R^1f_*\mathcal{N}(n))\). Now, for \(n\) large enough, \(R^1f_*\mathcal{N}(n) = 0\) (EGA III 2.2.1).
1.5.10. Let \(\mathcal{L}\) be an invertible sheaf on \(\overline{X}\) trivialized along \(Y\), and \(s \in S\). Consider the conditions

(1.5.10.1) Every section of \(\mathcal{L} \otimes k(s)\) on \(X_s\), equal to 1 on \(Y_s\), lifts to a section of \(\mathcal{L}\) on the inverse image \(U\) of a neighbourhood of \(s\), equal to 1 on \(Y|U\).
(1.5.10.2) There exist 4 sections \(m_i\) of \(\mathcal{L} \otimes k(s)\) on \(X_s\), equal to 1 on \(Y\), and linearly independent at the generic point of every irreducible component of \(X_s\).

(1.5.10.3) \(m\) is equal to 1 on \(Y\) and the subscheme \(Z(m)\) of \(X\) with equation \(m = 0\) is a relative divisor over \(S\) (which means that it is quasi-finite over \(S\), hence finite over \(S\), since \(X = \overline{X} - Y\) is smooth over \(S\)).

(1.5.10.5) Likewise, \(\lambda m_1 + \mu m_2 + (1 - \lambda - \mu)m_3\) satisfies (1.5.10.3).

blocks.html:
Lemma 1.5.11

Let \(\mathcal{L}\) be an invertible sheaf on \(X\), trivialized along \(Y\), and \(\bar{s}\) a geometric point of \(S\) with image \(s\) in \(S\). If \(\mathcal{L}\) satisfies (1.5.10.1) and (1.5.10.2) at \(s\), then:

(I) If \(n\) sections \(m_i\) of \(\mathcal{L}\) satisfy (1.5.10.3), there exist an étale neighbourhood \(U\) of \(\bar{s}\) and a section \(k\) of \(\mathcal{L}|f^{-1}(U)\) such that the pairs \((m_i, k)\) satisfy (1.5.10.4).

(II) Let \(m_1\), \(m_2\), \(k_1\), \(k_2\) be four sections of \(\mathcal{L}\) such that the pairs \((m_i, k_j)\) satisfy (1.5.10.4). Then there exist an étale neighbourhood \(U\) of \(\bar{s}\) and a section \(k\) of \(\mathcal{L}|f^{-1}(U)\) such that the triples \((m_i, k_j, k)\) satisfy (1.5.10.5).
For \(k(s)\) infinite, one could be content to take \(U\) to be a Zariski neighbourhood.

1.5.12. Let now \(\mathcal{L}\) be an invertible sheaf on \(\overline{X}\) rigidified along \(Y\), and \(K\) a \(G\)-torsor on \(X\), where \(G\) is as in 1.5.7. We propose to define a \(G\)-torsor \(\langle\mathcal{L}, K]\) on \(S\), generalizing the one studied in 1.3, and additive in \(\mathcal{L}\).

Let \((m_1, m_2)\) be a pair of sections of \(\mathcal{L}\) satisfying (1.5.10.4). With the notation of 1.5.10.3 and 1.5.10.4, the trace, from \(\lambda m_1 + (1 - \lambda)m_2 = 0\) to \(\mathbb{E}^1_S\), of the torsor \(g'^*K\) is a torsor \(K_{1,2}\) on \(\mathbb{E}^1_S\). Its inverse image by the section \(\lambda = 0\) (resp. \(\lambda = 1\)) is the torsor \(K_2 = \operatorname{Tr}_{Z(m_2)/S}(K)\) (resp. \(K_1 = \operatorname{Tr}_{Z(m_1)/S}(K)\)). By 1.5.7, the torsor \(K_{1,2}\) is canonically the inverse image of a torsor under \(G\) on \(S\); whence a canonical isomorphism between \(K_1\) and \(K_2\).
If \(m_1\), \(m_2\) and \(k\) are three sections of \(\mathcal{L}\) such that the pairs \((m_i, k)\) satisfy (1.5.10.4), one again obtains by composition an isomorphism
\[(1.5.12.1)\qquad \Psi_k : K_1 = \operatorname{Tr}_{Z(m_1)/S}(K) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } K_2 = \operatorname{Tr}_{Z(m_2)/S}(K)\]
If \(E\) is a relative divisor on \(X\), finite over \(S\), the sections \(m_i' = m_i \otimes 1\) of \(\mathcal{L} \otimes \mathcal{O}(E)\) again satisfy (1.5.10.3); we have (for \(i = 0, 1\))
\[(1.5.12.2)\qquad K_i' = \operatorname{Tr}_{Z(m_i')/S}(K) \simeq K_i + \operatorname{Tr}_{E/S}(K)\]
and the isomorphism \(\Psi_{k \otimes 1} : K_1' \to K_2'\) is deduced from \(\Psi_k\):
\[(1.5.12.3)\qquad \Psi_{k \otimes 1} = \Psi_k + \operatorname{id}_{\operatorname{Tr}_{E/S}(K)} \;.\]

To verify that \(\Psi_k\) does not depend on \(k\), it suffices to do so in the étale neighbourhood of each point \(s\) of \(S\), and, by 1.5.12.3 and 1.5.9, one reduces to the case where the conditions (1.5.10.1) (1.5.10.2) are satisfied. With the notation of 1.5.11. (II), \(\Psi_{\lambda k_i + (1 - \lambda)k} - \Psi_{k_i}\) is a morphism from \(\mathbb{E}^1_S\) to \(G\), zero at \(\lambda = 1\), hence zero, and \(\Psi_{k_i} = \Psi_k\), hence \(\Psi_{k_1} = \Psi_{k_2}\).

Let \(m_1\) and \(m_2\) be two sections of \(\mathcal{L}\) satisfying 1.5.10.3 and \(K_i = \operatorname{Tr}_{Z(m_i)/S}(K)\). To define an isomorphism \(\Psi_{m_2, m_1} : K_1 \to K_2\), it suffices to do so in the étale neighbourhood of each point \(s\) of \(S\), in a manner compatible with base change. If \(E\) is a relative divisor on \(X\), finite over \(S\), such that \(\mathcal{L} \otimes \mathcal{O}(E)\) satisfies (1.5.10.1) (1.5.10.2) (see 1.5.9), and if the pairs \((m_i \otimes 1, k)\) satisfy (1.5.10.4), one sets (cf. 1.5.12.3)
\[\Psi_{m_2, m_1} + \operatorname{Tr}_{E/S}(K) = \Psi_k \;.\]

This defines \(\Psi_{m_2, m_1}\) and one verifies by (1.5.11. (I)) that \(\Psi_{m_3, m_2}\, \Psi_{m_2, m_1} = \Psi_{m_3, m_1}\). These constructions are compatible with base change. If there exists a section \(m\) of \(\mathcal{L}\) satisfying (1.5.10.3), one will set
\[\langle\mathcal{L}, K] = \operatorname{Tr}_{Z(m)/S}(K)\]
and, by what precedes, this torsor does not depend, up to canonical isomorphism, on the choice of \(m\).

Let us note, in the general case, that to define \(\langle\mathcal{L}, K]\) it suffices to define it in the étale neighbourhood of each point \(s\) of \(S\), in a manner compatible with base change. If, as above, \(\mathcal{L} \otimes \mathcal{O}(E)\) satisfies (1.5.10.1) (1.5.10.2), then \(\mathcal{L} \otimes \mathcal{O}(E)\) admits sections satisfying (1.5.10.3), and one sets
\[\langle\mathcal{L}, K] = \langle\mathcal{L} \otimes \mathcal{O}(E), K] - \operatorname{Tr}_{E/S}(K) \;.\]

1.5.13. Under the hypotheses 1.5.8, if \(x\) and \(y\) are two sections of \(f_*\mathbb{G}_m(\underline{m})\), then \(\lambda x + (1 - \lambda)y\) is again a section for \(\lambda\) in an open set with non-empty fibres of the affine line over \(S\).
One can translate this by saying that
(1.5.13.1) "\(f_*\mathbb{G}_m(\underline{m})\) is arcwise connected".

Every morphism from an open set with non-empty fibres of the affine line to \(G\) is constant. There therefore exists no non-trivial homomorphism from \(f_*\mathbb{G}_m(\underline{m})\) to \(G\), and the automorphisms of \(\mathcal{L}\) act trivially on \(\langle\mathcal{L}, K]\). The torsor \(\langle\mathcal{L}, K]\) therefore depends only on \(K\) and on the section of \(R^1f_*\mathbb{G}_m(\underline{m})\) defined by \(\mathcal{L}\). By globalization, this allows one to define a symbol \(\langle\lambda, K]\) for \(\lambda\) a section of \(R^1f_*\mathbb{G}_m(\underline{m})\). The torsor \(\langle\lambda, K]\) is additive in \(\lambda\), and therefore corresponds to an extension \(e(K)\) of \(R^1f_*\mathbb{G}_m(\underline{m})\) by \(G\) (see 1.4.23 or SGA 7 VII 1.1.6 and 1.2).
The formation of \(e(K)\) is compatible with every base change and with the addition of torsors, whence an additive functor
\[e : f_*\operatorname{ch}(G[1]) \to \operatorname{EXT}(R^1f_*\mathbb{G}_m(\underline{m}), G) \;.\]
Let \(j\) be the canonical map from \(X\) to \(R^1f_*\mathbb{G}_m(\underline{m})\), \(j : t \mapsto (\text{class of } \mathcal{O}(t))\). The inverse image by \(j\) is an additive functor
\[j^* : \operatorname{EXT}(R^1f_*\mathbb{G}_m(\underline{m}), G) \to f_*\operatorname{ch}(G[1])\]
and one trivially has \(j^*e \sim \operatorname{Id}\). One verifies as in 1.3.10 and 1.5.2 that, in the fppf topology
