Proposition 1.5.14

Under the hypotheses 1.5.8, the functors \(e\) and \(j\) of 1.5.13 are inverse equivalences of one another. By 1.4.19, 1.4.23 one deduces an isomorphism

\[\operatorname{Ext}^1(R^1f_*\mathbb{G}_m(\underline{m}), G) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } H^1(X, G) \;.\]
1.5.15. Let \(f_i : X_i \to S\) (\(i = 1, 2\)) be two curves compactified as in 1.5.8.

Let \(\bar{u} : \overline{X}_1 \to \overline{X}_2\) be a morphism such that \(Y_1\) is a subscheme of the inverse image of \(Y_2\) and which induces a finite and flat morphism from \(X_1\) to \(X_2\). We then have, for \(\mathcal{L}\) an invertible sheaf on \(X_2\) and \(K\) a torsor on \(X_1\),
\[\langle\mathcal{L}, \operatorname{tr}_{X_1/X_2}(K)] \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \langle\bar{u}^*\mathcal{L}, K] \;,\]
and from this we deduce the commutativity of the diagram

\[(1.5.15.1)\qquad \xymatrix@C=3em{ \operatorname{Ext}^1(R^1f_{1*}\mathbb{G}_m(\underline{m}), G) \ar[r]^-{\sim} \ar[d]_{\operatorname{Ext}^1(u^*, \operatorname{Id})} & H^1(X_1, G) \ar[d]^{\operatorname{tr}_{X_1/X_2}} \\ \operatorname{Ext}^1(R^1f_{2*}\mathbb{G}_m(\underline{m}), G) \ar[r]_-{\sim} & H^1(X_2, G) }\]

If \(\bar{u} : \overline{X}_1 \to \overline{X}_2\) is finite and flat, and satisfies \(Y_1 \supset \bar{u}^{-1}Y_2\) (as schemes), we have, for \(\mathcal{L}\) an invertible sheaf on \(X_1\) and \(K\) a torsor on \(X_2\),
\[\langle\mathcal{L}, u^*K] \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \langle N_{\overline{X}_1/\overline{X}_2}\mathcal{L}, K]\]
and from this we deduce the commutativity of the diagram

\[(1.5.15.2)\qquad \xymatrix@C=3em{ \operatorname{Ext}^1(R^1f_{2*}\mathbb{G}_m(\underline{m}), G) \ar[r]^-{\sim} \ar[d]_{\operatorname{Ext}^1(N_{X_1/X_2}, \operatorname{Id})} & H^1(X_2, G) \ar[d]^{u^*} \\ \operatorname{Ext}^1(R^1f_{1*}\mathbb{G}_m(\underline{m}), G) \ar[r]_-{\sim} & H^1(X_1, G) }\]
One could of course make this result more precise in terms of Picard stacks.
1.6. An effacement theorem.
The present n°, from 1.6.6 (2nd proof) to the end, can be read independently of n° 2 to 5.

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 1.6.1

Let \(X\) be a scheme and \(Y\) a closed subscheme of \(X\) with complement \(U\), defined by an ideal \(\underline{m}\).

\[U \xrightarrow{\ j\ } X \xleftarrow{\ i\ } Y\]

Let \(\mathbb{G}_m(\underline{m})\) be the fpqc sheaf whose sections over an \(X\)-scheme \(X_1\) are the sections of \(\mathcal{O}_{X_1}^\times\) equal to 1 on the inverse image of \(Y\). For \(n \geqslant 1\) invertible on \(X\), the sequence

\[0 \to j_!\mu_n \to \mathbb{G}_m(\underline{m}) \xrightarrow{\ n\ } \mathbb{G}_m(\underline{m}) \to 0\]

is an exact sequence of sheaves on the big étale site (XVII 0.10) of \(X\).
Let \(i\) be the morphism of big étale sites \(i : Y \to X\) induced by \(i\):
The functor \(i_*\) is exact. In the diagram

\[(1.6.1.1)\qquad \xymatrix@C=1.8em@R=1.8em{ & 0 \ar[d] & 0 \ar[d] & 0 \ar[d] & \\ 0 \ar[r] & j_!\mu_n \ar[r] \ar[d] & \mathbb{G}_m(\underline{m}) \ar[r]^-{n} \ar[d] & \mathbb{G}_m(\underline{m}) \ar[r] \ar[d] & 0 \\ 0 \ar[r] & \mu_n \ar[r] \ar[d] & \mathbb{G}_m \ar[r]^-{n} \ar[d] & \mathbb{G}_m \ar[r] \ar[d] & 0 \\ 0 \ar[r] & i_*\mu_n \ar[r] \ar[d] & i_*\mathbb{G}_m \ar[r]_-{n} \ar[d] & i_*\mathbb{G}_m \ar[r] \ar[d] & 0 \\ & 0 & 0 & 0 & }\]
the columns are exact, as are the last two rows (IX 3.2). The first row is therefore exact.
1.6.2. Let \(k\) be a field and

an exact sequence of abelian sheaves on the big fppf site of \(\operatorname{Spec}(k)\). We recall that if \(G_1'\) and \(G_2'\) are representable of finite type, and \(G_2''\) and \(G_1''\) representable locally of finite type, then \(G\) is representable and locally of finite type.
If \(P\) is a connected commutative algebraic group of finite type over \(k\), and \(n\) an integer invertible in \(k\), the sequence
\[(1.6.2.1)\qquad 0 \to {}_n P \to P \xrightarrow{\ n\ } P \to 0\]
is exact. If \(G\) is a finite étale commutative group over \(k\), annihilated by \(n\), the first group and the last arrow of the exact sequence
\[\operatorname{Hom}(P, G) \to \operatorname{Hom}({}_n P, G) \xrightarrow{\ j\ } \operatorname{Ext}^1(P, G) \xrightarrow{\ n\ } \operatorname{Ext}^1(P, G)\]
are zero, whence an isomorphism
\[(1.6.2.2)\qquad j : \operatorname{Hom}({}_n P, G) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \operatorname{Ext}^1(P, G) \;.\]
1.6.3. Under the hypotheses of 1.6.1, suppose \(X\) proper over the spectrum of a field \(k\)
The exact sequence
\[0 \to \mathbb{G}_m(\underline{m}) \to \mathbb{G}_m \to i_*\mathbb{G}_m \to 0\]
defines an exact cohomology sequence of fppf sheaves on \(\operatorname{Spec}(k)\), which it is easy to interpret directly

\[(1.6.3.1)\qquad 0 \to p_*\mathbb{G}_m(\underline{m}) \to p_*\mathbb{G}_{mX} \to (pi)_*\mathbb{G}_{mY} \xrightarrow{\ j\ } R^1p_*\mathbb{G}_m(\underline{m}) \to \operatorname{Pic}_{X/k} \to \operatorname{Pic}_{Y/k} \;.\]

The sheaves \(p_*\mathbb{G}_{mX}\) and \(p_*\mathbb{G}_{mY}\) are representable by group schemes of finite type. The sheaves \(\operatorname{Pic}_{X/k}\) and \(\operatorname{Pic}_{Y/k}\) are representable by group schemes locally of finite type. By 1.6.2, the sheaves \(p_*\mathbb{G}_m(\underline{m})\) and \(R^1p_*\mathbb{G}_m(\underline{m})\) are representable. By (1.3.13.1), the first is representable by a connected (and finite-type) group scheme; the second is locally of finite type.

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 1.6.4

Under the preceding hypotheses, we denote by \(\operatorname{Pic}_{\underline{m}, X/k}\) the group scheme that represents \(R^1p_*\mathbb{G}_m(\underline{m})\). We denote by \(\operatorname{Pic}^0_{\underline{m}, X/k}\) its identity component and by \(\operatorname{Pic}^\tau_{\underline{m}, X/k}\) the inverse image in \(\operatorname{Pic}_{\underline{m}, X/k}\) of the torsion subgroup of \(\operatorname{Pic}_{\underline{m}, X/k}/\operatorname{Pic}^0_{\underline{m}, X/k}\).

The scheme \(\operatorname{Pic}_{\underline{m}, X/k}\) represents the fppf sheaf generated by the presheaf which to each \(k\)-scheme \(S\) associates the set of isomorphism classes of invertible modules on \(S \times_k X\), trivialized along \(S \times_k Y\) (1.5.8).
The Kummer exact sequence 1.6.1 yields, for \(k\) algebraically closed and \(n\) invertible in \(k\), an isomorphism
\[(1.6.4.1)\qquad H^1_c(U, \mu_n) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } {}_n\operatorname{Pic}^\tau_{\underline{m}, X/k}(k) \;.\]

1.6.5. Let \(X\) be a smooth curve over an algebraically closed field \(k\), \(\overline{X}\) the projective smooth curve containing \(X\) as a dense open subset, \(Y\) a subscheme of \(\overline{X}\) such that \(X = \overline{X} - Y\), \(\underline{m}\) the ideal defining \(Y\), \(n\) an integer invertible in \(k\) and \(G\) a finite abelian group killed by \(n\).

The group \(\operatorname{Pic}_{\underline{m}, \overline{X}/k}\) is non-canonically the product of the subgroup \(\operatorname{Pic}^0_{\underline{m}, \overline{X}/k}\) and a free abelian group. By 1.6.4.1, 1.6.2.2, and 1.5.14, we thus have a canonical composite isomorphism

\[\begin{aligned} \operatorname{Hom}(H^1_c(X, \mu_n), G) &\xleftarrow{\ \sim\ } \operatorname{Hom}({}_n\operatorname{Pic}^\tau_{\underline{m}, \overline{X}/k}(k), G) = \operatorname{Hom}({}_n\operatorname{Pic}^0_{\underline{m}, \overline{X}/k}, G) \\ &\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \operatorname{Ext}^1(\operatorname{Pic}^0_{\underline{m}, \overline{X}/k}, G) \xleftarrow{\ \sim\ } \operatorname{Ext}^1(\operatorname{Pic}_{\underline{m}, \overline{X}/k}, G) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } H^1(X, G) \end{aligned}\]
If \(u : X \to Y\) is a finite morphism between smooth curves over \(k\), we deduce from XVII 6.3. and (1.5.15.2) the commutativity of the diagram

\[(1.6.5.1)\qquad \xymatrix@C=3em{ \operatorname{Hom}(H^1_c(Y, \mu_n), G) \ar[r]^-{\sim} \ar[d]_{\operatorname{Hom}(\operatorname{Tr}_u, G)} & H^1(Y, G) \ar[d]^{u^*} \\ \operatorname{Hom}(H^1_c(X, \mu_n), G) \ar[r]_-{\sim} & H^1(X, G) }\]

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 1.6.6

Let \(X\) be a smooth curve over an algebraically closed field \(k\), \(n\) an integer invertible in \(k\) and \(u : X' \to X\) a tame étale covering. The morphism

\[\operatorname{Tr}_u : H^1_c(X', \mathbb{Z}/n) \to H^1_c(X, \mathbb{Z}/n)\]

is then (non-canonically) isomorphic to the transpose of the morphism

\[u^* : H^1(X, \mathbb{Z}/n) \to H^1(X', \mathbb{Z}/n) \;.\]
1st proof. Since \(\mu_n\) is isomorphic to \(\mathbb{Z}/n\), 1.6.6 is a special case of 1.6.5.1 for \(G = \mathbb{Z}/n\) .

2nd proof. If \(k\) is the field \(\mathbb{C}\) of complex numbers, then, by the comparison theorems, the morphisms \(\operatorname{Tr}_u\) and \(u^*\) are identified with the analogous morphisms, defined by the continuous map between topological spaces \(u : X'(\mathbb{C}) \to X(\mathbb{C})\):
\[\operatorname{Tr}_u : H^1_c(X'(\mathbb{C}), \mathbb{Z}/n) \to H^1_c(X(\mathbb{C}), \mathbb{Z}/n) \quad\text{and}\]
\[u^* : H^1(X(\mathbb{C}), \mathbb{Z}/n) \to H^1(X'(\mathbb{C}), \mathbb{Z}/n) \;.\]
These two homomorphisms are transposes of one another by Poincaré duality.

By the Lefschetz principle, assertion 1.6.6 is still true for \(k\) of characteristic 0 (the cohomology groups under consideration are indeed invariant under change of algebraically closed base field).

If \(k\) is of characteristic \(p > 0\), let \(W(k)\) be the ring of Witt vectors over \(k\). Let \(\overline{X}\) be the projective smooth curve that completes \(X\). By (SGA 1 III 7.4), the curve \(\overline{X}\) lifts to a projective smooth curve \(\overline{X}_1\) over \(W(k)\). Since \(\overline{X}\) is smooth, each point \(s_i \in S = \overline{X} - X\) lifts to a section \(s_i'\) of \(\overline{X}\) over \(W(k)\); we set \(S_1 = \bigcup_i s_i'(\operatorname{Spec}(W(k)))\) and \(X_1 = \overline{X}_1 - S_1\).

Let us recall (SGA 1 XII) that the covering \(X'\) of \(X\) lifts to an étale covering \(X_1'\) of \(X_1\), and that \(X_1'\) is obtained from a projective smooth curve \(\overline{X}_1'\) over \(W(k)\) by removing the union \(S_1'\) of a finite number of disjoint sections.
\[\xymatrix@R=2.4em@C=1.4em{ X_1 & & X \ar[ll] \\ X_1' \ar[u]^{u_1} \ar[d]_{f_1'} & & X' \ar[u]_{u} \ar[ll] \ar[d]^{f_1} \\ \operatorname{Spec}(W(k)) & & \operatorname{Spec}(k) \ar[ll] }\]

The étale sheaves \(R^1f'_{1*}(\mathbb{Z}/n)\), \(R^1f'_{1!}(\mathbb{Z}/n)\), \(R^1f_{1!}(\mathbb{Z}/n)\) and \(R^1f'_{1!}(\mathbb{Z}/n)\) are locally constant, of formation compatible with base change, as shown by the exact sequences relating the cohomologies of \(\overline{X}_1\), \(X_1\) and \(S_1\), or \(\overline{X}_1'\), \(X_1'\) and \(S_1'\).
The special or generic geometric fibres of the morphisms
\[\operatorname{Tr}_{u_1} : R^1f'_{1!} \mathbb{Z}/n \to R^1f_{1!} \mathbb{Z}/n\]
or
are therefore isomorphic, and this reduces us to the already-treated case where \(k\) is of characteristic zero.

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 1.6.7

Let \(X\) be a connected smooth curve over an algebraically closed field \(k\) of characteristic exponent \(p\), and \(n\) an integer prime to \(p\). There exists a principal covering (\(=\) finite étale Galois (surjective)) \(u : X' \to X\), of degree dividing a power of \(n\), such that the trace morphism

\[\operatorname{Tr}_u : H^1_c(X', \mathbb{Z}/n) \to H^1_c(X, \mathbb{Z}/n)\]

is zero.

Let us recall that the group \(H^1(X, \mathbb{Z}/n)\) is finite (IX 4.6 or XVI 5.2). Let \(u : X' \to X\) be the largest connected abelian principal covering of \(X\) with Galois group killed by \(n\) (its Galois group is denoted \(H_1(X, \mathbb{Z}/n)\)). By construction, the homomorphism
\[u^* : H^1(X, \mathbb{Z}/n) \to H^1(X', \mathbb{Z}/n)\]
is zero. By 1.6.6, the homomorphism
\[\operatorname{Tr}_u : H^1_c(X', \mathbb{Z}/n) \to H^1_c(X, \mathbb{Z}/n)\]
is therefore zero.
Let us recall the following lemma (EGA IV 15.6.5):

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 1.6.8

Let \(f : X \to S\) be a smooth morphism and \(x\) a section of \(f\). Then there exists a Zariski open subset \(U\) of \(X\), containing \(x\), and such that the geometric fibres of \(f|U\) are connected.

blocks.title: Fundamental lemma
blocks.html:
Fundamental lemma 1.6.9

Let \(f : X \to S\) be a compactifiable (XVII 3.2.) smooth curve (1.1.2), \(x\) a geometric point of \(X\), \(s\) its image in \(S\) and \(n \geqslant 1\) an integer invertible on \(S\). There exist an étale neighbourhood \(V\) of \(s\) in \(S\) and an étale neighbourhood \(U\) of \(x\) in \(f^{-1}(V) = V \times_S X\)

\[(1.6.9.1)\qquad \xymatrix@C=2em@R=2.4em{ x \ar[r] \ar[d] & U \ar[r]^-{u} \ar[d]_{f'} & f^{-1}(V) \ar[r] \ar[d]^{f_V} & X \ar[d]^{f} \\ s \ar[r] & V \ar@{=}[r] & V \ar[r] & S \;, }\]

such that \(R^0f'_! \mathbb{Z}/n = 0\), such that the arrow XVII 6.2

\[\operatorname{Tr}_u : R^1f'_! \mathbb{Z}/n \to R^1f_{V!} \mathbb{Z}/n\]

is zero, and such that the trace morphism

\[\operatorname{Tr}_{f'} : R^2f'_! \mathbb{Z}/n(1) \to \mathbb{Z}/n\]

is an isomorphism.

For \(R^0f'_!\mathbb{Z}/n = 0\), it suffices that \(f'\) be quasi-affine; for \(\operatorname{Tr}_{f'}\) to be an isomorphism, it suffices that the geometric fibres of \(f'\) be connected (1.1.9); thanks to 1.6.8, these properties of \(f'\) are easy to obtain, locally on \(S\) for the étale topology. It remains to prove, for \(X\) with connected geometric fibres, the existence of a diagram (1.6.9.1) for which the arrow \(\operatorname{Tr}_u\) under consideration is zero: it will suffice to shrink \(U\) and \(V\) so that the two other required properties of \(f'\) are satisfied.

The problem is local on \(S\) in a neighbourhood of \(s\); by XVII 5.2.6 (base change), we reduce immediately to the case \(S\) noetherian. By passage to the limit, and thanks to XVII 5.3.6 (constructibility), we reduce to the case \(S\) strictly local noetherian, with closed point the image of \(s\).
Let \(t\) be a geometric point of \(S\). By 1.6.7, there exists a principal covering of degree prime to the characteristic exponent \(p\) of \(k(s)\), \(u : X_t^1 \to X_t\), such that the arrow
\[\operatorname{Tr}_u : H^1_c(X_t^1, \mathbb{Z}/n) \to H^1_c(X_t, \mathbb{Z}/n)\]

is zero. By the acyclicity theorem XV 2.1 (or XV 2.6), there exists an étale neighbourhood \(v : U \to X\) of \(x\) in \(X\) such that \(X_t^1\) splits over \(U_t\), so that \(v_t : U_t \to X_t\) factors through \(X_t^1\). We therefore still have
\[\operatorname{Tr}_{v_t} = 0 : H^1_c(U_t, \mathbb{Z}/n) \to H^1_c(X_t, \mathbb{Z}/n) \;.\]
For every geometric point \(t\) of \(S\), there therefore exists an étale neighbourhood of \(x\) in \(X\)
\[\xymatrix@R=2.2em@C=1.6em{ U \ar[rr]^-{v} \ar[dr]_{f'} & & X \ar[dl]^{f} \\ & S & }\]
such that the fibre at \(t\) of
\[(1.6.9.2)\qquad \operatorname{Tr}_v : R^1f'_! \mathbb{Z}/n \to R^1f_! \mathbb{Z}/n\]
is zero (XVII 5.2.6).

For \(U\) varying, the images of the arrows (1.6.9.2) form a decreasing filtered system of subsheaves of the constructible sheaf \(R^1f_! \mathbb{Z}/n\), which becomes zero at any geometric point of \(S\). By noetherian induction, one verifies that such a system is always stationary, with stationary value zero. There therefore exists \(U\) such that (1.6.9.2) is zero, and this completes the proof of 1.6.9.
2. The trace morphism
The present § is devoted to the proof of Theorems 2.9 and 2.12. The proof of 2.9 uses only n°1 of § 1.

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 2.1

Let \(f : X \to S\) be a compactifiable morphism (XVII 3.2.1) of relative dimension \(\leqslant d\) and \(j : U \hookrightarrow X\) an open subscheme of finite type of \(X\), whose complement is fibre by fibre of dimension \(< d\) (for example: \(U\) dense fibre by fibre in \(X\)). If \(F\) is a torsion sheaf on \(X\), the canonical arrow

\[R^{2d}(fj)_! j^*F \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } R^{2d}f_! F\]

is an isomorphism.
Let \(i\) be the inclusion of \(Y = X - U\) in \(X\). The exact sequence (XVII 5.1.16.2) provides us with an exact sequence
whose extreme terms are zero by virtue of (XVII 5.2.8.1).

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 2.2

Let \(f : X \to S\) be a compactifiable morphism of relative dimension \(\leqslant d\), and \(u_i : X_i \to X\) a family of étale, separated, finite-type morphisms; let \(u_{ij} : X_{ij} = X_i \times_X X_j \to X\). For every torsion sheaf \(F\) on \(X\), the sequence

\[\bigoplus_{i,j} R^{2d}(fu_{ij})_! u_{ij}^*F \rightrightarrows \bigoplus_i R^{2d}(fu_i)_! u_i^*F \to R^{2d}f_! F \to 0\]

of arrows (XVII 6.2.7.2) is exact.
This follows immediately from the right exactness of the functor \(R^{2d}f_!\) and from XVII 6.2.9.

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 2.3

Let \(f : X \to S\) be a flat morphism of finite presentation. The open subset of \(X\) on which \(f\) is Cohen-Macaulay (EGA IV 6.8.1 and 12.2.1(vii)) is relatively of finite presentation and dense fibre by fibre.

The question is local on \(S\), which we may assume noetherian, whence the 1st assertion. The second is verified fibre by fibre, hence for \(S\) the spectrum of a field. The local rings of \(X\) at the maximal points of \(X\) are artinian, hence Cohen-Macaulay, whence the assertion, since "Cohen-Macaulay" is an "open" property.

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 2.4

Let \(f : X \to S\) be a flat, finite-presentation, Cohen-Macaulay morphism, with \(S\) quasi-separated. Every point of \(X\) has an open (Zariski) neighbourhood \(U\) such that there exists a quasi-finite and flat \(S\)-morphism of finite presentation from \(U\) to the standard vector bundle \(\mathbb{E}^d_S\).
This is a special case of EGA IV 15.4.3.

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 2.5

Let \(\underline{u} = (u_1, \ldots, u_d)\) and \(\underline{v} = (v_1, \ldots, v_d)\) be two systems of parameters of a Cohen-Macaulay local ring \(A\), of dimension \(d\) and with maximal ideal \(\underline{m}\). There exists a sequence \(\underline{w}_0 \ldots \underline{w}_n\) of systems of parameters of \(A\), such that \(\underline{w}_0 = \underline{u}\), \(\underline{w}_n = \underline{v}\) and each \(\underline{w}_{i+1}\) is obtained from \(\underline{w}_i\) by modifying a single one of the parameters.

We argue by induction on \(d\), the assertion being vacuous for \(d < 2\); we therefore assume \(d \geqslant 2\). For an element \(x \in \underline{m}\) to be \(A/u_1\)-regular (resp. \(A/v_1\)-regular), it is necessary and sufficient that \(x\) belong to no element of \(\operatorname{Ass}(A/u_1)\) (resp. \(\operatorname{Ass}(A/v_1)\)); since no finite union of prime ideals \(\neq \underline{m}\) equals \(\underline{m}\), there exists \(x \in \underline{m}\) which is \(A/u_1\)- and \(A/v_1\)-regular, hence also systems of parameters \(\underline{a} = (u_1, x, \ldots)\) and \(\underline{b} = (v_1, x, \ldots)\). We conclude by applying the induction hypothesis to \(\underline{u} - \{u_1\}\) and \(\underline{a} - \{u_1\}\) in \(A/u_1\), to \(\underline{a} - \{x\}\) and \(\underline{b} - \{x\}\) in \(A/x\), and to \(\underline{b} - \{v_1\}\) and \(\underline{v} - \{v_1\}\) in \(A/v_1\).

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 2.6

Let \(X\) be a Cohen-Macaulay scheme of finite type over an algebraically closed field \(k\) and \(u, v : X \to \mathbb{E}^d_k\) two quasi-finite and flat morphisms from \(X\) to a standard vector bundle. Every closed point \(x\) of \(X\) has an open (Zariski) neighbourhood \(U\), such that there exists a sequence of morphisms \(w_0 \ldots w_n : U \to \mathbb{E}^d_k\), such that \(w_0 = u|U\), \(w_n = v|U\) and \(w_{i+1}\) differs from \(w_i\) only by a single coordinate.

Suppose first that \(u(x) = v(x) = 0\). The germs at \(x\) of quasi-finite flat morphisms from \(X\) to \(\mathbb{E}^d_k\) sending \(x\) to 0 are then identified with the systems of parameters of the local ring \(\mathcal{O}_{X,x}\), and 2.6 follows from 2.5. In the general case, we begin by joining \(u\) and \(u - u(x)\) (resp. \(v\) and \(v - v(x)\)) by the chain of morphisms
\[u - (u_1(x), \ldots, u_d(x), 0 \ldots 0) \quad (\text{resp. } v - (v_1(x), \ldots, v_d(x), 0 \ldots 0)) \;.\]

2.7. Let \(X \xrightarrow{\ g\ } Y \xrightarrow{\ f\ } S\) be a composable pair of \(S\)-compactifiable morphisms. Suppose that \(f\) is of relative dimension \(\leqslant d\) and \(g\) of relative dimension \(\leqslant e\). For every torsion sheaf \(F\) on \(X\), the composition spectral sequence
\[(2.7.1)\qquad R^pf_! R^qg_! F \Longrightarrow R^{p+q}(fg)_! F\]
then provides us (maximal cycle argument) with an isomorphism
2.8. Let
\[a^d : \mathbb{E}^d_S \to S\]

be the standard vector bundle over a coherent scheme (i.e. quasi-compact quasi-separated) \(S\). If \(F\) is a torsion sheaf on \(S\), prime to the residue characteristics of \(S\), we define as follows, by induction on \(d\), a trace morphism
\[(2.8.1)\qquad \operatorname{Tr}_{a^d} : R^{2d}a^d_! F(d) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } F \;.\]
For \(d = 0\), \(\operatorname{Tr}_{a^0}\) is the identity. For \(d = 1\), \(\operatorname{Tr}_{a^1}\) is the isomorphism (1.1.6) (cf. 1.1.9). Finally, we have a canonical isomorphism
\[\mathbb{E}^{d+1}_S \simeq \mathbb{E}^1_S \times_S \mathbb{E}^d_S = \mathbb{E}^1_{\mathbb{E}^d_S}\]

and we define \(\operatorname{Tr}_{a^{d+1}_S}\) as the composite of the isomorphisms \(\operatorname{Tr}_{a^d_S}\) and \(Ra^d_{S!}(\operatorname{Tr}_{a^1_{\mathbb{E}^d_S}})\). (cf. the diagram Var 3 of 2.9).

The source (and target) of 2.8.1 are of formation compatible with any base change. Any algebraic group over \(S\) acting on \(\mathbb{E}^d_S\) thus acts on these sheaves; a connected algebraic group necessarily acts trivially. The group of permutations of the coordinates, contained in the affine group, thus acts trivially on the source (and target) of 2.8.1.
(2.8.2) The isomorphism 2.8.1 is invariant under permutation of the coordinates.
This point could also be verified by interpreting (2.8.1) in terms of cup-products (XVII 5.4.2.2 and 5.4.3.5.).

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 2.9

Consider the triples \((f, d, F)\) formed by a compactifiable morphism (XVII 6.3.) \(f : X \to Y\), an integer \(d\) and a torsion sheaf \(F\) on \(Y\) prime to the residue characteristics of \(Y\), the morphism \(f\) satisfying the condition: \((*)_d\) There exists an open subset \(U\) of \(X\) such that the restriction of \(f\) to \(U\) is a flat morphism of finite presentation with fibres of dimension \(\leqslant d\), and such that the fibres \(X - U\) are of dimension \(< d\).

It is possible in one and only one way to associate to each triple \((f, d, F)\) as above a trace morphism

\[\operatorname{Tr}_f : R^{2d}f_! f^*F(d) \to F\]

in such a way that the following conditions are satisfied:

(Var 1) (Functoriality). The trace morphism is functorial in \(F\).

(Var 2) (Compatibility with base change). For every cartesian square

\[\xymatrix@C=3em{ X' \ar[r]^-{g'} \ar[d]_{f'} & X \ar[d]^{f} \\ Y' \ar[r]_-{g} & Y }\]

with \(Y'\) quasi-compact quasi-separated, the diagram

\[\xymatrix@C=1.4em{ R^{2d}f'_! f'^* g^*F(d) \ar@{=}[r] \ar[d]_{\operatorname{Tr}_{f'}} & R^{2d}f'_! g'^* f^*F(d) & g^* R^{2d}f_! f^*F(d) \ar[l]_-{\sim} \ar[d]^{g^*(\operatorname{Tr}_f)} \\ g^*F \ar@{=}[rr] & & g^*F }\]

in which the horizontal isomorphism is the base change arrow (XVII 5.5.2.1), is commutative.

(Var 3) (Compatibility with composition). For every composable pair of \(Z\)-compactifiable morphisms

\[X \xrightarrow{\ g\ } Y \xrightarrow{\ f\ } Z \;,\]

integers \(d\) and \(e\) such that \(f\) satisfies \((*)_d\) and \(g\) satisfies \((*)_e\), and torsion sheaf \(F\) on \(Z\), the composite morphism \(fg\) satisfies \((*)_{d+e}\) and the diagram

\[\xymatrix@C=2em{ R^{2d}f_! R^{2e}g_! g^*f^*F(d)(e) \ar[r]^-{R^{2d}f_!(\operatorname{Tr}_g)} \ar[d]_{\wr} & R^{2d}f_! f^*F(d) \ar[d]^{\operatorname{Tr}_f} \\ R^{2(d+e)}(fg)_! (fg)^*F(d+e) \ar[r]_-{\operatorname{Tr}_{fg}} & F }\]

in which the vertical isomorphism is the arrow (2.7.2), is commutative.

(Var 4) (Normalizations).

(I) If \(f\) is finite locally free of rank \(n\) and if \(d = 0\), the composite morphism

\[F \to f_*f^*F = f_!f^*F \xrightarrow{\ \operatorname{tr}_f\ } F\]

is multiplication by \(n\).

(II) If \(f\) is the standard affine line \(f : \mathbb{E}^1_Y \to Y\), and if \(d = 1\), the trace morphism

\[\operatorname{Tr}_f \quad R^2f_!f^*F(1) \to F\]

is the isomorphism (2.8.1)

a) For \(d = 0\), the condition \((*)_d\) is that \(f\) be quasi-finite flat of finite presentation. By virtue of (XVII 6.2.3), for \(d = 0\), the trace morphism must coincide with the morphism constructed in loc. cit.
When \(f\) is the projection of the standard affine space \(\mathbb{E}^d_S\) onto \(S\), it follows from (Var 4 (II)) and (Var 3) that \(\operatorname{Tr}_f\) must be the isomorphism (2.8.1) (2.8.1).

b) Let \(f : X \to Y\) be a compactifiable morphism satisfying the condition: \((**)_d\) There exists a quasi-finite and flat \(Y\)-morphism of finite presentation \(u\) from \(X\) to the standard vector bundle \(a^d : \mathbb{E}^d_Y \to Y\).
Let \(t(f, u)\) be the morphism "composite of the trace morphisms (2.8.1) and (SGA XVII 6.2.3 ) (cf. (Var 3))
\[t(f, u) = \operatorname{Tr}_{a^d} \circ R^{2d}a^d_!(\operatorname{Tr}_u) \;.\]

This morphism \(t(f, u)\) satisfies (Var 1) and (Var 2). By base change, to verify that \(t(f, u)\) depends only on \(f\) and \(d\), and not on \(u\), it suffices to verify it for \(Y\) the spectrum of an algebraically closed field \(k\). By 2.2, the question is local on \(X\), so that by 2.6, it suffices to show that \(t(f, u) = t(f, v)\) when \(u\) and \(v\) differ only by a single coordinate which, by 2.8.2, we may suppose to be the first. Setting \(E = \mathbb{E}^{d-1}_Y\), we thus have a commutative diagram
\[\xymatrix@R=2em@C=2.2em{ X \ar[r]^-{u} \ar[dr]|(0.4){v} \ar[ddr]|(0.55){x} \ar[dddr]_{f} & \mathbb{E}^1_E \ar[dd]|{a} \ar[r]^-{g} & \mathbb{E}^1_E \\ & & \\ & E \ar[d]|{w} & \\ & Y & }\]
By construction (2.8) we have
\[\operatorname{Tr}_{wa} = \operatorname{Tr}_w \circ R^{2(d-1)}w_!(\operatorname{Tr}_a) \;;\]
we deduce that \(t(f, u)\) is the "composite" of \(\operatorname{Tr}_w\) and \(t(x, u)\):

\[\begin{aligned} t(f, u) &= \operatorname{Tr}_{wa} \circ R^{2d}(wa)_! (\operatorname{Tr}_u) \\ &= \operatorname{Tr}_w \circ R^{2(d-1)}w_! (\operatorname{Tr}_a) \circ R^{2d}(wa)_! \operatorname{Tr}_u \\ &= \operatorname{Tr}_w \circ R^{2(d-1)}w_! (\operatorname{Tr}_a \circ R^2a_! (\operatorname{Tr}_u)) \;. \end{aligned}\]
Moreover (1.1.7), \(t(x, u)\) is none other than the morphism \(\operatorname{Tr}_x\) of 1.1.6; we thus have \(t(x, u) = t(x, v) = \operatorname{Tr}_x\) and \(t(f, u) = t(f, v)\).

We denote by \(\operatorname{Tr}_f\) the morphism \(t(f, u)\) constructed above. By XVII 6.2.3, this trace morphism satisfies (Var 1), (Var 2), (Var 3) for \(e = 0\), and (Var 4). When it is defined, it necessarily coincides with the sought trace morphism, if the latter exists.

c) Let \(f : X \to Y\) be a Cohen-Macaulay compactifiable morphism, flat of finite presentation, purely of relative dimension \(d\). Let \((U_i)_{i \in I}\) be a covering of \(X\) by quasi-compact open subsets, such that there exists a quasi-finite and flat \(Y\)-morphism from \(U_i\) to \(\mathbb{E}^d_Y\) (2.4). By 2.2 and b), there then exists one and only one morphism \(\operatorname{Tr}_f\) making the following diagram commute, where the notations of 2.2 are used:

\[\xymatrix@C=1.4em@R=3em{ \bigoplus_{i,j} R^{2d}(fu_{ij})_!(fu_{ij})^*F(d) \ar@<0.5ex>[r] \ar@<-0.5ex>[r] & \bigoplus_i R^{2d}(fu_i)_!(fu_i)^*F(d) \ar[r] \ar[dr]_{\bigoplus_i \operatorname{Tr}_{fu_i}} & R^{2d}f_!f^*F(d) \ar[d]^{\operatorname{Tr}_f} \\ & & F }\]

This trace morphism does not depend on the chosen open covering (compare the two to the sum covering); it satisfies the conditions (Var 1), (Var 2), (Var 3) for \(e = 0\), (Var 4), as follows immediately from b).

d) Let \(f : X \to Y\) be a compactifiable morphism satisfying \((*)_d\), and \(j : U \hookrightarrow X\) the open subset promised by \((*)_d\). By 2.3, up to replacing \(U\) by a smaller open subset, we may suppose that \(fj\) is Cohen-Macaulay, and purely of dimension \(d\).
By 2.1, the canonical morphism
\[R^{2d}(fj)_!(fj)^*F(d) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } R^{2d}f_!f^*F(d)\]
is an isomorphism, and we define \(\operatorname{Tr}_f\) as being the composite
\[\operatorname{Tr}_f : R^{2d}f_!f^*F(d) \xleftarrow{\ \sim\ } R^{2d}(fj)_!(fj)^*F(d) \xrightarrow{\ \operatorname{Tr}_{fj}\ } F \;.\]

It is immediate, thanks to (Var 3) for \(e = 0\) established in c), that \(\operatorname{Tr}_f\) does not depend on the choice of \(U\). The trace morphism satisfies (Var 1), (Var 2), (Var 3) for \(e = 0\), (Var 4), and is the only one that can satisfy the imposed conditions. It remains to prove that it satisfies (Var 3), and to do so we reduce, by the preceding arguments, to considering only pairs \((f, d)\), \((g, e)\) satisfying \((**)_d\) and \((**)_e\) .
The reader who wishes to polish the arguments that follow will first verify the

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 2.9.1

Let \((f, g, h)\) be three composable \(T\)-compactifiable morphisms, satisfying \((**)_k\), \((**)_\ell\) and \((**)_m\).

\[X \xrightarrow{\ h\ } Y \xrightarrow{\ g\ } Z \xrightarrow{\ f\ } T \;.\]

If the pairs \((f, g)\) and \((g, h)\) satisfy (Var 3), then for \((f, gh)\) to satisfy (Var 3), it is necessary and sufficient that \((fg, h)\) satisfy (Var 3).
The condition considered in the conclusion also means that \(\operatorname{Tr}_{fgh}\) is the "composite" of \(\operatorname{Tr}_f\), \(\operatorname{Tr}_g\) and \(\operatorname{Tr}_h\).
e) Consider a commutative diagram:
\[\xymatrix@R=2.2em@C=2.4em{ X \ar[r]^-{v} \ar[d]_{g} & \mathbb{E}^e_Y \ar[r]^-{u'} \ar[d]|{c} & \mathbb{E}^{d+e}_Z \ar[d]^{b} \\ Y \ar[r]^-{u} \ar[dr]_{f} & \mathbb{E}^d_Z \ar[d]^{a} & \\ & Z & }\]

The trace morphism relative to \(fg\) is the "composite" of the trace morphisms relative to \(ab\) and \(u'v\); it is also, by construction for \(ab\), and by XVII 6.2.3 for \(u'v\), the "composite" of the trace morphisms relative to \(a\), \(b\), \(u'\) and \(v\). On the other hand, the "composite" of the trace morphisms relative to \(f\) and \(g\) is the "composite" of those relative to \(a\), \(u\), \(e\) and \(v\). We thus have to verify that for every cartesian diagram
\[(2.9.2)\qquad \xymatrix@C=3em{ \mathbb{E}^e_S \ar[r]^-{u'} \ar[d]_{b'} & \mathbb{E}^e_T \ar[d]^{b} \\ S \ar[r]_-{u} & T }\]
with \(u\) quasi-finite and flat of finite presentation, the diagram of trace morphisms (2.8.1) and XVII 6.2. )

\[(2.9.3)\qquad \xymatrix@C=2.6em{ R^{2e}b_! u'_! u'^*b^*F(e) \ar[r]^-{R^{2e}b_!(\operatorname{Tr}_{u'})} \ar@{=}[d] & R^{2e}b_! b^*F(e) \ar[r]^-{\operatorname{Tr}_b} \ar@{=}[d] & F \ar@{=}[d] \\ u_! R^{2e}b'_! b'^* u^*F(e) \ar[r]_-{u_!(\operatorname{Tr}_{b'})} & u_! u^*F \ar[r]_-{\operatorname{Tr}_u} & F }\]
is commutative.

By base change, it suffices to verify it for \(T\) the spectrum of an algebraically closed field \(k\). If \(S\) is a sum of schemes \(S_i\), we reduce to verifying the commutativity of (2.9.3) only for the diagrams (2.9.2) with base \(u_i : S_i \to T\). This allows us to suppose that \(S\) is the spectrum of a local artinian \(k\)-algebra \(A\), of finite degree \(n = [A : k]\). If we then identify the sheaves on \(T\) (resp. on \(\mathbb{E}^e_T\)) with the sheaves on \(S\) (resp. on \(\mathbb{E}^e_S\)) via the functor \(u^*\) (resp. \(u'^*\)) (VIII 1.1), the morphism \(\operatorname{Tr}_b\) is identified with the morphism \(\operatorname{Tr}_{b'}\) (compatibility of (2.8.1) with base change), while \(\operatorname{Tr}_u\) and \(\operatorname{Tr}_{u'}\) are identified with multiplication by \(n\), whence the assertion. This completes the proof of 2.9.
We have seen in the course of the proof that we have:

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 2.10

The trace morphisms XVII 6.2.3, 1.1.6 and (2.8.1) are special cases of the trace morphism 2.9.

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 2.10.1

One can show without difficulty that the trace morphism of 2.9 is an isomorphism if and only if the geometric fibres of \(f\) have exactly one irreducible component of dimension \(d\), and the "multiplicity" of the latter is prime to \(n\). We shall not give here the direct proof of this fact, which will follow immediately from the "global duality theorem" of § 3.
2.11. Let \(f : X \to S\) and \(g : Y \to S\) be two \(S\)-compactifiable morphisms satisfying respectively \((*)_d\) and \((*)_e\).
\[\xymatrix@R=2.2em@C=1.4em{ & X \times_S Y \ar[dl]_{\operatorname{pr}_1} \ar[dd]|{f \times g} \ar[dr]^{\operatorname{pr}_2} & \\ X \ar[dr]_{f} & & Y \ar[dl]^{g} \\ & S & }\]
The Kunneth isomorphism (XVII 5.4.3)
\[Rf_!(\mathbb{Z}/n) \overset{L}{\otimes}_{\mathbb{Z}/n} Rg_!(\mathbb{Z}/n) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } R(f\times g)_!(\mathbb{Z}/n)\]
induces an isomorphism
\[(2.11.1)\qquad R^{2d}f_!\mathbb{Z}/n \otimes R^{2e}g_!\mathbb{Z}/n \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } R^{2(d+e)}(f\times g)_!(\mathbb{Z}/n)\]
It is clear that \(f\times g\) satisfies \((*)_{d+e}\); we have the compatibility:

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 2.12

The following diagram

\[(2.12.1)\qquad \xymatrix@C=3em{ R^{2d}f_!\mathbb{Z}/n(d) \otimes R^{2e}g_!\mathbb{Z}/n(e) \ar[r]^-{\sim} \ar[d]_{\operatorname{Tr}_f \otimes \operatorname{Tr}_g} & R^{2(d+e)}(f\times g)_!\mathbb{Z}/n(d+e) \ar[d]^{\operatorname{Tr}_{f\times g}} \\ \mathbb{Z}/n \ar@{=}[r] & \mathbb{Z}/n \;, }\]

in which the first horizontal arrow is a twisted form of (2.11.1), is commutative.
To verify it, it suffices to use (Var 3), and the asymmetric interpretation of the Kunneth arrow used in the proof of XVII 5.4.3. (XVII 5.4.3.5).
2.13. Let \(f : X \to S\) be an \(S\)-compactifiable morphism satisfying \((*)_d\), \(\mathcal{A}\) a sheaf of rings on \(S\) and \(n\) an integer invertible on \(S\) such that \(n\mathcal{A} = 0\).
For every \(K \in D(S, \mathcal{A})\), we have (XVII 5.2.6)
\[(2.13.1)\qquad K \overset{L}{\otimes}_{\mathbb{Z}/n} Rf_!\mathbb{Z}/n(d) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } Rf_!(f^*K(d)) \;.\]
The trace morphism
\[\operatorname{Tr}_f : R^{2d}f_!\mathbb{Z}/n(d) \to \mathbb{Z}/n\]
can also be interpreted as a morphism
\[\operatorname{Tr}_f : Rf_!\mathbb{Z}/n(d)[2d] \to \mathbb{Z}/n \;.\]
By tensoring with \(K\), this morphism defines, via (2.13.1), a trace morphism
\[(2.13.2)\qquad \operatorname{Tr}_f : Rf_!(f^*K(d)[2d]) \to K \;.\]
As we shall see in 3.2.5. the following theorem is essentially equivalent to the global duality theorem in étale cohomology.

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 2.14

Let \(f : X \to S\) be a smooth and compactifiable morphism purely of relative dimension \(d\), and \(n\) an integer \(\geqslant 1\) invertible on \(S\). For every geometric point \(x\) of \(X\) with image \(s\) in \(S\), there exists an étale neighbourhood \(V\) of \(s\) in \(S\) and an étale neighbourhood \(U\) of \(x\) in \(f^{-1}(V)\)

\[(2.14.1)\qquad \xymatrix@C=2em@R=2.4em{ U \ar[r]^-{j} \ar[d]_{f'_V} & f^{-1}(V) \ar[r] \ar[d]|{f_V} & X \ar[d]^{f} \\ V \ar@{=}[r] & V \ar[r] & S }\]

such that the morphism (XVII 6.2.7.2)

\[R^i f'_{V!} \mathbb{Z}/n \to R^i f_V \mathbb{Z}/n\]

is zero for \(i < 2d\), and such that the morphism

\[\operatorname{Tr}_{f'_V} : R^{2d}f'_{V!} \mathbb{Z}/n(d) \to \mathbb{Z}/n\]

is an isomorphism.
Let us first prove the

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 2.14.2

Let \(\mathcal{A}\) be an abelian category, \(k\) an integer \(\geqslant 0\), \((K_i)_{0 \leqslant i \leqslant 2k}\) objects of \(D^b(\mathcal{A})\) such that \(H^p(K_i) = 0\) for \(p \notin [0, k]\), \(f_i : K_i \to K_{i+1}\) (\(0 \leqslant i \leqslant 2k-1\)) morphisms and \(f\) their composite. If \(H^p(f_i) = 0\) for \(p < k\), then there exists in \(D^b(\mathcal{A})\) a morphism \(\varphi\) from the complex \(H^k(K_0)[-k]\), reduced to \(H^k(K_0)\) placed in degree \(k\), to \(K_{2k}\), which makes the diagram commute

\[\xymatrix@C=3em{ K_0 \ar[r]^-{f} \ar[d] & K_{2k} \\ \sigma_{\geqslant k}(K_0) \ar@{=}[r] & H^k(K_0)[-k] \ar[u]_{\varphi} }\]

The lemma is trivial for \(k = 0\). Let us prove it by induction on \(k\). The induction hypothesis applied to the complexes \(\sigma_{\geqslant 1}(K_i)[1]\) provides the existence of a morphism \(\varphi' : H^k(K_0)[-k] \to \sigma_{\geqslant 1} K_{2k-2}\) which makes the following diagram commute, where \(f' = f_{2k-3}\ldots f_0\):
\[\xymatrix@C=3em{ K_0 \ar[r]^-{f'} \ar[d] & \sigma_{\geqslant 1}K_{2k-2} \\ \sigma_{\geqslant k}(K_0) \ar@{=}[r] & H^k(K_0)[-k] \ar[u]_{\varphi'} }\]
For every complex \(L\), the distinguished triangle
\[\xymatrix@R=1.4em@C=0.8em{ & \sigma_{\geqslant 1}(L) \ar[dl] & \\ \sigma_{\leqslant 0}(L) \ar[rr] & & L \ar[ul] }\]
provides, for every complex \(M\), an exact sequence

\[\ldots \to \operatorname{Hom}(M, \sigma_{\leqslant 0}(L)) \to \operatorname{Hom}(M, L) \to \operatorname{Hom}(M, \sigma_{\geqslant 1}L) \xrightarrow{\ j\ } \operatorname{Ext}^1(M, \sigma_{\leqslant 0}L) \;.\]
In particular, we have a diagram

\[(2.14.3)\qquad \xymatrix@C=0.9em@R=3em{ \operatorname{Hom}(\sigma_{\geqslant k}K_0, \sigma_{\leqslant 0}K_{2k-2}) \ar[r] \ar[d] & \operatorname{Hom}(\sigma_{\geqslant k}K_0, K_{2k-2}) \ar[r] \ar[d] & \operatorname{Hom}(\sigma_{\geqslant k}K_0, \sigma_{\geqslant 1}K_{2k-2}) \ar[r] \ar[d] & \operatorname{Ext}^1(\sigma_{\geqslant k}K_0, \sigma_{\leqslant 0}K_{2k-2}) \ar[d] \\ \operatorname{Hom}(K_0, \sigma_{\leqslant 0}K_{2k-2}) \ar[r] & \operatorname{Hom}(K_0, K_{2k-2}) \ar[r] & \operatorname{Hom}(K_0, \sigma_{\geqslant 1}K_{2k-2}) \ar[r] & \operatorname{Ext}^1(K_0, \sigma_{\leqslant 0}K_{2k-2}) }\]

which maps into the analogous diagrams relative to \(K_{2k-1}\) and \(K_{2k}\). By hypothesis, the morphism \(f'\) at ① has an image at ② which lifts to ③. The obstruction ④ to the element ③ lifting to ⑤ has zero image in the diagram (2.14.3) relative to \(K_{2k-1}\). In this new diagram, ③ therefore lifts to ⑤, and the difference between ① and the image of ⑤ has zero image at ⑥, hence is the image of an element ⑦. This element ⑦ has zero image in the diagram (2.14.3) relative to \(K_{2k}\); in this new diagram, \(f\) is therefore the image of ⑤, and this solves the posed problem.
Let us prove that, for a given value of \(d\), the statement 2.14 implies the

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 2.14.4

Under the hypotheses of 2.14, there exists a diagram (2.14.1) such that the morphism XVII 6.2.4, in \(D^b(V, \mathbb{Z}/n)\) admits a factorization

\[\xymatrix@R=2.4em@C=1em{ Rf'_{V!}\mathbb{Z}/n(d) \ar[rr] \ar[dr]_{t} & & Rf_{V!}\mathbb{Z}/n(d) \\ & \mathbb{Z}/n[-2d] \ar[ur]_{\varphi} & }\]

where \(t\) is the arrow

\[t : Rf'_{V!}\mathbb{Z}/n(d) \to \sigma_{\geqslant 2d}Rf'_{V!}\mathbb{Z}/n(d) = H^{2d}(Rf'_{V!}\mathbb{Z}/n(d))[-2d] \xrightarrow{\ \operatorname{Tr}\ } \mathbb{Z}/n[-2d] \;.\]
Set \(f'_0 = f\) and let us construct, by induction, \(4d\) diagrams
satisfying 2.14. Set \(V = V'_{4d}\) and \(U_i = U'_i \times_{V'_i} V\). We obtain a diagram
\[\xymatrix@C=1.4em@R=2.4em{ U_{4d} \ar[r] \ar@/_/[drrr]_{f_{4d}} & \cdots \ar[r] & U_1 \ar[r] \ar[dr]|{f_1} & U_0 \ar[r] \ar[d]|{f_0} & X \ar[d]^{f} \\ & & & V \ar@{=}[r] & S \;, }\]
with \(U_0 = f^{-1}(V)\), such that the arrows
\[R^i f_{k+1!}\mathbb{Z}/n(d) \to R^i f_{k!}\mathbb{Z}/n(d)\]
are zero and such that the arrow
\[\operatorname{Tr} : R^{2d}f_{4d!}\mathbb{Z}/n(d) \to \mathbb{Z}/n\]
is an isomorphism. By 2.14.2, the corollary is verified for \(U = U_{4d}\).
We are now ready to prove 2.14 by induction on \(d\). The case \(d = 0\) is trivial and the case \(d = 1\) is none other than 1.6.9. We thus suppose \(d \geqslant 2\).

The problem being of local nature on \(X\) and \(S\), we may suppose that \(f\) admits a factorization \(f = gh\), with \(g\) and \(h\) smooth compactifiable, purely of dimension \(d'\) and \(d''\) and with \(d'\), \(d'' < d = d' + d''\). Let us apply 2.14.4 to \(g\) and to the morphisms deduced from \(h\) by base change, so as to obtain a diagram

\[\xymatrix@C=1.6em@R=2.2em{ U \ar[r]^-{u} \ar[dr]_{h'_0} & f^{-1}W \ar[r] \ar[d]|{h_0} & X \ar[d]^{h} \\ V \ar[r]^-{v} \ar[dr]_{g'_0} & g^{-1}W \ar[r] \ar[d]|{g_0} & Y \ar[d]^{g} \\ W \ar@{=}[r] & W \ar[r] & S \;, }\]
such that the morphisms (XVII 6.2.7.3) admit factorizations
\[Rh'_{0!}\mathbb{Z}/n(d'') \xrightarrow{\ \operatorname{Tr}\ } \mathbb{Z}/n[-2d''] \xrightarrow{\ \varphi\ } Rh_{0!}\mathbb{Z}/n(d'')\]
\[Rg'_{0!}\mathbb{Z}/n(d') \xrightarrow{\ \operatorname{Tr}\ } \mathbb{Z}/n[-2d'] \xrightarrow{\ \psi\ } Rg_{0!}\mathbb{Z}/n(d')\]
and such that \(\operatorname{Tr}_{h_0}\) and \(\operatorname{Tr}_{g_0}\) are isomorphisms.
Let \(h_1\) and \(h_1'\) be the morphisms deduced from \(h_0\) and \(h'\) by the base change \(V\), and let \(f' = g_0'h_1'\), \(f_W = g_0h_0\) .
The following diagram is commutative:

\[\xymatrix@C=1.6em{ Rf'_!\mathbb{Z}/n(d) \ar[rr] \ar@{=}[d] & & Rf_{W!}\mathbb{Z}/n(d) \ar@{=}[d] \\ Rg'_{0!} Rh'_{1!}\mathbb{Z}/n(d) \ar[r] & Rg_{0!} Rh'_{0!}\mathbb{Z}/n(d) \ar[r] & Rg_{0!} Rh_{0!}\mathbb{Z}/n(d) \;, }\]
as well as the diagram

\[\xymatrix@C=1.2em@R=1.8em{ Rg'_{0!} Rh'_{1!}\mathbb{Z}/n(d) \ar@{=}[d] \ar@/_5em/[dddd] & & \\ Rg'_{0!} v^* Rh'_{0!}\mathbb{Z}/n(d) \ar[rr]^-{Rg'_{0!}v^*(t)(d')} & & Rg'_{0!}\mathbb{Z}/n(d')[-2d''] \ar[d]^{t[-2d'']} \\ & & \mathbb{Z}/n[-2d] \ar[d]^{\psi[-2d'']} \\ & & Rg_{0!}\mathbb{Z}/n(d')[-2d''] \ar[dr]^{Rg_{0!}(\psi)(d')} & \\ Rg_{0!} Rh'_{0!}\mathbb{Z}/n(d) \ar[urr]^-{Rg_{0!}(t)(d')} \ar[rrr] & & & Rg_{0!} Rh_{0!}\mathbb{Z}/n(d) }\]
For the diagram
\[\xymatrix@C=1.6em@R=2.2em{ U_1 \ar[r] \ar[dr]_{f'} & f^{-1}W \ar[r] \ar[d]|{f_W} & X \ar[d]^{f} \\ & W \ar@{=}[r] & S \;, }\]

the canonical arrow from \(Rf'_!\mathbb{Z}/n(d)\) to \(Rf_{W!}\mathbb{Z}/n(d)\) thus factors through \(\mathbb{Z}/n[-2d]\); the arrows from \(R^i f'_!\mathbb{Z}/n(d)\) to \(R^i f_{W!}\mathbb{Z}/n(d)\) are thus zero for \(i < 2d\). Finally, \(\operatorname{Tr}_{f'}\) is an isomorphism as the composite of the isomorphisms \(\operatorname{Tr}_{g'_0}\) and \(Rg'_{0!} \operatorname{Tr}_{h'_1}\).
This completes the proof of 2.14.
3. The global duality theorem
3.1. The functor \(Rf^!\)
We shall need a variant of the canonical flasque resolutions.

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 3.1.1

Let \(X\) be a coherent scheme (i.e. quasi-compact quasi-separated). The functor \(\varinjlim\) induces an equivalence between the category of Ind-objects of the category of constructible sheaves of sets (resp. of groups, resp. of abelian groups) and the category of sheaves of sets (resp. sheaves of Ind-finite groups, resp. abelian torsion sheaves).
Follows from IX 2.7.2 and IX 2.7.3 .

3.1.2. Let \(\mathfrak{F}\) be an abelian torsion sheaf on a scheme \(X\), a filtered inductive limit of constructible sheaves \((\mathfrak{F}_i)_{i \in I}\), and \(X_0\) a conservative set of points of \(X\). We define the modified canonical flasque resolution of \(\mathfrak{F}\) by the formula
\[C^*_\ell(\mathfrak{F}) = \varinjlim_i C^*(\mathfrak{F}_i) \;,\]

where the \(C^*(\mathfrak{F}_i)\) are the canonical flasque resolutions of XVII 4.2.2 . By 3.1.1., for \(X\) coherent, this definition does not depend on the choice of the \(\mathfrak{F}_i\). It moreover commutes with localization; this fact allows us to define \(C^*_\ell(\mathfrak{F})\) by globalization for \(\mathfrak{F}\) a torsion sheaf on an arbitrary scheme \(X\), not necessarily coherent.

The complex \(C^*_\ell(\mathfrak{F})\) is a resolution of \(\mathfrak{F}\), functorial in \(\mathfrak{F}\), whose formation commutes with localization and with filtered inductive limits; the functors \(C^n_\ell\) are exact.

It follows that for a sheaf of rings \(\mathcal{A}\) on \(X\), the functors \(C^n_\ell\) transform \(\mathcal{A}\)-Modules into \(\mathcal{A}\)-Modules; they likewise transform torsion sheaves into torsion sheaves. It is well known that

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 3.1.3

Let \(\mathcal{A}\) be an abelian \(\mathcal{U}\)-category having a small generating set and such that the inductive limits indexed by a small filtered ordered set are representable in \(\mathcal{A}\), and are exact. For a functor \(F\) from \(\mathcal{A}^o\) to (Ens) to be representable, it is necessary and sufficient that it transform (arbitrary) small inductive limits into projective limits.
Cf. e.g. SGA 4 I 8.12.5, where one does not suppose \(\mathcal{A}\) abelian nor the filtered \(\varinjlim\) exact.

We shall apply this lemma to the category \(\operatorname{Mod}(X, \mathcal{A})\) of sheaves of modules on a ringed site \((X, \mathcal{A})\). In this special case, if the functor \(F\) is represented by the sheaf \(\underline{F}\), we have
\[(3.1.3.1)\qquad \underline{F}(U) = F(\mathcal{A}_U) \;.\]
This description of \(\underline{F}\) allows a direct verification of 3.1.3 in the case considered.
Recall that if \(f : X \to S\) is a compactifiable morphism (XVII 3.2.), then \(S\) is quasi-compact quasi-separated (sic), and the dimension of the fibres of \(f\) is bounded.

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 3.1.4

Let \(f : X \to S\) be a compactifiable morphism and \(\mathcal{A}\) a sheaf of torsion rings on \(S\). Then, the functor

\[(3.1.4.1)\qquad Rf_! : D(X, f^*\mathcal{A}) \to D(S, \mathcal{A})\]

admits a partial right adjoint

\[(3.1.4.2)\qquad Rf^! : D^+(S, \mathcal{A}) \to D^+(X, f^*\mathcal{A}) :\]

for \(K \in \operatorname{Ob} D(X, f^*\mathcal{A})\) and \(L \in \operatorname{Ob} D^+(S, \mathcal{A})\), we have a functorial isomorphism

\[(3.1.4.3)\qquad \operatorname{Hom}(Rf_!K, L) \simeq \operatorname{Hom}(K, Rf^!L) \;.\]

Equipped with the translation morphism making the diagram commute

\[(3.1.4.4)\qquad \xymatrix@C=1.4em{ \operatorname{Hom}(Rf_!(K[1]), L) \ar@{=}[d] & \operatorname{Hom}(K[1], Rf^!L) \ar[l]_-{\text{adj.}} \ar@{=}[r] & \operatorname{Hom}(K, (Rf^!L)[-1]) \ar@{=}[d] \\ \operatorname{Hom}(Rf_!K[1], L) \ar@{=}[r] & \operatorname{Hom}(Rf_!K, L[-1]) \ar[r]^-{\text{adj.}} & \operatorname{Hom}(K, Rf^!(L[-1])) }\]

this functor \(Rf^!\) is a triangulated functor.
N.B. The notation \(Rf^!\) is abusive in that \(Rf^!\) is in general not the derived functor of a functor \(f^!\).
Proof. Let \(d\) be an integer such that every fibre of \(f\) is of dimension \(< d\), and let us choose a compactification
\[\xymatrix@R=2em@C=1.6em{ X \ar[r]^-{j} \ar[dr]_{f} & \overline{X} \ar[dl]^{\overline{f}} \\ & S }\]
If \(K\) is a complex of \(f^*\mathcal{A}\)-Modules on \(X\), we have
\[Rf_! K \simeq R\overline{f}_*(j_! K) \;.\]
For every sheaf \(F\) on \(X\), the components \(F^i\) of the complex \(\tau_{\leqslant 2d}C^*_\ell j_! F\) satisfy
\[(3.1.4.5)\qquad R^k \overline{f}_* F^i = 0 \text{ for } k > 0 \;.\]
Indeed, for \(i \neq 2d\), \(F^i\) is an inductive limit of flasque sheaves, and for \(i = 2d\) and \(k > 0\), we have (XVII 5.2.8.1)

The simple complex associated with the double complex given by the truncated modified canonical flasque resolution of \(K\) is a resolution of \(K\). By virtue of (3.1.4.5), we thus have (notation of XVII 1.1.15)
\[(3.1.4.6)\qquad R\overline{f}_*(j_! K) \xleftarrow{\ \sim\ } \overline{f}_* \tau''_{\leqslant 2d} C^*_\ell j_! K \;.\]
We denote by \(f_!^i\) the functor from the sheaves of modules on \(X\) to the complexes of sheaves on \(S\) defined by
\[(3.1.4.7)\qquad f_!^\bullet(F) = \overline{f}_* \tau_{\leqslant 2d} C^*_\ell j_! F \;.\]

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 3.1.4.8

(i) The functors \(f_!^i\) are exact and commute with filtered inductive limits; we have \(f_!^i = 0\) for \(i \notin [0, 2d]\).

(ii) The functor \(f_!^\bullet\), being bounded with exact components, derives (XVII 1.2.10) trivially to \(Rf_!^\bullet\) or simply \(Rf_! : D(X, f^*\mathcal{A}) \to D(S, \mathcal{A})\). The arrow 3.1.4.6 is an isomorphism of functors

\[Rf_!^\bullet \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } Rf_! \;.\]

The functors \(C_\ell^i\) are exact and commute with filtered inductive limits (3.1.2). They transform every sheaf into an acyclic sheaf. The functors \(\overline{f}_*\) and \(j_!\) commute with filtered inductive limits. We deduce that
a) the functors \(\overline{f}_*C_\ell^i j_!\), hence also the functors \(f_!^i\), commute with filtered inductive limits;
b) for \(i < 2d\), the functors \(f_!^i = \overline{f}_*C_\ell^i j_!\) are exact. For \(i = 2d\), one verifies that \(f_!^i\) is exact by (3.1.4.5).
The remaining assertions of 3.1.4.8 are trivial.

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 3.1.4.9

The definition of \(f_!^i\) is independent of the sheaf of rings \(\mathcal{A}\), and retains a meaning for every abelian sheaf. The assertion 3.1.4.8 (i) remains valid in the categories of abelian torsion sheaves on \(X\) and \(S\).
By 3.1.4.8 and 3.1.3, the functor
\[f_!^i : \operatorname{Mod}(X, f^*\mathcal{A}) \to \operatorname{Mod}(S, \mathcal{A})\]
has a right adjoint \(f_i^!\); since \(f_!^i\) is exact, \(f_i^!\) transforms injectives into injectives.
With the sign convention (XVII 1.1.12), the functors \(f_i^!\) form a complex of left exact functors, zero in cohomological degree \(n \notin [-2d, 0]\):
\[(3.1.4.10)\qquad f_\bullet^! : \operatorname{Mod}(S, \mathcal{A}) \to C^b(X, f^*\mathcal{A}) \;.\]
The functor \(f_\bullet^!\) derives (XVII 1.2.10) to a triangulated functor
\[(3.1.4.11)\qquad Rf^! : D^+(S, \mathcal{A}) \to D^+(X, f^*\mathcal{A}) \;,\]

right adjoint to the functor \(Rf_!\) (\(= Rf_!^\bullet = Lf_!^\bullet\)) ("trivial duality formula"). More precisely, if \(I \in \operatorname{Ob}C^+(S, \mathcal{A})\) is a complex of injective sheaves of \(\mathcal{A}\)-modules, the \(\mathcal{A}\)-modules \(f_i^! I^n\) are injective, and we have an isomorphism of triple complexes (XVII 1.1.12)
\[(3.1.4.12)\qquad \operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(f_!^\bullet K, I) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(K, f_\bullet^! I) \;.\]
Passing to the \(H^0\) of the associated simple complex (computed by products), we obtain the adjunction statement. We leave to the reader the task of verifying the compatibility (3.1.4.4).

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 3.1.5

Suppose that the functor \(Rf^!\) is of finite cohomological amplitude. By XVII 1.2.10 the functor \(f_\bullet^!\) then admits a derived functor

\[(3.1.5.1)\qquad Rf^! : D(S, \mathcal{A}) \to D(X, \mathcal{A}) \;.\]

This derived functor is again right adjoint to the functor \(Rf_!\) (3.1.4.1). Indeed, we have

\[\operatorname{Hom}_{D(S)}(Rf_!K, L) \simeq \varinjlim_{L \to L'} \operatorname{Hom}_{K(S)}(f_!^\bullet K, L') \simeq \varinjlim_{\substack{K' \to K \\ L \to L'}} \operatorname{Hom}_{K(S)}(f_!^\bullet K', L')\]

\[\operatorname{Hom}_{D(X)}(K, Rf^!L) \simeq \varinjlim_{K' \to K} \operatorname{Hom}_{K(X)}(K', Rf^!L) \simeq \varinjlim_{\substack{K' \to K \\ L \to L'}} \operatorname{Hom}_{K(X)}(K', f_\bullet^! L')\]

and, by adjunction,

\[\operatorname{Hom}_{K(S)}(f_!^\bullet K', L') = H^0 \operatorname{Hom}(f_!^\bullet K', L') \simeq H^0 \operatorname{Hom}(K', f_\bullet^! L') = \operatorname{Hom}_{K(X)}(K', f_\bullet^! L') \;.\]

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 3.1.6

The triangulated functor

\[Rf^! : D^+(S, \mathcal{A}) \to D^+(X, f^*\mathcal{A})\]

(or, under the hypotheses of 3.1.5 ,

\[Rf^! : D(S, \mathcal{A}) \to D(X, f^*\mathcal{A}) \;),\]

right adjoint to the functor \(Rf_!\) (3.1.4.1) is called the extraordinary inverse image functor.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 3.1.7

Suppose the compactifiable morphism \(f : X \to S\) is of relative dimension \(\leqslant d\).

(i) If \(L \in \operatorname{Ob}D^+(S, \mathcal{A})\) satisfies \(H^i(L) = 0\) for \(i \leqslant k\), then \(H^i Rf^!L = 0\) for \(i \leqslant k - 2d\) .

(ii) For \(L \in \operatorname{Ob}D^b(S, \mathcal{A})\), we have

\[\dim \operatorname{inj} (Rf^!L) \leqslant \dim \operatorname{inj} (L) \;.\]

The functor \(Rf^!\) is the right derived functor of \(f_\bullet^! : \operatorname{Mod}(S, \mathcal{A}) \to C^b \operatorname{Mod}(X, f^*\mathcal{A})\). Assertion (i) follows from the fact that \((f_\bullet^!)^i = 0\) for \(i < -2d\), and assertion (ii) follows from the fact that \((f_\bullet^!)^i = 0\) for \(i > 0\), and that the functors \(f_i^!\) transform injective into injective.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 3.1.8

Let \(f : X \to S\) be a quasi-finite compactifiable morphism.

(i) The functor \(f_! : \operatorname{Mod}(X, f^*\mathcal{A}) \to \operatorname{Mod}(S, \mathcal{A})\) admits a right adjoint \(f^! : \operatorname{Mod}(S, \mathcal{A}) \to \operatorname{Mod}(X, f^*\mathcal{A})\), and \(Rf^!\) is the derived functor of the functor \(f^!\).

(ii) If \(f\) is a closed immersion, then \(f^!\) is the functor "sections with support in \(X\)".

(iii) If \(f\) is étale, then \(f^!\) is identified with the functor \(f^*\), with

\[\operatorname{Tr}_f : f_! f^* F \to F\]

as adjunction morphism.

Assertion (i) follows immediately from the special case \(d = 0\) of the proof of 3.1.4: we have \(f_!^\bullet = f_!\) and \(f_\bullet^! = f^!\) . Equivalently, the existence of an adjoint functor \(f^!\) follows from 3.1.3 and from the fact that \(f_!\) is exact and commutes with filtered inductive limits; the adjunction \((f_!, Rf^!)\) is a "trivial duality formula".
Assertion (ii) is clear, and (iii) is XVII 6.2.
3.1.9. Let \(f : X \to S\) be a compactifiable morphism, \(\mathcal{A}\) a sheaf of torsion rings on \(S\), and let us ring \(X\) by the inverse image of \(\mathcal{A}\).
Let \(K \in \operatorname{Ob} D^-(X, f^*\mathcal{A})\), \(L \in \operatorname{Ob} D^+(X, f^*\mathcal{A})\) and let us represent \(L\) by a bounded-below complex of injective sheaves, so that
\[R\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}(K, L) \simeq \underline{\operatorname{Hom}}(K, L) \;.\]
The complex \(\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}(K, L)\) has flasque components, and thus
\[(3.1.9.1)\qquad Rf_*R\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}(K, L) \simeq f_*\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}(K, L) \;.\]
Let us choose a compactification of \(f\) and an integer \(d\) as in the proof of 3.1.4, whence a functor \(f_!^\bullet\) (3.1.4.7) .

\[(3.1.9.2)\qquad \xymatrix@C=1.4em@R=2em{ X_V \ar[r]^-{k_X} \ar[d]_{j_V} & X \ar[rr]^-{j} \ar[dd]|(0.35){f} & & \overline{X} \ar[dd]^{\overline{f}} \\ \widetilde{X}_V \ar[d]_{f_V} \ar@/^1.5em/[urrr]^{k_{\overline{X}}} & & & \\ V \ar[rrr]_-{k} & & & S \;. }\]
For every \(V \in \operatorname{Ob} S_{\text{ét}}\), we have an isomorphism
\[(3.1.9.3)\qquad k^*f_!^\bullet \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } f_{V!}^\bullet k_X^* \;,\]
so that
\[\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}^\bullet(f_!^\bullet K, f_\bullet^! L)(V) \simeq \operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(f_{V!}^\bullet(k_X^* K), f_{V!}^\bullet(k_X^* L)) \;.\]
The functoriality of \(f_{V!}^\bullet\) provides us with
\[\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}^\bullet(K, L)(X_V) = \operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(k_X^* K, k_X^* L) \to \operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(f_{V!}^\bullet(k_X^* K), f_{V!}^\bullet(k_X^* L)) \;,\]
whence an arrow, at the level of complexes,
\[(3.1.9.4)\qquad f_*\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}^\bullet(K, L) \to \underline{\operatorname{Hom}}^\bullet(f_!^\bullet K, f_!^\bullet L) \;.\]
By (3.1.9.1), this arrow derives to
\[(3.1.9.5)\qquad Rf_*R\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}(K, L) \to R\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}(Rf_!K, Rf_!L) \;.\]
Now let \(K \in \operatorname{Ob} D^-(X, \mathcal{A})\) and \(L \in \operatorname{Ob} D^+(S, \mathcal{A})\). The adjunction arrow from \(Rf_!Rf^!L\) to \(L\) and (3.1.9.4) provide a composite arrow
\[Rf_*R\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}(K, Rf^!L) \to R\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}(Rf_!K, Rf_!Rf^!L) \to R\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}(Rf_!K, L) \;,\]
a local form on \(S\) of the adjunction isomorphism:
\[(3.1.9.6)\qquad Rf_*R\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}(K, Rf^!L) \to R\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}(Rf_!K, L) \;.\]

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 3.1.10

The arrow 3.1.9.6 is an isomorphism.
Let \(V \in \operatorname{Ob} S_{\text{ét}}\) and let us resume the notations of (3.1.9.2). The isomorphism ("of transitivity")
whose existence is the root of the theory of the functor \(Rf_!\), transposes to a localization isomorphism (3.1.8.(iii))
represented at the level of complexes by a morphism
\[k_X^* f_\bullet^! \to f_{V\bullet}^! k^* \;.\]
To verify that 3.1.9.6 is an isomorphism, it suffices to verify that for every \(V \in \operatorname{Ob}S_{\text{ét}}\), (3.1.9.6) induces an isomorphism

\[(3.1.10.2)\ ;\quad \operatorname{Hom}(k_X^* K, k_X^* Rf^!L) \simeq H^0(V, Rf_*R\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}(K, Rf^!L)) \to H^0(V, R\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}(Rf_!K, L)) \simeq \underline{\operatorname{Hom}}(k^*Rf_!K, k^*L)\]
For \(V = X\), this is none other than 3.1.4.3. The general case follows from it via the following compatibility, which the writer has not verified:

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 3.1.10.3

The diagram

\[\xymatrix@C=2.4em{ \operatorname{Hom}(k_X^* K, k_V^* Rf^!L) \ar[r]^-{(3.1.10.2)} \ar@{=}[d]^{(3.1.10.1)} & \operatorname{Hom}(k^* Rf_!K, k^*L) \ar@{=}[d]^{\text{(localization)}} \\ \operatorname{Hom}(k_X^* K, Rf_V^! k_X^* L) & \operatorname{Hom}(Rf_{V!} k_X^* K, k^*L) \ar[l]_-{\sim}^-{\text{(3.1.4.3 on } V)} }\]

is commutative.
3.1.11. Consider a cartesian square
\[(3.1.11.1)\qquad \xymatrix@C=3em{ X' \ar[r]^-{g'} \ar[d]_{f'} & X \ar[d]^{f} \\ S' \ar[r]_-{g} & S \;, }\]

with \(f\) compactifiable, \(\mathcal{A}\) a sheaf of torsion rings on \(S\), \(\mathcal{B}\) a sheaf of torsion rings on \(S'\) and \(M\) a bounded-above complex of \((f'^*\mathcal{A}, \mathcal{B})\)-bimodules. We then have, at the level of complexes, a morphism of functors in \(K\) (\(K \in \operatorname{Ob}C(X, f^*\mathcal{A})\))
\[(3.1.11.2)\qquad M \otimes_\mathcal{B} g'^*f_!^\bullet K \to f'^{!}_{\bullet}(f'^*M \otimes_\mathcal{A} g'^*K) \;,\]
which transposes to a morphism of functors in \(L\) (\(L \in \operatorname{Ob}C(S', \mathcal{B})\))
\[(3.1.11.3)\qquad g'_! \underline{\operatorname{Hom}}_\mathcal{B}(f'^*M, f'^{!}_{\bullet}L) \to f^! g_* \underline{\operatorname{Hom}}_\mathcal{B}(M, L) \;.\]
This morphism derives to a morphism of functors in \(L\), from \(D^+(S', \mathcal{B})\) to \(D^+(X, f^*\mathcal{A})\):
\[(3.1.11.4)\qquad Rg'_* R\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}_\mathcal{B}(f'^*M, Rf'^!L) \to Rf^! Rg_* R\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}_\mathcal{B}(M, L) \;,\]
which makes the following diagram commute, where \(K \in \operatorname{Ob} D^-(X, f^*\mathcal{A})\) and \(L \in \operatorname{Ob} D^+(S', \mathcal{B})\):

\[\xymatrix@C=0.7em@R=2.4em{ \operatorname{Hom}(K, Rg'_* R\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}_\mathcal{B}(f'^*M, Rf'^!L)) \ar[r]^-{①} \ar[d] & \operatorname{Hom}(K, Rf^! Rg_* R\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}_\mathcal{B}(M, L)) \ar[r]^-{\text{adj}} & \operatorname{Hom}(Rf_!K, Rg_* R\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}_\mathcal{B}(M, L)) \ar[d] \\ \operatorname{Hom}(g'^*K, R\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}_\mathcal{B}(f'^*M, Rf'^!L)) \ar[d] & & \operatorname{Hom}(g^*Rf_!K, R\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}_\mathcal{B}(M, L)) \ar[d] \\ \operatorname{Hom}(f'^*M \overset{L}{\otimes}_\mathcal{A} g'^*K, Rf'^!L) & \operatorname{Hom}(Rf'_!(f'^*M \overset{L}{\otimes}_\mathcal{A} g'^*K), L) \ar[l]_-{\text{adj}} \ar[r]^-{②} & \operatorname{Hom}(M \overset{L}{\otimes}_\mathcal{B} g^*Rf_!K, L) \;. }\]
In this diagram, ② (deduced from the arrow XVII 5.2.2.1) is an isomorphism (XVII 5.2.6). The arrow ① is thus an isomorphism for every \(K\), and this implies that (3.1.11.4) is an isomorphism.
The base change theorem for a proper morphism thus transposes into the

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 3.1.12

The arrow 3.1.11.4 is an isomorphism.
We call this isomorphism the induction isomorphism.
Here are 3 special cases of it.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 3.1.12.1

Let \(f : X \to S\) be a compactifiable morphism, \(\mathcal{A}\) and \(\mathcal{B}\) two sheaves of torsion rings on \(S\), and \(\varphi : \mathcal{B} \to \mathcal{A}\) a homomorphism. We denote by \(\rho\) the restriction of scalars from \(\mathcal{B}\) to \(\mathcal{A}\). We then have, for \(K \in \operatorname{Ob} D^+(S, \mathcal{B})\)

\[\rho Rf^!K \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } Rf^!(\rho K) \;.\]
It suffices in 3.1.11.3 to take \(S = S'\), \(X = X'\), \(\mathcal{A} = \mathcal{A}\), \(\mathcal{B} = \mathcal{B}\), \(M = \mathcal{A}\).
We thus see that the sheaf of rings plays a dummy role in the construction of \(Rf^!\).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 3.1.12.2

Let \(f : X \to S\) be a compactifiable morphism, \(\mathcal{A}\) a sheaf of torsion rings on \(S\) and \(K \in \operatorname{Ob} D^-(S, \mathcal{A})\), \(L \in \operatorname{Ob} D^+(S, \mathcal{A})\). We have the induction formula

\[R\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}(f^*K, Rf^!L) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } Rf^! R\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}(K, L)\]

(take \(S = S'\), \(X = X'\)) .

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 3.1.12.3

For every square 3.1.11, and every \(L \in \operatorname{Ob} D^+(S', \mathcal{A})\), we have

\[Rg'_* Rf'^! L \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } Rf^! Rg_* L\]

(take \(\mathcal{B} = f^*\mathcal{A} = M\)) .
3.1.13. For a composite \(gh\) of \(S\)-compactifiable morphisms
\[X \xrightarrow{\ h\ } Y \xrightarrow{\ g\ } Z\]
the composition isomorphism
\[c_{g,h} : Rg_! Rh_! \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } R(gh)_!\]
transposes to a composition morphism
\[(3.1.13.1)\qquad c_{g,h}^! : Rh^! Rg^! \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } R(gh)^!\]

satisfying the usual cocycle condition for a triple composite. In other words, the categories \(D^+(X, f^*\mathcal{A})\) form the fibres of a fibred and cofibred category over the category whose objects are the \(S\)-schemes \(f : X \to S\), with arrows the \(S\)-compactifiable morphisms, the direct image (resp. inverse image) functors being the functors \(Rf_!\) (resp. \(Rf^!\)). For every commutative square of compactifiable morphisms,
\[\xymatrix@C=3em{ X' \ar[r]^-{g} \ar[d]_{f'} & X \ar[d]^{f} \\ S' \ar[r]_-{g'} & S \;, }\]
we thus have a co-base change morphism (XVII 2.1.3 )
3.1.14. Consider a cartesian square
\[\xymatrix@C=3em{ X' \ar[r]^-{g'} \ar[d]_{f'} & X \ar[d]^{f} \\ S' \ar[r]_-{g} & S }\]

with \(f\) compactifiable, and let \(\mathcal{A}\) be a sheaf of torsion rings on \(S\). We ring \(S'\), \(X\) and \(X'\) by the inverse images of \(\mathcal{A}\), still denoted \(\mathcal{A}\) by abuse of notation. The base change isomorphism
\[(3.1.14.1)\qquad g^*Rf_! \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } Rf'_! g'^*\]

allows us to consider the categories \(D(S, \mathcal{A})\), \(D(X, \mathcal{A})\), \(D(S', \mathcal{A})\) and \(D(X', \mathcal{A})\) as the fibres of a cofibred category over the category of the commutative diagram
\[\xymatrix{ X \ar[d] & X \ar[l] \ar[d] \\ X & X \ar[l] }\;,\]

the direct image functors being the functors \(Rf_!\), \(Rf'_!\), \(g^*\) and \(g'^*\) (sic). When one restricts to the categories \(D^+\), one even obtains a fibred and cofibred category over this diagram, the direct image functors being the functors \(Rf^!\), \(Rf'^!\), \(Rg_*\) and \(Rg'_*\) (sic). We deduce
a) a "transitivity isomorphism" (sic) for the "inverse image" functors
\[Rg_* Rf^! \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } Rf^! Rg_*\]
already obtained in 3.1.12.3 (with the same definition by transposition of (3.1.14.1)).
b) a "base change morphism" (XVII 2.1.3 )
which, by loc. cit., can be described in the two following ways:
a) by adjunction, giving a morphism (3.1.14.2) amounts to giving a morphism
The base change theorem provides such a morphism as a composite
\[Rf'_! g'^* Rf^! \xleftarrow{\ \sim\ } g^* Rf_! Rf^! \xrightarrow{\ g^* \times \text{adj.}\ } g^* \;.\]
b) by adjunction, giving a morphism (3.1.14.2) amounts to giving a morphism
The isomorphism (3.1.12.3) provides such a morphism as a composite
\[Rf^! \xrightarrow{\ Rf^! \times \text{adj.}\ } Rf^! Rg_* g^* \xleftarrow{\ \sim\ } Rg'_* Rf'^! g^* \;.\]

By their interpretations in terms of fibred and cofibred category, it is clear that the morphisms (3.1.12.3), (3.1.13.2) and (3.1.14.2) each satisfy two compatibilities of the type XII 4.4 for \(f\) or \(g\) a composite of two morphisms.
The results of general topology that follow will be used in the next section.
3.1.15. Let \(f : X \to S\) be a morphism of sites. We denote by \(\Gamma(f)\) the following site
a) The category \(\Gamma(f)\) is the category of triples \((U, V, \varphi)\) with
\[U \in \operatorname{Ob}(X), \quad V \in \operatorname{Ob} S, \quad \varphi \in \operatorname{Hom}_X(U, f^*V) \;.\]
b) A family of morphisms \((u_i, v_i) : (U_i, V_i, \varphi_i) \to (U, V, \varphi)\) is covering if, in \(X\), the morphisms \(u_i : U_i \to U\) cover \(U\).
We then have
(3.1.15.1) The functor from \(\Gamma(f)\) to \(X\) given by
\[(U, V, \varphi) \mapsto U\]
is an equivalence of sites \(\gamma : X \to \Gamma(f)\) .
(3.1.15.2) The functor \(f_\Gamma^*\) from \(S\) to \(\Gamma(f)\)
\[V \mapsto (f^*V, V, \operatorname{Id}_{f^*V})\]

is a morphism of sites, denoted \(f_\Gamma : \Gamma(f) \to S\), or simply \(f\) by abuse of notation. It satisfies \(f_\Gamma\gamma = f\) . The functor \(f_\Gamma^*\) admits a right adjoint \(f_{\Gamma*}\) :
\[f_{\Gamma*} : (U, V, \varphi) \mapsto V \;.\]
The functor \(f_\Gamma\) is thus a comorphism of sites from \(\Gamma(f)\) to \(S\), and defines the same morphism of topoi as the morphism of sites \(f_\Gamma\) .
\[(3.1.15.3)\qquad \xymatrix@R=2em@C=1em{ X \ar[rr]^-{\approx} \ar[dr]_{f^*} & & \Gamma(f) \ar[dl]|{f_\Gamma^*} \ar@/^2em/[dll]^{f_\Gamma} \\ & S & \;. }\]
From this we deduce the following rule for computing the inverse image of a sheaf
(3.1.15.4) Let \(\mathfrak{F}\) be a sheaf on \(S\), and \(f_\Gamma^*\mathfrak{F}\) the presheaf on \(\Gamma(f)\) given by
\[f_\Gamma^*\mathfrak{F}(U, V, \varphi) = \mathfrak{F}(V) \;,\]
and \(af_\Gamma^*\mathfrak{F}\) the sheaf it generates. Then
\[f^*\mathfrak{F}(U) \simeq af_\Gamma^*\mathfrak{F}(U, V, \varphi) \;.\]

3.1.16. Let \(f : X \to S\) be a morphism of sites, \(\mathcal{A}\) a sheaf of rings on \(S\), \(\mathcal{B}\) a sheaf of rings on \(X\), and \(d\) an integer. Let \(K\) be an object of the following type

(3.1.16.1) \(K\) associates to each object \(U\) of \(X\) a complex \(K(U)\) of \((\mathcal{A}, f_*(\mathcal{B}|U))\) -modules on \(S\), zero in degree \(> d\), and \(K(U)\) is a covariant functor of \(U\).

For every sheaf of \(\mathcal{A}\)-modules \(\underline{F}\) on \(S\), we denote by \(K^!\underline{F}\) the complex of sheaves on \(X\) generated by the complex of presheaves of \(\mathcal{B}\)-modules:
\[U \mapsto \operatorname{Hom}_\mathcal{A}(K(U), \underline{F}) \;.\]
We denote by \(RK^!\) the derived functor of \(K^!\)
\[RK^! : D^+(S, \mathcal{A}) \to D^+(X, \mathcal{B}) \;.\]
If \(U : K_1 \to K_2\) is a morphism of objects (3.1.11.1), then \(U\) induces morphisms of functors
\[{}^t u : K_2^! \to K_1^! \quad\text{and}\quad RK_2^! \to RK_1^! \;.\]
Under the preceding hypotheses, we have

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 3.1.17

(i) For every point \(x\) of \(X\) and every \(L \in \operatorname{Ob} D^+(S, \mathcal{A})\), we have, denoting by \(V(x)\) the category of neighbourhoods of \(x\)

\[(3.1.17.1)\qquad \underline{H}^n(RK^!L)_x \simeq \varinjlim_{U \in \operatorname{Ob}V(x)} \operatorname{Ext}^n(K(U), L) \;.\]

(ii) We thus have a spectral sequence

\[(3.1.17.2)\qquad E_2^{pq} = \varinjlim_{U \in \operatorname{Ob}V(x)} \operatorname{Ext}^p(\underline{H}^{-q}(K(W)), L) \Longrightarrow \underline{H}^n(RK^!L)_x \;.\]

(iii) If \(X^0\) is a conservative set of points of \(X\), and \(u : K_1 \to K_2\) a morphism of objects (3.1.11.1), then, in order for

\[{}^t u : RK_2^! \to RK_1^!\]

to be an isomorphism, it is necessary and sufficient that for every \(n\) and every \(x \in X^0\), the morphism of pro-objects of \(\operatorname{Mod}(S, \mathcal{A})\)

\[(3.1.17.3)\qquad u_x : \text{"}\varprojlim\text{"}_{U \in \operatorname{Ob}V(x)} \underline{H}^n K_1(U) \to \text{"}\varprojlim\text{"}_{U \in \operatorname{Ob}V(x)} \underline{H}^n K_2(U)\]

is an isomorphism.
To prove (i), we take for \(L\) a complex of injectives, so that (3.1.17.1) is trivial; it is clear that (i)\(\Longrightarrow\)(ii).

That condition (3.1.17.3) of (iii) is sufficient follows immediately from (3.1.17.2). We shall not need to make use of the fact that it is necessary. If \({}^t u\) is an isomorphism, then, by (3.1.16.1), for every injective sheaf \(I\) on \((S, \mathcal{A})\), we have
\[\operatorname{Hom}(\text{"}\varprojlim\text{"}_{V(x)} \underline{H}^n K_2(U), I) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \operatorname{Hom}(\text{"}\varprojlim\text{"}_{V(x)} \underline{H}^n K_1(U), I) \;,\]

and we conclude by noting that in every abelian category having enough injectives (here, \(\operatorname{Mod}(S, \mathcal{A})\)), the functors \(\operatorname{Hom}(\times, I)\) for \(I\) injective of \(\mathcal{A}\) form a conservative system of functors on \(\operatorname{Pro}(\mathcal{A})\).

blocks.html:
Example 3.1.18

Let \(f : X \to S\) be a compactifiable morphism of schemes, and \(\mathcal{A}\) a sheaf of torsion rings on \(S\). We ring \(X\) by \(f^*\mathcal{A}\). Let us choose an integer \(d\) bounding above the dimension of the fibres of \(f\), together with a compactification of \(f\), and set (3.1.4.7))

\[(3.1.18.1)\qquad K(U) = f_!^\bullet((f^*\mathcal{A})_U) \;.\]

By formula (3.1.3.1) for the adjoint of \(f_!^\bullet\), we have an isomorphism

\[(3.1.18.2)\qquad f_\bullet^! \simeq K^! : \operatorname{Mod}(S, \mathcal{A}) \to C^b \operatorname{Mod}(X, f^*\mathcal{A}) \;.\]

and thus

\[(3.1.18.3)\qquad Rf^! \simeq RK^! : D^+(S, \mathcal{A}) \to D^+(X, f^*\mathcal{A}) \;.\]

blocks.title: Example
blocks.html:
Example 3.1.19

Let \(f : X \to S\), \(\mathcal{A}\), \(\mathcal{B}\) and \(d\) be as in 3.1.16. Let \(K\) be an object of the following type

(3.1.19.1) For every \(W = (U, V, \varphi) \in \operatorname{Ob}\Gamma(f)\) (3.1.15), \(K(W)\) is a complex of \((\mathcal{A}_V, \varphi_*\mathcal{B}|U)\)-Modules on \(V\), functorial in \(W\): for every morphism \((u, v) : W_1 = (U_1, V_1, \varphi_1) \to W_2 = (U_2, V_2, \varphi_2)\) it is given by

\[K(u, v) : K(W_1) \to v^*K(W_2) \;, \quad\text{i.e.}\]

To every object \(K\) (3.1.19.1) is associated an object \(K'\) (3.1.16.1) relative to \(f_\Gamma : \Gamma(f) \to S\), given by

\[(3.1.19.2)\qquad K'(U, V, \varphi) = j_! K(U, V, \varphi)\]

where \(j\) is the "inclusion morphism" of \(V\) into \(S\). We set

\[K^! \underset{\text{defn}}{=} K'^! \quad\text{and}\quad RK^! \underset{\text{defn}}{=} RK'^! \;.\]

Example 3.1.20

With the notation of 3.1.19, take \(\mathcal{B} = f^*\mathcal{A}\) and set

\[(3.1.20.1)\qquad K(U, V, \varphi) = \mathcal{A}_V \quad (\text{in degree } 0)\]

By 3.1.15.4, we then have isomorphisms of functors

\[(3.1.20.2)\qquad K^! \simeq f^*\]

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 3.2.2

If the functor \(Rf^!\) is of finite cohomological dimension, then \(t\) is still defined as a morphism between functors from \(D(S, \mathcal{A})\) to \(D(X, f^*\mathcal{A})\), (definition in 3.1.5).
We have another method for constructing an arrow (3.2.1.2), by adjunction from (2.13.2)
\[\operatorname{Tr} : Rf_!(f^*L(d)[2d]) \to L \;.\]
These two arrows coincide:

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 3.2.3

For \(L \in \operatorname{Ob}D^+(S, \mathcal{A})\) (resp. \(D(S, \mathcal{A})\) if the functor \(Rf^!\) is of finite cohomological dimension), the diagram

\[\xymatrix@C=3em{ Rf_!(f^*L(d)[2d]) \ar[r]^-{Rf_!(t_f)} \ar[d]_{\operatorname{Tr}_f} & Rf_! Rf^!L \ar[d]^{\text{adjunction}} \\ L \ar@{=}[r] & L }\]

is commutative.

Let us first give a variant of the definition of \(t\), in terms of the functor \(f_\bullet^!\) (3.1.4.10). Let \(U \in \operatorname{Ob}X_{\text{ét}}\), \(V \in \operatorname{Ob}S_{\text{ét}}\) and \(\varphi \in \operatorname{Hom}_f(U, V)\). By definition,
\[f_\bullet^!(L)(U) = \operatorname{Hom}(f_!^\bullet\mathcal{A}_U, L) \;;\]
the trace morphism defines a morphism
\[\operatorname{Tr}_f : f_!^\bullet\mathcal{A}_U \to \mathcal{A}_V(-d)[-2d]\]
which transposes into
\[t_\varphi : f_\bullet^!(L)(U) \leftarrow L(d)[2d](V) \;.\]
The morphisms \(t_\varphi\) define a morphism
\[t_f : f^*L(d)[2d] \to f_\bullet^!L\]

which we leave to the reader to verify coincides, in the derived category, with (3.2.1.2). This description shows that the following diagrams are commutative at the level of complexes, for \(L\) a complex of Modules:

\[\xymatrix@C=2em{ \operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(\mathcal{A}_V, L) \ar[r] \ar[d]_{\operatorname{Tr}_f} & \operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(f^*\mathcal{A}_V(d)[2d], f^*L(d)[2d]) \ar[d]^{t_f} \\ \operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(f_!^\bullet\mathcal{A}_V(d)[2d], L) \ar[r]^-{\sim} & \operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(f^*\mathcal{A}_V(d)[2d], f_\bullet^!L) \;. }\]
By functoriality of the arrows of this diagram in \(\mathcal{A}_V\), we deduce that for every sheaf, or every complex of sheaves \(K\), the following diagram is commutative:

\[\xymatrix@C=2em{ \operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(K, L) \ar[r] \ar[d]_{\operatorname{Tr}_f} & \operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(f^*K(d)[2d], f^*L(d)[2d]) \ar[d] \\ \operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(f_!^\bullet K(d)[2d], L) & \operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(f^*K(d)[2d], f_\bullet^!L) \ar[l]_-{\sim} }\;.\]
Taking \(K = L\) and \(\operatorname{Id} : L \to L\), we recover 3.2.3 at the level of complexes.
I would be grateful if anyone who has understood this proof would explain it to me.

3.2.4. We deduce immediately from this lemma and from the definition (3.1.13) of the composition isomorphisms by adjunction that if \(f\) is the composite of two flat compactifiable morphisms of finite presentation, purely of relative dimension \(d_1\) and \(d_2\): \(f = gh\), and if \(d = d_1 + d_2\), then the diagram
\[\xymatrix@C=3em{ h^*(g^*L(d_2)[2d_2])(d_1)[2d_1] \ar[r]^-{\sim} \ar[d]_{t_h * t_g} & (gh)^*L(d)[2d] \ar[d]^{t_{gh}} \\ Rh^! Rg^! L \ar[r]^-{\sim} & R(gh)^!L }\]
is commutative.

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 3.2.5

(Poincaré duality). Let \(f : X \to S\) be a smooth compactifiable morphism (\(S\) is thus quasi-compact quasi-separated (sic)), \(d\) the locally constant function on \(X\) "relative dimension of \(f\) ", \(n \geqslant 1\) an integer invertible on \(S\), and \(\mathcal{A}\) a sheaf of rings on \(S\) satisfying \(n\mathcal{A} = 0\). Then the functor

\[Rf_! : D(X, f^*\mathcal{A}) \to D(S, \mathcal{A})\]

admits as right adjoint the functor from \(D(S, \mathcal{A})\) to \(D(X, f^*\mathcal{A})\):

\[K \mapsto f^*K(d)[2d]\]

with the morphism (2.13.2)

\[\operatorname{Tr}_f : Rf_! f^*K(d)[2d] \to K\]

as adjunction arrow:

\[\operatorname{Hom}(K, f^*L(d)[2d]) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \operatorname{Hom}(Rf_!K, L) \;.\]

Proof. We reduce to the case \(d\) constant. By the description 3.2.1 of the arrow \(t_f\) (3.2.1.2), Theorem 2.14, combined with criterion 3.1.17.(iii), implies that the arrow \(t_f\) is an isomorphism (for \(L \in D^+(S, \mathcal{A})\))
\[t_f : f^*L(d)[2d] \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } Rf^!L \;.\]
In particular, the functor \(Rf^!\) is of finite cohomological dimension, hence is defined on the entire derived category. The morphism \(t_f\) remains an isomorphism for \(L \in D(S, \mathcal{A})\).

By definition, \(Rf^!\) is the right adjoint of the functor \(Rf_!\); by 3.2.3, the adjunction arrow from \(Rf_! Rf^! K\) to \(K\) is identified, via \(t_f\), with \(\operatorname{Tr}_f\), and this completes the proof of 3.2.5.
Henceforth we shall identify, by means of \(t_f\), the functors \(f^*L(d)[2d]\) and \(Rf^!L\).

3.2.6. Let \(S\) be the spectrum of an algebraically closed field \(k\), \(X\) a compactifiable scheme, smooth over \(k\), purely of relative dimension \(d\), \(n\) an integer invertible in \(k\), and \(F\) a locally constant constructible sheaf of \(\mathbb{Z}/n\)-modules, i.e. a "system of coefficients" killed by \(n\). Denoting by \(\vee\) the \(\mathbb{Z}/n\)-dual, we have
\[R\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}(F, \mathbb{Z}/n) = F^\vee \quad (\text{in degree } 0) \;.\]
This formula follows from the fact that \(\mathbb{Z}/n\) is an injective \(\mathbb{Z}/n\)-module. The isomorphism 3.2.5.1, or rather the isomorphism deduced from it
\[R\Gamma\, R\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}(F, \mathbb{Z}/n(d)[2d]) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } R\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}(R\Gamma_c(F), \mathbb{Z}/n) \;,\]
thus reads here
\[(3.2.6.1)\qquad R\Gamma\, (F^\vee(d)[2d]) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } R\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}(R\Gamma_c(F), \mathbb{Z}/n) \;.\]
Passing to the cohomology groups, and using again that \(\mathbb{Z}/n\) is an injective \(\mathbb{Z}/n\)-module, this gives
\[(3.2.6.2)\qquad H^{2d-i}(X, F^\vee(d)) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } H^i_c(X, F)^\vee \;,\]
which is the usual form of Poincaré duality.
